Zambia’s Hichilema begins second term amid disputed vote and arrests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
16:47:47 UTC
01:47:47 KST

Zambia’s Hichilema begins second term amid disputed vote and arrests
Economic gains face growing scrutiny as political tensions deepen after the vote.
Lusaka, Zambia – President Hakainde Hichilema has begun a second and final term promising to make sure ordinary Zambians feel the benefits of an economic recovery he says has put the country on a more stable footing.
But his inauguration on Tuesday came against a far less settled political backdrop: election observers have raised concerns about the conduct and counting of the August 13 vote, while opposition figures, including Hichilema’s main rival, have been arrested and charged with treason.
Hichilema won about 60 percent of the vote, according to the official results, against about 38 percent for opposition challenger Brian Mundubile. Mundubile rejected the result and alleged irregularities.
The European Union Election Observation Mission said voters had been offered a competitive choice, but the election was held on an uneven playing field. It also said the transparency of the tabulation process deteriorated significantly after the counting of results was temporarily suspended.
The observations did not amount to a finding that Hichilema had lost the election, but they have cast a shadow over the start of a second term for a president who came to power in 2021 promising to strengthen democracy, the rule of law and state institutions.
From economic recovery to political unease
Hichilema has substantial economic achievements to point to.
When he took office, Zambia was emerging from one of the worst economic crises in its recent history. The southern African country had defaulted on its sovereign debt in 2020, becoming the first African country to do so during the COVID-19 pandemic.
His government has since overseen a major debt restructuring and worked with the International Monetary Fund on a programme of economic reforms. The efforts have helped restore investor confidence and encouraged new investment, particularly in mining.
That matters well beyond Zambia’s borders. The country is one of Africa’s leading copper producers, and its mineral wealth has made it increasingly important to countries looking to secure supplies of copper and other critical minerals needed for the global energy transition.
But the improving economic picture has not necessarily translated into an easier life for many Zambians.
High food and energy costs remain a source of frustration, while the removal of fuel subsidies has put additional pressure on household budgets.
Mundubile made the cost of living a central theme of his campaign, arguing that Hichilema’s economic gains had not reached enough Zambians.
Hichilema acknowledged those frustrations during his inauguration.
“We know that many of our families have challenges with the cost of living and that the benefits of our stabilisation have not yet been felt at every level,” he told thousands of people at the ceremony in Lusaka.
“Economic growth must mean something at the dinner table to all our people,” he said.
What happened after the election?
The vote was largely peaceful at polling stations, but tensions rose as ballots were counted.
The Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) temporarily suspended the tabulation and announcement of results on August 14 after violence at some counting centres and allegations of the theft of election materials.
The EU mission later reported problems at several counting centres, including extended breaks and cases in which returning officers appeared to wait for instructions before announcing results. It also reported a heavy military presence that observers said had an intimidating effect.
The result was eventually declared in Hichilema’s favour, but Mundubile sought to challenge it through the courts.
On August 24, Zambia’s High Courts were closed and access to the premises restricted. The closure came as the deadline for filing a presidential election petition approached.
Human Rights Watch said the move essentially prevented access to the courts for those seeking to challenge the result, while authorities cited security concerns.
The dispute then took a more serious turn.
Mundubile and his running mate, Makebi Zulu, were taken into custody and charged with treason. Authorities have not publicly disclosed detailed evidence underpinning the allegations, and Mundubile has rejected them.
Before their detention, the two men sought refuge at a United Nations facility in Lusaka before surrendering to police. They remain in custody.
A deadly confrontation
The political confrontation had already turned violent in the immediate aftermath of the election.
On August 14, security forces raided a property in Lusaka linked to Mundubile. Former cabinet minister Mutotwe Kafwaya was fatally shot during the operation, while 11 other people were arrested.
Authorities said weapons were recovered and security forces acted in self-defence. Mundubile disputed that account, saying those at the property were not an armed militia.
“We see things like this in countries like Tanzania, Rwanda but not here,” political scientist Neo Simutanyi told Al Jazeera.
“Zambia has had a distinguished record in so far as democracy is concerned,” he said.
Since the end of one-party rule in 1991, Zambia has generally been regarded as one of the more stable multiparty democracies in the region, where power changes hands through elections.
After years as an opposition leader and five unsuccessful presidential bids, Hichilema defeated then-President Edgar Lungu in an election that was praised for its peaceful transfer of power and was seen as an important moment for Zambia’s democracy.
Economic confidence vs political concerns
Investors have so far largely looked past the political turmoil as Zambia’s bonds remain resilient after the election and markets are focused on debt restructuring and economic continuity.
Both China and the United States congratulated Hichilema on his re-election and sent representatives to his inauguration, underscoring Zambia’s importance as a major copper producer and potential source of critical minerals.
For Hichilema, that creates a sharp contrast.
International investors may see continuity in government and an improving economic outlook while opposition groups and observers are increasingly focused on the treatment of political opponents and the strength of democratic institutions.
Mundubile’s lawyer, Milner Katolo, told Al Jazeera there was “sincere hope” that now that Hichilema had secured his second term, a negotiated settlement could help “heal the nation” after a highly acrimonious contest.
“We hope the African Union and SADC [Southern African Development Community] can come in and encourage the state and our clients to sit and find room to resolve this dispute in an amicable way through a settlement,” Katolo said.
Whether such a settlement is possible remains unclear.
“There is a small dent on his image, on democracy and human rights, but most investors are happy that there is continuity because that means their investments are safe. They don’t pay a damn about human rights,” Simutanyi said.

Netanyahu says Israel ‘not retreating’ during Gaza visit
JERUSALEM - Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sept 2 visited Israeli forces in the Gaza Strip, where he vowed not to pull back troops despite a recent push by mediators to advance a US-backed ceasefire plan calling for their withdrawal.

Uber to cut 3,300 corporate jobs in management overhaul
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
16:45:02 UTC
01:45:02 KST

Uber plans to cut its global workforce by about 10% as part of a major restructuring, slashing about 3,300 corporate jobs.
The boss of the US-based ride-hailing app, Dara Khosrowshahi, told staff Wednesday that the changes would create a “simpler and faster” business by cutting layers of management and merging teams. Uber also plans to ask more employees to work in the office.
Uber, which has its headquarters in San Francisco, did not specify how many roles would be affected in each location that it has offices, including in London. The cuts are the largest since 2020 when Uber laid off 6,700 people in response to a major downturn in rides during the Covid pandemic.
Staff affected have been notified, but some countries will have their own local process to follow, according to the firm.
Khosrowshahi said in his message that Uber had been growing in the past five years and the business was performing well.
“But that growth has also brought complexity: more layers, more coordination, more fragmented ownership, and in some cases structures that made sense when businesses were smaller but no longer serve us well at our current scale,” he said.
“The changes we’re making today are designed to do two things: make Uber simpler and faster, and create more capacity to invest in our future.”
Uber is also asking the majority of its staff to come into an office, meaning less than about 1% of employees will be working remotely. The move will reinforce a hybrid work policy which requires three days a week in the office.
Khosrowshahi laid out organisational changes including combining operational and tech teams, and reducing the number of “micro-teams” – where one or two employees report to a single manager – by nearly 50%.
The number of employees who sit more than seven layers from the chief executive has also been cut by 20%.
“The decisions we’re making today are difficult, but they will help us build an even stronger Uber for the years ahead,” Khosrowshahi said.
Uber is preparing to launch self-driving taxis for the first time on UK roads after partnering with the robotaxi business Wayve and being granted approval by Transport for London last month. The company plans to spend $10bn toward developing its autonomous vehicle business, aiming to form a grip on the burgeoning market of self-driving.
Uber also recently struck a $14.8bn deal to acquire the German company Delivery Hero as it jockeys for dominance in the global food delivery market. The company’s UberEats service faces intense competition from rival apps such as DoorDash.
Uber expanded rapidly after launched in San Francisco in 2010, and is now valued at more than $150bn.

"In light of the above, I propose summoning the head of the Administrative Cassation Court, Ihor Dashutin, to address questions regarding his possible use of his administrative powers to influence other judges of the Administrative Cassation Court and the course of cases in which he did not participate as a judge," she said.
As previously reported, the Appeals Chamber of the High Anti-Corruption Court (HACC), at a hearing on Wednesday, upheld the pretrial detention measure imposed on the suspect in cases involving money laundering and corporate raiding (the "Forrest Gump" and "Themis"): detention with the option of bail set at UAH 20 million.
On August 19, the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO) released a video regarding a special operation called "Forrest Gump:" individuals who laundered UAH 150 million to pay bail for a suspect in the Midas case were exposed and charged. The group included, among others, the deputy head of the President's Office of Ukraine and a former member of parliament. Later that day, Zelenskyy signed a decree dismissing Mudra from her position as deputy head of the President's Office.
On Thursday, August 20, NABU and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO) released a second video regarding corruption involving the same high-ranking officials, titled "Themis"– exposing the illegal acquisition of real estate and corporate assets through document forgery. The former deputy head of the President's Office also appears in this episode.
Later on August 20, NABU and SAPO commented on the videos they had previously released, titled "Forrest Gump" and "Themis," which exposed corruption schemes involving high-ranking officials of the President's Office, as well as former and current members of parliament. "The criminal organization's activities, among other things, were aimed at seizing high-value real estate properties, as well as other assets of legal entities, through unauthorized interference in the operation of information (automated) networks of the Ministry of Justice of Ukraine, and the forgery of court decisions and documents of title," the NABU said on its Telegram channel on Thursday.
NABU also said that certain members of the criminal organization, in collusion with representatives and officials of one of the state-owned banks, organized and facilitated the laundering of criminally obtained funds throughout June 2026.
"Based on the evidence obtained, NABU detectives and SAPO prosecutors have served notices of suspicion to members of the criminal organization and the individuals they recruited, under Articles 255, 191, 206-2, 209, 358, and 361 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine," the SAPO said in the statement.

E.U. Chief Says Alleged Russian Drone Plot Had 'Hallmarks of State-Sponsored Terrorism'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
16:43:53 UTC
01:43:53 KST

An alleged Russian drone plot at a German airport last month had “all the hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism,” European Union’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas asserted Wednesday, a day after Germany said Russia was responsible.
“We have already summoned Russian ambassadors,” Kallas told reporters in Ireland, ahead of a meeting with European foreign ministers. Kallas said E.U. member states would consider adding further sanctions on Russian military assets, in addition to working with Ukraine on efforts to put additional pressure on Moscow to end the war.
Germany’s Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said Russia was responsible for the attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle airport in early August, which saw the discovery of an explosive-laden drone close to a runway. Germany's Bild newspaper reported that the drone had been found lying near a Ukrainian cargo aircraft. Federal police and a bomb disposal unit were deployed to safely dispose of the drone.
Leipzig/Halle has served as a European base for Ukraine's Antonov jets since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. The airport is also used by NATO for transportation needs, as well as by the German military.
Wadephul said “the means used to commit the attack, including the drone’s configuration, various components, explosives and ignition technology, are familiar to us from other Russian hybrid operations and from Russia’s war against Ukraine.”
He described the technology found at the airport as “professional” and said the drone’s components demonstrated “a high degree” of technical expertise. “Through the attempted attack in Leipzig, the Russian leadership consciously chose to damage further our already severely strained bilateral relationship,” he alleged.
Wadephul announced retaliatory measures, relaying how Germany intends to close the Russian consulate in Bonn from Sep. 18. The lease for the Russian House in Berlin, an institute showcasing Russian culture, will be terminated.
There will also be tighter entry controls for Russian nationals and additional pressure will be placed on Moscow's shadow fleet.
Russia has denied responsibility for the drone plot.
Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova said that no evidence for the allegations had been presented, and that “under a completely far-fetched and far-fetched pretext, Berlin has once again escalated bilateral relations,” according to Russian state news agency TASS.
In response to the retaliatory actions taken by Germany, Russia’s Deputy Foreign Minister Alexander Grushko told reporters Wednesday that Moscow “will respond as we deem necessary, when we are ready for it.” This came after Russian President Vladimir Putin called the German response a “grave mistake” that “clearly runs counter to the interests of the German people,” according to TASS reporting.
TIME has approached the Russian Foreign Ministry and the Kremlin for comment.
European officials lead support for Germany
Europe has rallied behind Germany and vowed to display a strong, united front.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said “the United Kingdom stands in full solidarity with Germany following Russia’s egregious and reckless attack in Leipzig. Russian attempts to undermine our united resolve and our willingness to support Ukraine are futile and doomed to fail.”
French President Emmanuel Macron said Russia's alleged involvement “cannot go unanswered,” calling for European allies to remain united and stand in support of Ukraine.
Further afield, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said "attacking a Ukrainian cargo plane on German soil was an egregious attempt by Russia to weaken our resolve and our collective defence—and it will fail."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he had discussed the incident with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz. “This is yet another Russian escalation, and it is important that Germany responded,” Zelensky said. “I assured him that Ukraine is ready to help—with expertise, experience, or in other areas where Germany may need it.”
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, meanwhile, expressed “full solidarity” with Germany. “The evidence is clear,” he said, voicing his backing of Berlin’s measures against Moscow. “Russia’s attempts to intimidate us, to undermine our unity and our willingness to support Ukraine are futile and will fail.”
The U.S. ambassador to NATO Matthew Whitaker said the U.S. "stands in solidarity with Germany and all allies in the face of efforts to cause harm and chaos on NATO territory."
Since President Donald Trump’s return to Office, Washington has maintained that European allies must do more to prop up its defensive capabilities, rather than relying heavily on the U.S.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced a review of U.S. troops stationed in Europe in June, expressing the Trump Administration’s disappointment over the “shameful” response from allies to the war with Iran and the lack of support for Washington’s military actions.
NATO has largely heeded the call, with members pledging higher defense spending, but there have still been clashes over key issues, such as Trump’s expressed interest in annexing Greenland.

After the flood: human suffering on an unfathomable scale in Nepal’s worst-hit districts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
16:42:00 UTC
01:42:00 KST

Searching for the body of his wife in the mud, Dil Bahadur Shrestha lamented that he did not even have a shovel left. For now, he has been using his hands to try to find her as he picks through the ruins of his house.
On Wednesday morning last week, Jamuna Shrestha, his wife of 50 years, had been at home in Betrawati on the banks of Nepal’s Trishuli River, feeding her beloved chickens and goats.
As deadly flash floods coursed down the river valley, Jamuna was last seen going back into her house, trying to usher her chickens to safety, while others fled uphill. Now that house stands like a muddy carcass, everything inside it destroyed or washed away by the violent force of the water and debris that killed more than 1,200 people in Nepal and Tibet.
Dil Bahadur Shrestha, 70, had been tending to his rice fields and feeding his cows on the opposite bank when he felt the ground tremble and saw a black wave, hundreds of metres high, coming down the valley. He ran to safety in the forest, but not before watching two bridges get swept away behind him. “When it hit, everything was destroyed within two minutes,” he said.
He knows in his heart that his wife is gone, but like thousands caught up in the disaster, her body has yet to be found and she is counted among the missing. More than 5,000 people are reported missing in Nepal and a further 546 in the Tibet region of China.
Rescue workers have still not reached Dil Bahadur Shrestha’s home, so he returned to try to retrieve her body himself. “Maybe she thought the flood wouldn’t reach inside the house,” he said, wiping away tears.
The couple had already rebuilt their home once after an earthquake in 2015 that killed about 9,000 people. As he spoke, his frail body collapsed to the barren, muddy ground where his neighbour’s house once stood.
“Even now, I cannot believe that she is gone,” he said. “I cannot forget her. That’s why I keep walking around looking for her. I still feel as if she might be walking around somewhere here. I keep getting this feeling that she might still be here, looking after the chickens and the goats.”
The scale of the tragedy in Betrawati is unfathomable. It was 8.37am when a melting glacier high up in the Himalayas on the border between Nepal and Tibet crashed into the valley below, setting off deadly flash floods down Nepal’s Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers. By 8.50am, with only a few minutes’ warning, the settlement of Betrawati was engulfed.
This once-thriving market town was submerged in mud so thick that only the top two floors of a six-storey building are visible. Most houses were washed away entirely or flipped on their sides by the sheer force of the floods. School buses lie overturned. A grocery shop was swept 200 metres from its original location and lies in ruins. The river itself has diverted to a new path that cuts through where the highway once was.
Fragments of the lives of the thousands who lived here lie scattered in the debris: kettles, teddy bears, a record-keeping book, saucepans, medicine packets, a pair of glasses. At least 250 people are missing, Dil Bahadur Shrestha’s brother and sister-in-law among them.
As Dil Bahadur Shrestha surveyed the ruins of his life, search and rescue teams stood on the opposite bank, looking for the dead. By the end of the day, they had pulled 24 bodies from a single house. A helicopter thundered overhead, white body bags swinging underneath.
“I feel there could still be hundreds of bodies here,” said Dil Bahadur Shrestha. “So many people were swept away all at once, carried off by the raging water.” His voice broke: “Now I’m alone. I am completely alone.”
A few metres away, Santamaya Lawat, 57, stood shaking a thick cake of dirt from the few clothes and blankets she had been able to retrieve from her brother’s home, now only partly standing, with a gaping hole in the side. Her own house, built just 10 months ago with her life’s savings, was still so filled with mud she had not yet been able to get inside. Five members of her family are gone.
“My heart broke when I came back,” she said. “This was supposed to be the house I lived in for the rest of my life, but everything is gone. It was like heaven here and now it has been turned into hell.”
Further up the river, in the district of Rasuwa, on the border with Tibet, the scale of destruction only gets worse. Many of the villages here were swept away entirely and are only accessibly by army helicopter. Some are still so cut-off and the ground conditions so precarious that the fate of hundreds of people remains unknown. On Tuesday, police search and rescue teams confirmed they had finally been able to begin ground operations in the border village of Timure, recovering 90 bodies so far.
A week after the disaster, survivors who fled up mountainsides were still being collected by army helicopters and evacuated to the army base in Dhunche, Rasuwa district’s administrative headquarters.
The mountain village of Syabru Besi was among those wiped clean away, with even the road to the village gone. According to local government officials, at least 500 people there are missing, a quarter of the population. The village resembles nothing more than a muddy riverbed, just one building left standing.
Chhiring Dorje, a 50-year-old farmer, was among those who managed to escape Syabru Besi, but five of his family are missing. “There were 15 or 16 of us from the village who made it safely to the forest,” said Dorje. “We stayed there for two days before the army came in a helicopter. We had nothing to eat. We survived by drinking water from the forest.”
He stood tightly holding the hand of his nine-year-old granddaughter, Ritu Tamang, who wore a big pink rucksack as they waited at Dhunche army base for a ride down to Kathmandu. Rescue helicopters thundered in and out every few minutes. She said quietly that there was “nothing left where our house used to be. I used to go to school and was in Grade 1. Now the school is gone. There are no teachers either.”
With the highways washed away, the only road from Kathmandu to Rasuwa is a perilous unpaved track of mud and stones, weaving through tiny mountain villages. The journey often takes more than 12 hours. The treacherous conditions have made it difficult for aid to reach the worst-hit areas and hindered the rescue and relief operations. Many aid trucks are now stuck in Dhunche, unable to drive further north.
At a small relief camp on the road between Betrawati and Dhunche set up by Nepal’s Dhulikhel hospital, people collected medicine and food supplies. Doctors said dozens of the children here had lost their parents in the floods. More than 200 children from the local Nilakantha school, most aged between five and 11, are also missing, believed to have been washed away as they walked to morning classes.
Prakash Nepal, a teacher, said the school had received a warning just 10 minutes before the flood waters hit, when the school bus was already picking up students.
“Luckily, we immediately contacted the bus driver and the vehicle stopped midway so the students were able to survive,” he said. “The surge of water did reach the vehicle, but thankfully it did not cause much damage.”
However, many of the local families had been displaced by the 2015 earthquake and still lived in informal settlements along the riverbank. Most of those children had been walking to school when the flood struck. Prakash Nepal’s eyes welled with tears: “We could not save the students who were still on the road.”
Amid the tragedy, there were also small stories of hope. Sitting on the porch of their village home in Lachyang, Ram Krishna Neupane, 69, and his wife, Muiya Neupane, 66, said their only son had been working as a vet in Syabru Besi when the village was hit.
For two days afterwards they heard nothing and feared he was dead. Then they received a phone call. “He called up from a hospital in Kathmandu; he had been rescued by the army,” said Ram Krishna Neupane. “He could not speak, he was crying so much and we were crying.”
It was, added his wife, “a miracle”.

US President Donald Trump on Wednesday suggested renaming the Strait of Hormuz as “Trump Strait”, asserting US control of the vital waterway even as fighting raged there with Iran.

“It’s got a nice ring to it,” the White House post added.

Kallas pushes back on Franco-German reform plans for EU diplomatic service
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
16:39:56 UTC
01:39:56 KST

Kaja Kallas take part in a joint press conference following an informal meeting of EU Foreign Affairs ministers, at Druids Glen in Wicklow, south of Dublin, Ireland, on September 2, 2026. | Paul Faith/ AFP via Getty Images
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas on Wednesday poured cold water on plans to overhaul the bloc’s diplomatic branch, arguing that better enforcement of the current rules would make its foreign policy more effective.
France and Germany have floated plans for root-and-branch reforms of Kallas’s European External Action Service, or EEAS, according to a discussion paper seen by POLITICO. The plans include giving her oversight of policy units in the European Commission that deal with external relations.
But after a debate on the proposed reforms among EU foreign ministers in Wicklow, Ireland, Kallas said that a “majority” of envoys had supported “the current institutional setup” of the EEAS. She added that there was “broad support” from member countries to make it work without big institutional changes.
Advertisement
“The problem is not the treaties, the institutional setup,” Kallas told a news conference. “The problem is the implementation.”
Debate over the future of EU foreign policy — and the fate of the EEAS — is intensifying amid budget constraints and criticism that it is no longer fit for purpose in an era of increasingly brutal relations between global powers.
Meanwhile, the European Commission’s growing interest in foreign policy, including the creation of a unit dedicated to the Middle East and Africa, has sparked a turf war with Kallas’s EEAS.
The Franco-German paper, among other ideas, proposed addressing this issue by giving Kallas oversight of external-facing policy units within the Commission, including migration, trade and development aid.
Kallas pushed back, arguing that EU treaties and legal texts already gave her this responsibility in theory — but were not properly enforced.
Kallas’s role sits astride the Commission, where she is a vice president under President Ursula von der Leyen, and the European Council where she is tasked with coordinating the foreign policy positions of 27 EU states.
Advertisement
“There was not support for concentrating everything in the Commission without having this role practically implemented,” said Kallas, referring to her position as high representative and vice president. “If I have somebody above me who is actually deciding, then it doesn’t work that way.”
Ahead of the meeting in Wicklow, three EU diplomats, who were granted anonymity to discuss the reforms, said that Kallas was unlikely to support plans that could be seen as giving von der Leyen more direct authority over her actions.

Russia: Detention of charity leader Lida Moniava for anti-war social media posts a brazen attack on freedom of expression
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
16:39:00 UTC
01:39:00 KST

Reacting to the detention of Lidiya (Lida) Moniava, a Russian civil society activist and prominent charity leader, for alleged “dissemination of false information” about the Russian Armed Forces, Marie Struthers, Amnesty International’s Director for Eastern Europe and Central Asia, said:
“The criminal case against Lida Moniava is yet another brazen attempt by Russia’s authorities to crackdown on any expression of anti-war sentiment. This assault on one of Russia’s most prominent charity leaders is designed to silence not only her, but the entire civil society.”
“The Russian authorities must immediately end the criminal prosecution of Lida Moniava for peacefully exercising her right to freedom of expression. They must repeal the country’s repressive ‘war censorship’ legislation and release all those imprisoned solely for the peaceful exercise of their right to express opposition to the war.”
This assault on one of Russia’s most prominent charity leaders is designed to silence not only her, but the entire civil society
Marie Struthers, Amnesty International’s Director for Eastern Europe and Central Asia
Background
Lida Moniava has worked in the charity sector since 2008, including with “Podari Zhizn” (Gift a Life) foundation, which helps children with oncological and haematological diseases, and “Vera” (Faith), a hospice where she coordinated palliative care for children. In 2014, she became deputy director of the children’s hospice “Dom s Mayakom” (House with a Lighthouse) and in 2018 became director of its charitable foundation.
On 2 September 2026, Lida Moniava was detained in Moscow under charges of “public dissemination of knowingly false information about the use of the Armed Forces of the Russian Federation” (Article 207.3 of the Criminal Code). Her home was searched and she was questioned by members of the Investigation Committee, a stand-alone agency tasked with investigating serious crime. On the same day, she was placed in a temporary detention facility for two days until the court decides on her pretrial restrictions.
According to her lawyer, the criminal case concerns a Telegram post by Lida Moniava in February 2023.
In February 2026, a court fined Lida Moniava 45,000 roubles (US$ 580) for allegedly “discrediting” the Russian Armed Forces. The proceedings concerned three posts on her Telegram channel, including posts referring to Russia’s war against Ukraine and to reported Russian strikes in Kryvyi Rih and Sumy.

Frecciarossa in Germany: tests begin for Rome and Milan rail links to Munich
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
16:38:22 UTC
01:38:22 KST

Trial runs of Frecciarossa trains in Germany and Austria are paving the way for high-speed links between Rome, Milan and Munich. The first services are planned for summer 2027.
From Rome to Munich on a Frecciarossa train, via Innsbruck. Ferrovie dello Stato (FS) has begun test runs of the Frecciarossa trains operated by Trenitalia in Germany and Austria, as part of the international certification phase.
The FS Group has announced that the launch of services between Milan and Munich and between Rome and Munich is scheduled for the summer of 2027 "following the successful completion of the approval process for the new trains".
After France and Spain, and with the goal of reaching the United Kingdom via the Channel Tunnel by 2029, Italy's state railways are now arriving in the heart of Europe as well. The initiative is being carried out in partnership with the German and Austrian national railways, Deutsche Bahn and ÖBB.
The opening of the Brenner Base Tunnel will cut journey times by around an hour and, from December 2028, the full service will consist of ten connections between Italy and Germany, covering the routes between Milan, Rome and Munich and later extended to Naples and Berlin.
Where will the new services stop?
The commercial offer envisages four connections on the Milan - Munich and Rome - Munich routes.
On the Milan - Munich route, with a journey time of about six and a half hours, the main intermediate stops will be Brescia, Verona, Rovereto, Trento, Bolzano and Innsbruck.
On the Rome - Munich route, with a journey time of about eight and a half hours, the main stops will be Florence, Bologna, Verona, Rovereto, Trento, Bolzano and Innsbruck.
Towards the new 'European Metro' network
"The start of test runs in Germany and Austria is a step towards delivering a project that confirms our ambition to make the train the benchmark mode of transport for mobility across Europe," said FS chief executive and general manager Gianpiero Strisciuglio.
"Thanks to our partnership with Deutsche Bahn and ÖBB, we are moving towards creating the High-Speed 'European Metro', offering passengers a service able to bring regions, people and economies closer together," Strisciuglio explained.
The FS chief added that Frecciarossa "is thus continuing its international growth path, taking the FS Group's technological and industrial excellence abroad and helping to develop an increasingly integrated European rail network".
The Minister for Infrastructure and Transport, Matteo Salvini, has also expressed satisfaction with the milestone achieved. Salvini described it as "a further step confirming the growth of the FS Group and its ability to win new markets abroad, while providing better services and infrastructure in Italy. More jobs, more connections, more Italy in Europe".
The agreement between Trenitalia and Deutsche Bahn will also make it possible to share technical expertise so that the trains can adapt to different power-supply and signalling systems, speeding up the required technical process and keeping associated costs under control. At the same time as the prototypes were being built, training programmes for German and Austrian driving staff were also launched.
The Frecciarossa, compliant with European interoperability technical specifications, has been designed and built to run in Italy and on the rail networks of France, Germany, Spain, Austria, Switzerland, the Netherlands and Belgium.
The new connection will also affect rail links with other countries, capturing demand for travel to destinations such as Frankfurt and Krakow.

HK activist Joshua Wong pleads guilty
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
16:37:41 UTC
01:37:41 KST

Hong Kong democracy advocate Joshua Wong (黃之鋒) yesterday pleaded guilty to conspiracy to collude with foreign forces to endanger national security under a Beijing-imposed law.
It was the second prosecution of Wong, a former student leader in the democracy movement in the territory and one of its most recognizable faces, under the National Security Law introduced in Hong Kong in 2020 to quell massive anti-government protests the year before.
Wong, 29, who wore a blue shirt, appeared thinner as he entered his plea.
Photo: EPA
After hearing his lawyer’s arguments for a lesser prison term, Judge William Tam (譚耀豪) said that a sentence would be delivered as soon as possible, without specifying a date.
The offense is punishable by a prison term of three to 10 years, or up to life imprisonment if the offense is deemed to be “of a grave nature.”
Pleading guilty could typically result in a reduced sentence and his lawyers expressed hope for a penalty that would not be crushing.
Wong was already serving a prison term of four years and eight months after entering a guilty plea in a separate national security case linked to an unofficial political primary.
Before he was arrested for the collusion-related offense in June last year, Wong had been expected to be freed in January next year.
Critics say Wong’s case showed the authorities’ determination to silence prominent dissidents, chilling civic activism.
Wong jotted notes during the hearing and said “bye bye” to the public gallery before leaving the courtroom.
The prosecution alleged that Wong and fellow rights advocate Nathan Law (羅冠聰) had agreed in or around 2016 to lobby internationally to achieve their goal of democratic self-determination.
Before the security law, they and others sought foreign forces to impose sanction, blockades or engage in other hostile measures against Hong Kong and China, it said.
Wong expressed support for the special status previously given by Washington to Hong Kong to be reviewed through the Hong Kong Human Rights and Democracy Act at a hearing in 2019 of the US Congressional-Executive Commission on China, the prosecution said, and pointed to his other lobbying efforts.

Thai city beckons US Navy sailors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
16:37:38 UTC
01:37:38 KST

There is no getting around the fact that Thailand’s seaside resort of Pattaya has a lingering reputation for sex tourism, even though that is only part of the story for the city that is an expected shore leave destination of crew members aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln.
Pattaya, about 100km southeast of Bangkok, is where many of the 5,000 or so sailors and Marines in the Lincoln’s strike group are expected to visit for some rest and recuperation this week after the big ship’s tour of duty in the Middle East.
They would be following in the wake of millions of other tourists, including a significant number of US military personnel who take part every year in major land and sea exercises nearby with their Thai counterparts.
Photo: Bloomberg
Social media ahead of the Lincoln’s visit have been awash with jibes about lusty sailors, but recent visitors say the development of more family-friendly attractions makes the new Pattaya overshadow its former seedy self.
Many US Navy ships dock at nearby deep-water facilities such as Laem Chabang Port and the Sattahip Royal Thai Navy Base, both less than an hour away by road.
Shore leave spending boosts the local economy, and mission duties often include community outreach in and around the city, such as specialized medical care for villagers or putting in volunteer time at orphanages.
Photo: Reuters
However, when hundreds or thousands of sailors have a chance to enjoy some onshore liberty, the US Navy deploys members of its shore patrol to work side by side with Thai police to defuse any trouble.
Navy personnel are likely to have been reminded that, although rarely enforced, the law in Thailand technically bans prostitution and paying for sex is a punishable offense under Article 134 of the Uniform Code of Military Justice, the legal framework for the US armed forces.
The military connection goes back at least to the Vietnam War era, when at its height, 40,000 to 50,000 US service personnel were stationed in Thailand, largely in support of the conflict’s air operations. Bases used by US forces dotted Thailand and all attracted their share of nightlife activities.
Pattaya was close to the Sattahip naval base and the Thai Navy’s U-Tapao airfield, which hosted US Air Force B-52s.
Elizabeth Becker, author of Overbooked: The Exploding Business of Travel and Tourism, wrote that US soldiers during the Vietnam War flocked to Pattaya, a once-quiet fishing village, “and it turned into a raunchy seaside playground.”
The military facilities brought a continuous stream of personnel through Pattaya, while the 1966 Entertainment Places Act created a legal gray area allowing the sex trade to operate semiopenly in bars and massage parlors — as something of a private arrangement between customer and employee — despite a 1960 law criminalizing prostitution.
Pattaya’s infrastructure of go-go clubs and other entertainment venues was then marketed to travelers arriving in greater numbers due to cheaper air travel and a boom in package tours. Sex tourism became entrenched.
Pattaya underwent another evolution in the 1990s, with a new wave of tourists coming from what had been the Soviet Union after communism there collapsed in late 1991.
Embracing modern globalized tourism, the newcomers came on direct charter flights to the civilian airport at U-Tapao, benefiting from a 30-day visa-free agreement.
Signs in Cyrillic sprouted around Pattaya as businesses catered to this new clientele.
Russians were not the only people calling Pattaya their home away from home.
The agreeable climate and allegedly laissez-faire attitude of local law enforcement attracted fugitives from justice and criminals from all over the world, including Russian, eastern and western European gangsters, as well as drug-dealing motorcycle gangs from Australia.
Pattaya has tried with some success this century to rebrand itself as a family destination, with parks, malls and luxury resorts largely in surrounding areas that attract large numbers of Thais and visitors from other Asian nations.
A water park is themed around Cartoon Network shows. The Nong Nooch Tropical Botanical Garden displays vast stretches of flora and hosts cultural shows.
Travelers can still get a taste of old Pattaya with a nocturnal stroll down “Walking Street,” at the heart of the city’s nightlife district.

Cricketers to get best rooms at Asian Games, Japan says

Cricketers at this month’s Asian Games in Japan would have better accommodation than athletes from many other sports, the head of Japanese cricket said yesterday, after concerns were raised about a lack of five-star hotels for players.
A Sri Lankan official this week said that some of Asia’s top teams had raised doubts over facilities and accommodation at the Games, which are taking place in Nagoya and the wider Aichi area from Sept. 19.
Cricket is a minor sport in Japan and games would be played at a new purpose-built ground with reports of tents serving as dressing rooms and distant washroom facilities.
Photo: AFP
There is no dedicated athletes’ village at the Games, with organizers instead relying on cabins in a cruise ship, rooms in temporary wooden containers and hotels.
Organizers last week said that accommodation was already stretched to the limit after the number of Asian Games athletes ballooned to 17,000. By comparison there were about 11,000 at the 2024 Paris Olympics.
The cricket tournament is being run by the Asian Games organizing committee in collaboration with the Asian Cricket Council.
Japan Cricket Association CEO Naoki Alex Miyaji said that the two bodies had been discussing accommodation options “for a long time.”
“The participating teams in cricket are being offered hotel accommodation,” Miyaji said yesterday. “Many other sports are being accommodated in much more limited facilities such as a cruise ship or container hotels.”
Matches are to be played at Korogi Sports Park, a converted baseball field that is a 40-minute train ride away from central Nagoya.
Media reports in India said the country’s cricket board was unhappy with arrangements and might send a second-string squad after originally naming 15 players led by Shreyas Iyer and including 15-year-old rising star Vaibhav Sooryavanshi.
Miyaji said that Japanese organizers “only had 17 months to prepare and had to start from scratch” for cricket at the Games.
They had been working “to ensure that the best facilities are provided within the limited timeline and facility restrictions,” he said.
“Despite being temporary, the facilities will provide as comfortable a space as possible for the players and officials,” he said.
Miyaji said the pitch, which is being prepared by the curator of the 35,000-capacity Pallekele International Cricket Stadium in Sri Lanka, would be of a high standard.
“From what I have seen, the playing surface and field will be the best seen in cricket’s inclusion in the Asian Games,” he added.

The Alex Eala fans came bearing Philippine flags, and wearing hats telling her to fight on (“Laban Alex”). They cheered her sizzling groundstrokes, documented her volleys and serves in photos and video, and in some cases FaceTimed with friends or family — and this was only at the practice courts.
It was about four hours before Eala was to take the court for her first-round US Open match on Tuesday, and every seat at the practice court was filled. Many of Eala’s fans did not have tickets for the evening session, but they had come to see their idol hit some tennis balls.
It was hardly surprising, given the enormous, ardent, ever-growing fan base that surrounds the charismatic 21-year-old.
Photo: AFP
This summer, Eala beat Iga Swiatek at Wimbledon and won her first tour singles title. She is at a career-best 18th in the world, and she breezed into the second round of the US Open with a 6-1, 6-2 victory over Mary Stoiana — closing it out with a confident smile.
One of the fans watching practice on a rainy afternoon was Andrea Belen, at 21 the same age as Eala.
Belen, a premed student at New York University, said that she had not been a big tennis fan until Eala came along — someone who looked just like her.
Photo: AP
Belen’s father back home in Cleveland (the family’s originally from Laguna in the Philippines) also became a tennis fan out of pure admiration for Eala.
“It’s his new obsession,” Belen said. “It’s become the family hobby.”
She and her friend, Sarah Frederick, had arrived at the practice court long before Eala was to appear, surmising correctly that the seats would fill quickly.
In the Philippines, basketball and boxing reign supreme, and the sports heroes are men, Belen said.
“It’s just really nice to see a woman out there,” she said. “Also, she speaks in our native language, Tagalog.”
As Belen chatted and Eala pounded her groundstrokes, a voice from the row behind Belen called out: “Yay, Alex.”
Ellene Santos had come to the tournament from Orlando, Florida. Like Belen and Frederick, she did not have tickets for the evening match, but the 67-year-old was thrilled to get her Eala fix, just the same.
“I’m happy now,” she said.
With practice over, four retired nurses, all friends, headed for the exit. They were wearing bright blue hats emblazoned with the phrase, “Laban Alex,” an exhortation to “fight.”
“I love how Alex shows she is so proud to be from the Philippines,” Joy Rodriguez, 65, said.
Her friend, Maria Espiritu, 67, said this was the first tennis tournament she had ever attended.
Nearby, Frances Arespacochaga, 77, was taking photos with fellow attendees. Arespacochaga lives in Manila, and was in the US visiting her sister in Massachusetts. Together they drove down to see Eala at the US Open — bearing flags.
“She’s very intelligent, very articulate,” Arespacochaga said of Eala. “In her interviews you can see her values.”
Belen, who FaceTimed with her father during the practice session so he could see Eala, spoke of a special Filipino pride in the achievements of countrymen. Like gymnast Carlos Yulo, who won two gold medals at the 2024 Paris Olympics.
“Everyone went crazy,” she said. “We’re not that big of a country so those golds meant so much.”
“We’re very loud when it comes to supporting our people,” Belen said.

Notes from Central Taiwan: Taiwan’s drone bill has a kill switch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
16:37:33 UTC
01:37:33 KST

The Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT)-controlled legislature in February 2006 established the National Communications Commission (NCC). One of the purposes of the NCC was to circumvent the control of the Government Information Office (GIO), long the KMT’s tool for overseeing the local media, by the administration of Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) president Chen Shui-bian (陳水扁).
The NCC’s commissioners were originally apportioned according to the ratio of party control of the legislature. However, the Council of Grand Justices later ruled that agencies required greater coordination with the Executive Yuan, which then began sending a list of expert nominees for approval by the legislature.
That commission system was revived by the KMT and its sock puppet, the Taiwan People’s Party (TPP), in the recent drone funding bill. The Act on Strengthening Defense Autonomy and Developing the Unmanned Vehicles Industry (強化國防自主暨無人載具產業發展條例) was passed on Aug. 27 to great media fanfare.
Photo: Yen Hung-chun, Taipei Times
Many commentaries were cautiously approving, but noted that by requiring the drone procurement budget to be included in the annual budget, procurement may fail to become stable and regular. Observers also pointed out the apparent unconstitutionality of the legislature adding budget items to the regular budget.
Some analysts worried that the KMT could hold up the government budget as it did this year, introducing delays into drone procurement, which would force drone makers out of the business or at least, out of government contracting. However, the bill’s most critical proviso was neglected in much of the international commentary.
NCC REDUX?
Photo: AP
The bill requires the Executive Yuan to establish a “National Uncrewed Vehicle Industry Development Strategy Special Committee.” That special committee is to be responsible for coordinating industrial policies and reviewing industrial development guidelines (including funding needs and financial resource planning). The bill mandates that more than half of the committee members must be nominated by the various party caucuses in the Legislative Yuan.
That is the same basic structure as the NCC. The special committee also appears to have many of the same coordinating functions as the NCC.
As a sharp commentary by legislative staffer Gahon Chiang (江佳紘) this week observed in this paper, this would allow “caucus-nominated members to participate directly in an Executive Yuan policy coordination and review mechanism.”
Photo: Reuters
A Ministry of Economic Affairs (MOEA) news report observed that if the Legislative Yuan caucus delays the process of nominating committee members, or if nominated members obstruct the committee’s proceedings, the committee may be unable to convene or review drone industry development guidelines. This implies that if the special committee becomes dysfunctional, drone development will grind to a halt. The MOEA’s comments did not consider a third possibility: defunding (more of which below).
The KMT playbook is simple: delay, deny, defund. That is exactly what has happened under the current administration of President William Lai (賴清德). The KMT-controlled legislature since July last year has refused to confirm new NCC commissioners. The terms of the last three commissioners’ expired on July 31. As an excellent commentary at Global Taiwan Institute (GTI) on the NCC’s woes observed: “Starting from August 1, the lack of commissioners prevents the NCC from holding even advisory meetings.”
This year’s budget passed by the legislature slashes the NCC budget for administrative operations by 56 percent, according to the GTI piece. This means the NCC has vastly reduced ability to pay for utilities, rent and maintenance. The GTI commentary notes that the NCC’s dysfunctionality affects more than the media because the NCC also has authority over communications equipment for emergency vehicles, along with radio devices, including radars, mounted on ships and aircraft and installed on Taiwan’s islands. The transportation safety and national security implications of this are obvious.
The KMT can easily focus its NCC playbook on the new special committee for drone development. If the presidency remains in DPP hands, it can fail to confirm new committee members and allow current members’ terms to expire (it passed an amendment to the NCC banning third terms or extended terms for NCC committee members). It can slash the committee’s funding to hinder its work.
This also works if the central government flips to the KMT. The drone budget’s special committee will then become a hindrance to drone development, safely out of sight of the public.
KMT ASSAULT ON GOVERNANCE
The other aspect of the KMT playbook revealed by the special committee on drone development is the party’s assault on governance. The proposed committee would overlap legislative and executive responsibilities instead of legislative oversight clearly distinguished from the central government, with the concomitant degradation of central government authority. In fact, as several commentaries have described, mechanisms and processes within the central government to carry out the committee functions already exist and function smoothly. Hence, an “oversight” committee dependent on the legislature’s goodwill can have only one function: gunking up the process.
A commentary for the Australian Strategic Policy Institute’s (ASPI) Strategist said: “Yet the Kuomintang (KMT), Taiwan’s largest opposition party, did make concessions.”
The Ministry of National Defense was permitted to retain authority over the extra spending, and local content rules were rendered less stringent, according to the commentary. The reason it made those concessions should now be clear: as long as the KMT controls the legislature, they don’t matter.
The NCC and the special committee on drone development are related in another way. As the GTI report makes clear, NCC dysfunction itself can paralyze drone development because it is responsible for regulating radio frequencies, on which drone development depends.
“Even with three commissioners, the NCC struggled to maintain operations,” GTI reports. “Now, with none, its functions are impaired to the point that drones cannot clear manufacturing or import review.”
Control of either the NCC or the special committee gives the legislature the ability to severely impair drone development. Thus, the KMT-controlled legislature has given itself a broad toolkit to block drones, a critical national security necessity.
Drones are also an important industrial domain like bicycles, electronics and textiles, the kind of rapidly changing, constantly upgrading industry that Taiwan’s nimble small and medium-sized companies are especially good at. Based on its past experience in related technologies, Taiwan should become a major player in the drone field. For countries like the US attempting to develop non-Chinese supply chains for critical national security technologies, Taiwan’s drone industry is a must.
Former KMT vice chairman Andrew Hsia (夏立言) last month attended the opening of a cross-strait civic group exchange summit in Beijing. According to a former official of the People’s Republic of China (PRC), the summit was intended to promote “Chinese national and cultural identity” among Taiwanese, to turn them into “righteous Chinese who protect the nation’s fundamental interests together.”
Whose interests are the righteous Chinese in the KMT promoting with this carefully constructed drone bill?
Notes from Central Taiwan is a column written by long-term resident Michael Turton, who provides incisive commentary informed by three decades of living in and writing about his adoptive country. The views expressed here are his own.

Ko attacked the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) for being behind on flood control measures, but as the city administration observed, there are many weaknesses in how the government can mitigate extreme rainfall. Nor is the river entirely under the management of the city. The low-lying Dianbao River

HORSE RACING
Romantic Warrior retires
Romantic Warrior, the Hong Kong star racehorse who won a world record HK$288.74 million (US$36.82 million) in prize money, was retired yesterday after sustaining a leg injury in training last week. Owner Peter Lau said he had decided to end the eight-year-old’s storied racing career after consulting Hong Kong Jockey Club veterinarians. Scans revealed “a change in one of the horse’s joints” similar to last year when Romantic Warrior had surgery on a fetlock, he said. The news comes just days before the start of Hong Kong’s racing season on Sunday at Sha Tin. Romantic Warrior extended his unrivaled record as the world’s highest earning racehorse with six wins out of six last season, including a triumph in the prestigious Group 1 QEII Cup for an unprecedented fourth time in April.

Kaepernick not watching NFL
Colin Kaepernick still watches football; just not the NFL. The former San Francisco 49ers quarterback told NBC News in an interview that he prefers to watch the college game instead. The 38-year-old, who led the 49ers to a Super Bowl after the 2012 season, has not played since the 2016 season finale, an exile that began not long after he started taking a knee during the national anthem to highlight social injustices. “I’m not gonna support an organization that one, is actively blackballing me, but two, has targeted my brothers who have been protesting as part of this as well,” Kaepernick said. Kaepernick and former teammate Eric Reid, who knelt alongside Kaepernick, sued the NFL citing collusion. The two sides settled in early 2019.

Kroenke Sports and Entertainment on Tuesday said that it would purchase a controlling interest in the Los Angeles Angels from Arte Moreno in a deal that is expected to close in the first quarter of next year. Lifelong learning for national resilience
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
16:37:28 UTC
01:37:28 KST

Taiwan has become a super-aged society, with people aged 65 or older accounting for more than 20 percent of the population. As the demographic structure undergoes a dramatic transformation, the government has over the past few years promoted a long-term care program, health promotion and disability-prevention policies to reduce the burden on the healthcare and elderly care systems. Yet we are still overlooking an earlier form of public infrastructure: learning for older adults.
Lifelong learning for older people has long been misunderstood as little more than a leisure activity. What it builds is actually something far more important: the capacity to age well. Through health promotion, digital learning, lifelong education, social participation and volunteer work, older adults can maintain their physical and mental functioning, delay cognitive decline, expand their social support networks, and continue contributing to their families and communities.
True resilience is never built after a crisis has already struck. It is accumulated through capabilities developed earlier. The greatest challenge facing a super-aged society is not that there are more older people, but that the number of people living with disabilities might rise rapidly. If older adults lose their mobility, social connections and independence early, even the most comprehensive healthcare and long-term care systems would be overwhelmed.
Therefore, instead of directing the vast majority of resources toward care after disability occurs, we should move some investment upstream. By promoting learning and participation while people are healthy, we can help more people delay disability and extend their healthy life expectancy. It is not consumption spending, but a public investment with long-term returns.
We are willing to spend enormous sums building infrastructure and other public facilities, because we understand that physical infrastructure is essential to national development. However, a super-aged society needs more than visible infrastructure; it also needs invisible infrastructure: human capability.
Lifelong learning can change the way we view older adults. They should not be regarded merely as people who need to be cared for. They are also human capital capable of continuing to learn, serve and contribute.
When older adults become volunteers, lead community activities, participate in the workforce, pass on skills or support others, they not only bolster their sense of purpose and value, but also reinforce community solidarity and intergenerational integration.
Faced with a super-aged society, the government should fundamentally rethink the role of learning in later life and make it an integral part of national resilience. It should establish cross-ministerial cooperation linking lifelong learning with health promotion, long-term care, community-based services and the development of an older workforce. Education should no longer be viewed simply as the transmission of knowledge; it should become a core policy for building the capabilities of older people, promoting healthy aging and social participation.
Everyone will grow old. Investing in learning for older adults today is not merely an investment in today’s seniors; it is an investment in our own future.
A truly resilient society does not wait until people fall before reaching out to help them up. It gives people the strength to remain standing.
As Taiwan enters the era of a super-aged society, learning in later life should no longer be treated as an optional educational service. It should become a cornerstone of national resilience.
Hsieh Min-hsien is an adjunct assistant professor at National Chi Nan University’s Department of Counseling Psychology and Human Resource Development, and the CEO of Miaoli County’s Active Aging Learning Model Center.

When a passport becomes a prison
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
16:37:28 UTC
01:37:28 KST

Taiwan is home to thousands of foreign residents who build careers, families and lives here. However, what happens when one of those residents loses the ability to prove his identity — not because he has broken Taiwan’s laws, but because his own government refuses to renew his passport?
That is the situation my husband, Matteo (not his real name), a Nicaraguan national, has found himself in.
After about three years of attempts to renew his passport, our future in Taiwan remains uncertain.
It all comes back to Taiwan’s giant geopolitical issue: the multitude of countries cutting diplomatic ties with Taiwan in favor of the People’s Republic of China (PRC). Following Nicaragua’s decision to sever diplomatic relations with Taiwan in 2021 and recognize the PRC, Matteo’s circumstances changed dramatically. The Nicaraguan embassy in Taipei closed, leaving him to pursue passport renewal through Nicaragua’s diplomatic representatives in Japan and its Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Despite repeated efforts, his application remains indefinitely “on hold,” without a clear explanation or timeline.
This is particularly concerning given growing reports of the Nicaraguan government denying passports, restricting citizens’ abilities to return or leave the country, and stripping people of their nationality.
Matteo’s story is not unique; thousands of other Nicas abroad find themselves de facto stateless due to Nicaragua’s deliberate tools of transnational oppression. We have genuine fears that returning Matteo to Nicaragua could put him at risk of retaliation and potentially leave him unable to ever leave. Those concerns have also made us extremely cautious about speaking publicly, as we fear retaliation against his family members still in Nicaragua.
The consequences here in Taiwan have been profound. His legal stay has been maintained through one-month extensions from the National Immigration Agency (NIA), leaving us uncertain about what would happen from one month to the next. Without a valid passport and current alien resident certificate, Matteo has lost access to his bank account and the National Health Insurance system. He cannot renew his driver’s license, maintain his mobile phone service, pursue further education or work normally.
We have not passively waited for a solution. We have contacted Taiwanese authorities, human rights organizations, international human rights groups, as well as local and international lawyers. None of those options have resolved our situation. In January, Matteo was interviewed by the United Nations Group of Human Rights Experts on Nicaragua, who informed him that his circumstances constitute de facto statelessness — a situation in which a person cannot obtain protection or documentation from his country of nationality.
In February, Matteo applied for Spanish citizenship through the Carta de Naturaleza process as a possible long-term solution. However, we have learned that Spain is inundated with applications by thousands of other people who find themselves in the same situation, and Matteo’s application would expire after one year, thus leaving us in limbo while we wait for another country to determine whether he can obtain a new nationality.
In June, we traveled to Taipei for a meeting with representatives of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the NIA and the National Human Rights Commission. We presented documentation regarding Matteo’s situation, international human-rights information and our concerns about the potential consequences of returning him to Nicaragua. However, since that meeting we have received no substantive response to our inquiries and no apparent progress toward a resolution.
We are grateful that Taiwan continues to grant Matteo temporary extensions, but they are not a sustainable solution. Life as a stateless person in a country with no asylum laws or protections has taken its toll on us mentally, physically and financially. I have been hospitalized due to stress-induced illness, and Matteo battles newfound anxiety and depression, never knowing if he would see his family again or if we would be able to move forward with our lives.
Our case also raises a broader question about Taiwan’s place in the international community. Taiwan has long faced diplomatic isolation and pressure from Beijing. However, when diplomatic relations disappear, the consequences can extend beyond governments and treaties to ordinary people who suddenly find themselves caught between political realities.
For our family, this is not an abstract geopolitical issue. It is our life. For Taiwan, it is an opportunity to demonstrate that when extraordinary circumstances fall outside ordinary immigration procedures, compassion, human rights and practical solutions can coexist with the rule of law.
How Taiwan responds could matter not only to us, but to others who might one day find themselves in the same position.
Nicole Roberts, a pseudonym, is a permanent resident of Taiwan, and a certified teacher from the US with more than 16 years of experience in international education.

Tottenham splashed out ￡303 million as they rebuild after two successive seasons close to being relegated.

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電) is to establish a presence in the Baipu Industrial Park (白埔產業園區) in Kaohsiung to accelerate the testing and validation of semiconductor materials and equipment, a company executive said on Tuesday.
The company is working with the Ministry of Economic Affairs and the Kaohsiung City Government on the plan, which is expected to improve validation efficiency by 25 to 50 percent, TSMC vice president of advanced packaging technology and service Jun He (何軍) said at a 3D IC global summit held ahead of the Semicon Taiwan trade show, which opened in Taipei yesterday.
TSMC would also conduct process research and development at the park with the aim of building a world-class training base for advanced packaging talent and connecting local suppliers with global supply chains, He said.
Photo: CNA
The company is planning to develop a 3-hectare site in the Baipu Industrial Park that would include two buildings featuring modular facilities that can be reconfigured as technology evolves, he said.
The site would include small clean rooms and laboratories for testing and joint development involving advanced packaging technologies, equipment and materials, he said.
The move comes as demand for advanced packaging has surged amid the rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI) applications, he said.
Given that demand, TSMC expects its chip-on-wafer-on-substrate advanced packaging capacity to grow at a compound annual growth rate of more than 80 percent through next year, with growth expected to remain robust through 2029, He said.
Driven by skyrocketing demand for AI technology, revenue from Taiwan’s semiconductor industry is expected to increase by 40 percent this year, Taiwan Semiconductor Industry Association (台灣半導體產業協會) president Wu Chih-i (吳志毅) said yesterday.
“We are in a new era of the semiconductor industry from a technology point of view,” Wu said at the opening of Semicon Taiwan, adding that AI has pushed the development of new technology.
“This year Taiwan’s semiconductor industry has performed even better. Our total revenue is projected to be close to US$300 billion. That’s more than 40 percent growth over last year,” he said.
However, energy supply, talent and cybersecurity were “becoming more critical” for the industry and “no single country” could dominate the chip supply chain, he added.
“Continuous progress will require even closer semiconductor collaboration between many countries,” Wu said.
Also attending the event, SEMI president and chief executive officer Ajit Manocha said that global semiconductor revenue could reach US$2 trillion by 2030, as AI advances from training to inference and demand would grow for memory, higher bandwidth, advanced packaging and silicon photonics, creating new opportunities across the semiconductor ecosystem.
This would be the decade of AI, Manocha said, adding that the world is in the “early innings” and there would be “a lot more challenges” with the technology.
“It’s not going to be a straight line,” he said. “We’re going to have to learn how to deal with and navigate through the new opportunities and new headwinds.”

The company is on track to enter production of CPO later this year, Hsu said in another forum arranged by Imec in Taipei yesterday, about four months after TSMC announced its progress in CPO development in May.

Taiwan faces twin demographic milestones in 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
16:37:23 UTC
01:37:23 KST

Taiwan’s population faces two key milestones in 2027: the number of 18-year-olds will fall below 200,000 and the 85-and-older group will surpass 500,000 for the first time, according to the latest government projections.
Taiwan’s 18-year-olds, the typical age for entering college, will fall below 200,000 for the first time in the 2027 academic year to 195,309, down from 200,406 in 2026. The figure is projected to decline further to less than 150,000 by 2040, according to the National Development Council (NDC).
The 15-year-old high-school-bound population is projected to fall from 189,168 in the 2026 academic year to 122,566 by 2040 -- a drop of 66,602, or 35 percent, the report showed.
Photo: CNA
During the same period, populations in younger age groups will fall even more sharply, by more than half.
The number of junior high school entrants (age 12) is projected to fall from 207,790 in the 2026 academic year to 88,519 (down 57.3 percent) by 2040. Primary school entrants (age 6) will drop from 169,420 to 75,311 (down 55.6 percent), according to the NDC.
The demographic decline across all educational tiers will force school closures, mergers, and class reductions, weakening the nation’s labor supply and capacity for talent development, the NDC stated in a news release.
At the other end of the age spectrum, the 85-and-older group is projected to rise from 484,168 (9.97 percent of all seniors) in 2026 to 503,723 (9.99 percent) in 2027, surpassing the half-million mark for the first time, the projections by the National Development Council (NDC) released on Friday showed.
That figure is expected to top 1 million by 2039, the NDC said.
For the senior population as a whole, the NDC projected that the share of adults aged 65 and older will reach 30 percent of the population (6.52 million) by 2037, after crossing the 20 percent threshold in 2025, which at that time made Taiwan officially a super-aged society.
According to NDC projections, Taiwan’s population is set to drop from the current figure of 23.19 million to under 20 million by 2045. Meanwhile, the median age will climb from 46.4 to 57.2.
Projections show that seniors aged 65 and older will make up 41 percent of Taiwan’s total population by 2050, marking a historical peak.
By 2051, the working-age population (aged 15 to 64) will drop below 10 million, shrinking to 53.4 percent of the total population, according to NDC projections.
Meanwhile, the population aged 65 and older is projected to reach its peak around 2050 at roughly 7.7 million, before exceeding half of the total population (50.4 percent) by 2065.

Taiwan to launch NT$400m AI-assisted fishing project
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
16:37:20 UTC
01:37:20 KST

Taiwan is to launch a four-year, NT$400 million (US$12.61 million) project that would use artificial intelligence (AI) to help trawlers fish in the Pacific Ocean, Minister of Agriculture Chen Junne-jih (陳駿季) said.
The program, which is to begin next year, would use AI to integrate satellite imagery and oceanographic data to find fish, Chen said at an event celebrating National Fishers’ Day in Taipei on Tuesday.
The Ministry of Agriculture and the National Science and Technology Council’s joint program would enhance fishers’ ability to find tuna and mackerel in the high seas and predict yields ahead of time, he said.
Photo: CNA
Fishers need to make greater use of technology amid the challenges posed by climate change on global fisheries, he added.
Taiwan’s fishing trawlers last year reported a gross income of NT$96.5 billion, a worrisome sign of decline, Chen said.
Historically, fishing trawlers had an annual income of between NT$95 billion and NT$110 billion, while the fisheries industry typically generated NT$350 billion annually, he said.
The program would also monitor fisheries in Taiwan’s near seas, he said, adding that data about inland fisheries and fish farms would gradually be incorporated into the database.
Chen did not give a timeline for when the system would be available for fisheries, saying that it is still in early development.
Taiwan leads in data on Central and Western Pacific fisheries, Fisheries Agency Director-General Wang Mao-chen (王茂城) said.
Foreign partners in the program would likely include Australia and island nations in the Southern Pacific, although Taiwanese fishers would have priority access, he said.
The agency does not rule out commercializing access to the predictive data, should the technology prove successful, he added.
A Fisheries Agency spokesperson said the ministry is working on an AI-driven ecological monitoring and digital governance system that encompasses aquaculture, high seas fisheries management and harbor administration.
The event also awarded 12 exemplary fishery workers, including Wu Tien-nan (吳天南), a 95-year-old man from Tainan who became a fisher when he was 13.
Wu’s career as an aquafarmer, which focuses on prawns, sea bass, milkfish and groupers, is a microcosm of the sector’s history in Taiwan, agency officials said.
Wu received special commendation for his role in preserving the craft of bamboo raft making, old fishers’ rhymes for counting fries during trading and promoting educational programs that allow children to experience fishing village life, they said.
Wu said he still inspects his grow-out ponds daily.
Two of the fishery workers who received commendations were women.
Yu Chin-feng (于錦鳳), who designed a cutting-edge fish farm in Kaohsiung that utilizes smart technologies, liquefied natural gas-cooled water and cocktails of beneficial microbes, was awarded for introducing innovation in the industry.
Lei Xi-ying (雷細英), a naturalized Taiwanese national from China, was commended for holding classes on cooking fish at home to popularize seafood and charitable works in Yulin County.

Unknown Publisher
