6 Signs Your Venting Is Straining Your Relationships
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
11:00:02 UTC
20:00:02 KST

Twenty minutes ago, you called a friend to complain about something your boss said. Since then, you’ve reconstructed his exact tone—don’t you hate it when someone says “interesting” like that?—supplied three years of relevant backstory, and pulled up six Slack messages that prove this wasn’t an isolated incident. Your friend has contributed the occasional “ugh” and “wow.” You are nowhere near finished.
Sometimes, it just feels good to say the petty, uncharitable thing out loud to someone who won't forward it to HR. A venting session can be validating, cathartic, and even productive if it helps you figure out your next steps.
“Venting is discrete,” says Jenny Martin, a psychologist and founder of Gemstone Wellness, a trauma-informed practice in Chicago. “It has a beginning, a middle, and an end.”
But venting can also keep you stuck—not to mention, exhaust the person listening. The distinction isn’t whether you complain, get worked up, or talk for a long time. It’s whether the conversation eventually moves somewhere, and whether the other person still feels like a participant rather than an audience member trapped in the front row.
So how can you tell when blowing off steam has started straining your relationships? Therapists—who listen to people vent for a living—say there are a few consistent tells.
It’s a monologue, not a dialogue
Genuine, healthy venting isn’t one-sided. You talk; the other person asks a question, winces in solidarity, or says the same thing happened to them. Maybe they offer a perspective you hadn’t considered. Then you keep going from there. (There are, after all, far more exciting things to discuss, like the tacos and drinks you’ll be enjoying after work on Friday.)
When venting starts straining a relationship, that dynamic changes. “It’s more just a monologue as opposed to a dialogue,” says Stephanie Mahalec, a therapist in Los Angeles. When the listener asks a question, it registers as an interruption—and any advice is flicked away like lint from a sleeve. If they try to share a similar experience, you quickly steer the conversation back to yours.
That doesn’t mean every vent needs to be perfectly balanced. Sometimes a friend gets 45 minutes because their day was objectively worse. Look at the pattern instead: When you finish talking, could you summarize anything your friend said—or only what you told them?
The conversation has no off-ramp
A useful vent has an ending. You get it out, feel understood, and eventually move on, perhaps to the considerably more entertaining gossip your friend has been waiting to share.
That beginning-middle-end structure Martin describes can be easiest to spot in reverse: The listener keeps trying to supply the ending, and the speaker keeps reopening the case.
Perhaps your friend offers a natural exit—“Well, at least you don’t have to see him until Monday”—and you respond by introducing an entirely new piece of evidence. They try to change the subject, and three minutes later, you’re back to your boss. The conversation ends only because somebody has to attend a meeting, make dinner, or claim an urgent need to wash their hair.
One complaint turns into every complaint
You begin with the dishes that have been in the sink all week—but soon you’re talking about the laundry, the trash, and the fact that nobody seemed to care what restaurant you wanted to go to on your birthday.
Listen for two words: always and never. “You’re definitely talking about the past, because you’re not talking about the dish in the sink anymore,” says Matt Cartwright, a therapist in New York. What started as one irritation has opened the file drawer containing every related grievance going back years.
That expansion makes the problem feel bigger and harder to solve. A friend might have useful thoughts about today’s inconsiderate comment; there’s considerably less they can do with “This always happens to me, and nobody has ever respected me.”
When you notice one complaint expanding into a sweeping conclusion, Cartwright suggests pausing and telling yourself—or the person you’re venting to—“The story I’m telling myself is…” For example: “The story I’m telling myself is that because the dish is still in the sink, what I asked for didn’t matter.” Admittedly, it doesn’t exactly roll off the tongue. But that’s part of why it works: The phrase forces you to separate the dirty dish from the much larger case you’ve built around it.
You feel worse than when you started
A good vent doesn’t have to produce a solution. Cartwright describes venting as a “quick release”—sometimes feeling heard is the entire point. But ideally, something has shifted by the end: You’re calmer, clearer about why you’re upset, or have a better sense of what you want to do next.
Unproductive venting does the opposite. Cartwright says it can “activate the memory bank,” turning one offense into a reminder of every similar slight. You replay what happened until it feels freshly committed, then remember three incidents that make it even worse. That doesn’t release frustration; it exacerbates it.
The person listening can intensify the spiral, too. “Now we’ve got two people who can feel flooded, and depending on the dynamics of the relationship, it just feeds each other,” Cartwright says. Psychologists sometimes call this co-rumination: dwelling on a problem and its negative emotions together. Research suggests that it can make people feel closer while also being associated with greater anxiety.
If the listener matches every complaint with a more outraged one—“He said what? I would never put up with that”—the two of you may keep winding each other up. By the time you hang up, your boss hasn’t merely irritated you; he’s become a threat to justice everywhere.
Check in with your body afterward. Has your jaw unclenched? Do you understand the problem better? Or are you pacing faster and composing an email that absolutely should not be sent until morning—if ever?
You’re sharing at a 10 when the relationship is at a 2
Sometimes it isn’t the complaint itself that makes a conversation uncomfortable. It’s the gap between what you’re disclosing and how well you know the person hearing it.
“You’re giving information and providing detail that’s at an intimacy level of 10 when the relationship is actually at an acquaintance level of 2,” Martin says. The coworker you’ve eaten lunch with twice might be up for hearing that your divorce has been difficult. They may not be ready for a scene-by-scene account of your most brutal argument.
That mismatch can leave the other person frozen, with no idea how to react or respond. Are they supposed to offer advice? Ask questions? Hug you beside the office microwave?
Sharing with a near-stranger can feel surprisingly safe, Martin says. Their opinion may carry fewer stakes than the reaction of someone you love. The problem is that disclosure can outpace the relationship: You’re revealing more intimate information much faster than the connection itself is deepening. Before going further, consider how this person has responded to smaller disclosures—and whether the relationship is ready for something bigger.
People have stopped asking how you are
Most people won’t announce that your venting has become too much—but there will be signs.
Friends who once asked how you were feeling may switch to safer questions: “What are you doing this weekend? How’s the house project? Have you watched that show?” If the conversation edges toward an emotional subject, they quickly guide it elsewhere.
You might also notice that someone who used to spend time with you one-on-one now prefers group plans. “People want to have buffers around these people so that they’re not cornered,” Martin says. Or your calls increasingly go unanswered—and when you do connect, the other person seems ready to hang up before you’ve said anything at all.
None of these signs proves that your venting is the reason. People get busy, distracted, and overwhelmed by their own lives. But if several relationships seem to be shifting in the same direction, it’s worth getting curious rather than defensive. Are people avoiding you—or a role they’ve come to expect they’ll have to play?
How to vent without turning a friend into a complaint department
You don’t need to stop venting, nor does every complaint need to become a model of emotionally evolved communication. Sometimes the unhinged version is exactly what needs to come out first. The trick, Cartwright says, is being clear about what you want from the exchange.
For example: “Can I complain for 10 minutes? I don’t need advice—I just need you to hear how irritating this was.” Or: “Can I tell you what happened and get your honest take?” As Cartwright puts it: “Do you have a minute? Because I need to vent.” That lets your friend know whether you’re looking for validation, perspective, or help deciding what to do.
The time limit is useful, too. Mahalec describes healthy venting as time-limited—not because frustration expires at minute 11, but because a time boundary gives the conversation an off-ramp. When you reach it, take a breather. You can always ask whether your friend has the energy to keep going.

====================================================================================================

‘They destroy, we build’: Gazans rebuild their homes out of mud and rubble
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

Next to his destroyed home in Khan Younis, Fayez Abu Shamala, 76, a Palestinian academic and former mayor of Khan Younis, is building again.
Abu Shamala salvaged usable stones from the debris of destroyed buildings, collected and repaired them, and, with the help of his family, built a small house. Instead of cement, unavailable anywhere in Gaza, he used clay to hold the stones together.
He then fixed pieces of nylon over the walls to protect them from rain. He also recovered some windows and doors from the wreckage, modified them, and installed them in what is now his home.
“I am here on my land,” Abu Shamala said. “To my right is the house I built, and to my left is the house the Israeli army destroyed. They are the destroyers, and we are the builders.”
Abu Shamlah has slept in a mudhouse before, after he was displaced from his village in what is now the city of Ashkelon during the 1948 Nakba, when his family was forced from their land and lived for years in mud houses in the Gaza Strip. More than seven decades later, the cycle is being repeated across Gaza.
As Israel blocks the entry of cement, steel, and all conventional building materials, classifying them as “dual-use” items that could serve a military purpose, Abu Shamala and others across Gaza are constructing mud houses to brace for the cold and rainy season. By October 2025, UNOSAT satellite imagery found approximately 81 percent of all structures in the Gaza Strip had been damaged, with more than 123,000 destroyed outright. The UN estimates that the destruction generated 61 million tonnes of rubble. With large-scale reconstruction at a standstill, Palestinians are rebuilding with whatever they can salvage.
Alternatives to the alternatives
On August 15, the first two-story building in the Gaza Strip constructed entirely without banned building materials was unveiled. The building was constructed of steel rebar and aluminum on the inside and Jerusalem limestone on the outside. All the materials were extracted from the rubble.
The building, constructed by the Al-Rimal Company in Gaza City, will be used to run international organizations’ operations, including receiving and storing aid and overseeing its distribution across the Strip. Three engineers from the company planned and built the structure in collaboration with several professionals, technicians, and workers. It took them four months to complete.
“If it weren’t for the occupation, we would not have built this building,” said Younis Abu Mueilaq, one of the engineers who supervised the construction, meaning that the challenges imposed on Gaza ultimately forced the development of new and unprecedented approaches to rebuilding.
Al-Rimal Al-Taybeh is a partner of international organizations that operate warehouses across the Gaza Strip. As the war intensified and many of those warehouses were destroyed, the organizations began looking for alternatives once the situation became relatively calmer following the signing of the October 2025 ceasefire.
According to Abu Mueilaq, several alternative warehouses were established to replace those destroyed during the war, and as the company’s work with international organizations increased, an administrative building became necessary.
Israel continues to refuse to allow in the building materials needed for reconstruction, as well as the heavy machinery needed to remove the rubble, which has generated 61 million tonnes of debris — about as much as 15 Great Pyramids of Giza or 25 Eiffel Towers by volume, according to the UN. As a result, people in Gaza are turning to alternatives, some of which date back hundreds of years, such as mud houses, while others involve developing new methods that are expensive and beyond individuals’ means. Such projects are instead undertaken by companies and institutions, such as Al-Rimal Al-Taybeh, which constructed this building.
The building would ordinarily have been constructed with cement, Abu Mueilaq says, but since it remains unavailable due to Israel’s blockade, the team turned to construction metals recovered from destroyed buildings and modified them for reuse.
The external structure was mainly made of steel rebar fastened together with bolts. But when it came time to cover the structure with sheets of metal on the outside, as an alternative to cement, none was to be found.
“That was when we began looking for alternatives to the alternatives,” Abu Mueilaq said. “We started looking for whatever we could use. We found that there was a technique used in modern architecture in places such as Dubai, where the steel structure is covered with aluminum.”
Suitable aluminum was also unavailable in Gaza, either, so they eventually landed on another solution: Jerusalem limestone salvaged from destroyed buildings, cleaned and reused, to cover the structure. Each stone, five centimeters thick, was drilled at its four corners and fitted with a metal bracket to attach it to the steel structure.
“We placed one stone on top of another and secured them properly, and this beautiful structure emerged as a result of the hard work of the teams,” Abu Mueilaq said.
Once the exterior structure was resolved, the interior presented its own challenge.
Wood, cement, and suitable aluminum were all unavailable, but the team found aluminum used to manufacture kitchen cabinets — a material that had accumulated in warehouses because the other components needed to manufacture aluminum kitchens were unavailable. The aluminum was used to divide the building internally and create walls and partitions.
Abu Mueilaq says the project’s cost was extremely high, much like the cost of living in Gaza, he says, which increased many times over compared to before the genocide.
He also emphasizes that this experiment isn’t easily replicable. The materials used were recovered from within Gaza and cannot easily be salvaged or replaced.
“What we are using now cannot be used again later,” Abu Mueilaq explained.
The building, nevertheless, gave people something beyond shelter. “It gave people hope,” Abu Mueilaq said. “Hope that Gaza has the skilled workers, thinkers, and professionals capable of rebuilding their homeland if they are provided with the necessary resources.”
‘We are the builders’
Beyond the question of large-scale reconstruction, Palestinians have also resorted to ancient methods of building shelters that had been all but defunct for generations: using mud and clay to build houses.
Abu Shamala is one of them. The house he built from salvaged stones and clay is not large enough to accommodate his entire family, but it is a shelter. Still, it is a far cry away from what was once his family home of 500 square meters, made up of four stories that housed an extended family of over 20 people.
But Abu Shamala also worries about the approaching rainy season, since rain can dissolve the mud walls, and he cannot yet predict what will happen to the structure in such conditions.
“Obtaining clay is not straightforward either,” he explained. Khan Younis, where he lives, is divided into two areas: the eastern part, where clay can be located, and the western al-Mawasi area, which is sandy. The problem is that the clay-bearing eastern region is controlled by the Israeli military, beyond the so-called “Yellow Line” that demarcates the parts of Gaza divided between Israeli and Hamas control.
“Obtaining clay can sometimes come at the cost of lives,” Abu Shamala said. But despite the difficulties, he says building the house has given him a sense of movement toward stability, particularly after realizing that the Israeli occupation will not initiate or enable reconstruction and is instead increasing its restrictions on it.
“We are here, confronting the blockade and the aggression, trying to create life,” he said. “We are rebuilding our lives with our weak and limited resources, but we remain steadfast on our land.”
Abu Shamala says Israel accuses Palestinians of being destroyers, gesturing at the carnage surrounding him. “Here is a clear picture of who destroys and who builds. We build, and the enemy destroys.”
“This is the evidence of our love for our land,” he continued. “Of remaining steadfast on the land where we were born and raised, which gives back to us in equal measure to our affinity for it.”
He says he is part of a people that refuses to die and refuses to disappear.
“Despite the destruction, the bombing, the blockade, the deprivation of water and food, and the prevention of reconstruction, and despite all the crimes committed against us by the Israeli enemy, this is a people that builds its land with the barest of resources,” he said.

What do we know about the fatal US bombing of a wedding in Iran’s Sirik?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
10:57:16 UTC
19:57:16 KST

What do we know about the fatal US bombing of a wedding in Iran’s Sirik?
A residential building and a telecommunications tower were struck overnight, as Iran and the US launched more strikes over the control of Strait of Hormuz.
Tehran, Iran – The city of Kuhestak, located in southern Iran’s Sirik County in Hormozgan province, close to the Strait of Hormuz, was the target of multiple overnight attacks by the United States military, with local sources and authorities saying a wedding ceremony was struck.
The Hormozgan governor’s office on Wednesday identified four victims as four-year-old Amir Ali Karimi, 16-year-old Mohammad Malahi, 43-year-old Kolsoum Malahi and 43-year-old Zarkhatoun Taheri. More than 60 others were wounded, some seriously.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4UN watchdog urges access to Iran nuclear sites over proliferation concerns
- list 2 of 4Iran says US bombed a wedding party in Sirik, killing at least four people
- list 3 of 4‘We had an ordinary life’: Iran fisherwoman navigates uncertainty of war
- list 4 of 4Iran, US exchange new attacks: Who was hit in latest strikes?
Tim Hawkins, a spokesperson for US Central Command (CENTCOM), said they were aware of reports of civilian casualties “originated from Iranian state media”.
“The US military never targets civilians, unlike the IRGC,” he said, in reference to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
But while the operational details behind the strikes remain unclear, numerous videos and images from the area, witness accounts and official reports indicate that multiple projectiles hit Kuhestak, some to deadly effect.
Footage showed that several projectiles struck a telecommunications tower located near the city’s shoreline and destroyed it, with some locals saying they believed drones were among the weapons used. Based on fragments found in Kuhestak, defence experts say it might be a variant of the AGM-84K SLAM-ER, which manufacturer Boeing describes as an advanced precision-guided, air-launched cruise missile with “surgical strike capability”.
Wednesday morning’s footage, taken from some distance from the telecom tower, shows at least one direct hit to the roof of the building where the wedding was taking place.
More videos, released by locals and state media, showed partial destruction and debris inside the building, and electricity going out in the area. Women’s and children’s slippers could be seen scattered around. Several other adjacent residential buildings also sustained damage.
A state television reporter said three US missiles were used in the attack, with one penetrating through the roof and creating a 1.5-metre (5-foot) hole in the ground.
A man identified as Ali Malahi, the owner of the targeted building where his daughter’s wedding was taking place, told state television that people inside were all civilians.
State TV footage from a hospital in the area showed several wounded children and their families receiving medical care.
A young local man wounded in the attack said he and others were heading towards the house when they heard jets flying above, and the bombs caused massive explosions while they were arriving.
“Many young children and women were horribly wounded,” he said from the hospital bed.
A woman with bloodied hands said in a video released by state-linked SNN that she was there at the scene and could confirm that people present at the scene were civilians.
“This house was by no means close to any military site,” she said, adding that it appeared the munitions were directly targeting the building.
The Iranian Red Crescent Society said the incident was thoroughly documented, as it released several images from the site of the attack and the children who were injured.
It wrote to the Office of the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court, seeking legal action against the perpetrators of the “grave” attack.
Other prominent attacks on civilians
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs said the strikes in Kuhestak complete the “catalogue of atrocities against the nation of Iran” by the US.
“This cruelty cannot be separated from the chain of atrocities that preceded it in Minab, Lamerd, Qeshm and elsewhere nor from the strikes on military targets that were dressed in deceptive justifications,” spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei wrote on X.
“More dangerous than the bomb itself is the normalisation of bombing; and more dangerous than silence is the conversion of silence into legitimacy,” he said.
In Minab, also located in Hormozgan province, the deadliest strike of the war in terms of civilian casualties largely destroyed an elementary school packed with children on the first day of the war on February 28. The attack killed about 156 people, mostly schoolchildren, as well as teachers, parents and others.
Despite evidence that its Tomahawk missiles were used in the attack, the US military has refused to release findings from its investigation. CENTCOM commander Brad Cooper claimed the school was located “on an active IRGC cruise missile base”.
In the southern Fars province’s city of Lamerd, evidence and witness accounts pointed to a missile strike on a sports hall being used by a women’s volleyball team on the first day of the war, killing 21 people, including four children.
While CENTCOM denied responsibility and accused Iran, investigations by The New York Times, BBC and independent analysts concluded that a US Precision Strike Missile (PrSM) was responsible for the destruction.
The munition was designed to explode midair, scattering thousands of tungsten pellets that could claim casualties and deal damage to buildings and vehicles in a large area.
During over six months of war on Iran, the US and Israel have also struck critical infrastructure like oil and gas facilities, fuel depots, steel and petrochemical factories, airports, ports and bridges, as well as power installations, medical centres and water facilities.
More than 3,500 Iranians have been killed since the start of the war, including more than 50 during the 60-day truce amid renewed fighting in July, according to authorities.

Newly discovered ‘demon cave fish’ hid out in Alabama military installation for 40 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
10:57:07 UTC
19:57:07 KST

Some hills in northern Alabama are burial mounds from the Copena people who lived there 2,000 years ago. Some contain decommissioned nerve gas from the cold war. But one holds a portal to the underworld—a low-slung knoll in a restricted military installation leads to a cramped but sprawling limestone network called Bobcat Cave, where scientists have discovered a strange, eyeless creature they’ve dubbed the demon cave fish.
The cave isn’t exactly welcoming to human visitors. “You’re stooped to hands and knees, crawling, and depending on the water level, you could be in neck-deep,” says Matthew L. Niemiller, a cave biologist at the University of Alabama in Huntsville. But because the system is a stronghold for the endangered Alabama cave shrimp, monitoring teams have explored the cave nearly every month since the early 1990s.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Despite this scrutiny, the demon cave fish was discovered only recently and completely by chance. On a routine survey in February 2025, Niemiller slipped in the red Alabama mud and fell headlong into a deep pool of water—and found himself face-to-face with a creature he didn’t recognize. This fish had a humped back and a slightly duckbilled snout, and, unlike the slightly more colorful Southern cave fish already known to inhabit the system, it was so ghostly white it looked blue under their headlamps. “It’s a shock and kind of embarrassing, in a way,” that it escaped notice for so long, says Niemiller, lead author of a paper presenting the new species and genus in Scientific Reports.
Genetic analyses suggest the demon cave fish and the Southern cave fish aren’t closely related and made their way underground separately: it appears they lost their vision because of different mutations. The study authors say it’s surprising to see two cave fish species living in not just the same cave system but the same pools and chambers. Whereas other cohabitating cave fish are like neighbors, the demon and Southern cave fish are like roommates—if those roommates had been trapped together for millions of years and potentially snacked on each other’s children.
Niemiller and his team have named the new species Demogorgonichthys arcanus, a wink to the otherworldly creature that emerged in a secret federal lab in the Netflix series Stranger Things. The finding is a humbling reminder of how much biodiversity remains undocumented even in the best-explored caves, says Suzanne McGaugh, an ecologist and cave fish expert at the University of Minnesota, who wasn’t involved in the new study. “We owe a debt of gratitude to them for their discovery,” she says.

Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Pakistan advance steps for Mecca pact
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
10:53:46 UTC
19:53:46 KST

Breadcrumb
Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan agree to establish secretariat under Mecca pact
Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan have agreed to establish a general secretariat in Saudi Arabia under the Mecca Mutual Defence Agreement, the Saudi Foreign Ministry said Monday.
The secretariat will initially be headed by a Pakistani secretary-general for three years.
A joint statement issued by the Political and Strategic Defence Committee of the Mecca Agreement following its first meeting in Istanbul said the three countries would work to "enhance their defence capabilities and the cohesion of their armed forces through strong cooperation in the defence industries sector and the development of joint production and technologies".
According to the statement, the three countries reaffirmed their determination to work together under the Mecca Agreement to achieve sustainable peace and stability in their region by "supporting efforts aimed at de-escalation and restraint in a way that encourages peaceful solutions to crises".
The statement said the three countries had agreed to take further steps "to institutionalise their cooperation under the Mecca Agreement in a manner that strengthens their solidarity, ensures the credibility and effectiveness of collective deterrence and defence, and contributes to regional efforts and cooperative security aimed at achieving a just, comprehensive and lasting peace".
Earlier on Monday, 31 August, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said during a news conference that the Mecca Mutual Defence Agreement would gradually strengthen stability in the region and reduce uncertainty.
"With this agreement, a process of testing a new security and cooperative architecture has begun in our region," he said.
Fidan stressed that joint action by countries in the region for security, stability, prosperity and lasting peace, and institutionalising the steps they take in this direction, "has become an urgent need".
Door open for expansion
The Turkish minister also said the Mecca Mutual Defence Agreement was built based on keeping the door open for expansion.
"Thanks to the Mecca Defence Alliance, we will witness increasing consolidation of stability in the region and a decline in uncertainty," he stressed.
Fidan also said they were working on a roadmap for procedures for joining the alliance.
"The alliance was essentially formed for expansion. But, in the first stage, the foundations must be properly established, and its institutionalisation must also be achieved properly. Both Saudi Arabia and Pakistan are very keen on this, as are we," he remarked.
He noted the three parties agreed, on the one hand, to establish a strong and institutional foundation capable of dealing with problems and bringing stability, peace and prosperity to the region. On the other hand, they agreed to expand the alliance, noting that this would happen in stages.
The Turkish foreign minister stressed that any potential ally joining the alliance should join a structure with good infrastructure that is already established and operating efficiently.
"We are currently trying, together, to complete the establishment phase, which is the most difficult part," he added. "We will see this alliance gradually lead to greater consolidation of stability in the region, and uncertainty will decline. The positions of the parties will become clearer".
He noted that a decline in uncertainty would create an environment of stability in which investment could increase and further development could be achieved.
Netanyahu: 'a common enemy of humanity'
Meanwhile, regarding Israel considering Turkey a "strategic threat", Fidan said, "Since [Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu entered the election phase, he, his government and his supporters have increasingly adopted rhetoric targeting Turkey, and positions targeting our president [Recep Tayyip Erdogan] and some of our colleagues have also been issued by [the Israeli government]".
"First, one thing must be emphasised. Netanyahu, who has become a common enemy of humanity, the international community and security, and I stress this, Netanyahu, this criminal, the perpetrator of genocide, is not human in the true sense," he continued. "Netanyahu, his mentality and the group committing genocide and acting alongside him constitute a threat not only to Turkey but also to global security as a whole. It is a major mistake to think of this as a problem concerning Turkey alone".
Fidan further called on the international community to perform the task it has not yet carried out and "stop this criminal, the perpetrator of genocide, and prevent him from continuing to harm the region, Israel, the Jewish people and the entire world".
"This criminal who enjoys shedding the blood of Palestinians and Muslims must be stopped. The continuation of this is also causing serious harm to Israel, to the Palestinians, of course, and to the region," he added.
Fidan said that, in light of Netanyahu's statements, he did not want to establish a Palestinian state or end the occupation continuing in the countries of the region.
"He wants the continuation of the approach based on genocide and occupation and the approach that puts regional security and international security at risk. This is now not only a major threat to us but also to the entire region and the international community. The international system must confront this threat, Netanyahu's threat," the Turkish official remarked.
Earlier on Monday, the first meeting of the Political and Strategic Defence Committee established under the Mecca Mutual Defence Agreement between Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia began in Istanbul.
Turkey is hosting the first meeting of the committee, which includes the foreign and defence ministers and the chiefs of staff of the three countries, to provide strategic direction for activities to be carried out under the agreement.
The meeting began after participants posed for a group photograph.
The Turkish delegation includes Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, Defence Minister Yasar Guler and Chief of General Staff Selcuk Bayraktaroglu.
Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan, Defence Minister Khalid bin Salman and Chief of General Staff Fayyad bin Hamed Al-Ruwaili represent Saudi Arabia.
The Pakistani delegation includes Foreign Minister Muhammad Ishaq Dar, Federal Defence Minister Khawaja Muhammad Asif and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir.
The three countries are concerned about the military positions of Israel and Iran as the United States faces challenges in containing regional unrest that has caused a global energy crisis.
Mutual defence
On 7 August, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif signed the Mutual Defence Agreement in Mecca.
The agreement came as part of defence cooperation aimed at strengthening commitments to maintaining peace, stability and prosperity at the regional and global levels, based on the principle of burden-sharing and a shared understanding of security.
The agreement aims to strengthen collective deterrence against any act of aggression and stipulates that an armed attack against any of the three countries would be considered an attack against all of them.

That diamond ring on your finger could be enabling Gaza genocide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
10:53:12 UTC
19:53:12 KST

Breadcrumb
That diamond ring on your finger could be enabling Gaza genocide
Every diamond has a story. Yours likely began with a child knee-deep in Congolese mud, digging for stones that armed groups tax and smuggle. It passed through Dubai’s gleaming towers, where one billion carats of diamonds were exchanged last year – none mined in the UAE. It was cut in Surat, India, where exploited workers, prone to suicide, earn less than $5 a day polishing nine out of ten of the world’s gems.
It was certified “conflict-free” by the Kimberly Process (KP), which, over two decades, has found only two countries (Angola and Sierra Leone) worthy of the “blood diamond” label, while other countries have falsified certificates to circumvent the process.
That precious stone ended up in Tel Aviv, the fifth largest exporter of diamonds worldwide, where the Israeli Diamond Exchange, still shuttered by the war with Iran, has allegedly pumped roughly $1 billion annually into the military complex that perpetrated genocide in Gaza.
This is not a supply chain. It is a war machine engineered by a triad of occupation powers (Israel, India and the UAE) running on African blood.
US-Israel war on Iran
The Iran war exposed this architecture’s fragility but also reflected resilience. Missiles struck Israel’s Ramat Gan in 2025 and in April 2026, directly impacting the IDE's ability to continue trading. In March 2026, Dubai International Airport shut down for 48 hours, directly impacting the Dubai Multi Commodities Centre (DMCC) headed by Ahmed Bin Sulayem, who also presided over the KP in 2025, and through which major tender houses usually host auctions in the diamond sector.
Dubai reported a significant recovery in July 2026, suggesting record trade volumes, but the continued closure of the Strait of Hormuz and the expansion of the war is expected to impact on the market.
70% of India’s $30 billion gem sector, which routes through Dubai, also faced regional disruption. By March 2026, the $350 million Surat Diamond Bourse was virtually empty, with only about 250 of the over four thousand offices operational.
The IDE withdrew from the World Federation of Diamond Bourses in April 2025, before its closure under bombardment. Yet the financial architecture of genocide persists: for decades, the IDE poured approximately $1 billion per annum into Israel’s military and security apparatus.
The diamond sector and the war machine share the same financial ecosystem.
Israeli economist Shir Hever testified at the Russell Tribunal on Palestine in 2010, stating that “the Israeli diamond industry contributes about $1 billion annually to the Israeli military and security industries… every time somebody buys a diamond that was exported from Israel, some of that money ends up in the Israeli military.”
The Palestinian Boycott Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) National Committee also confirms that Israel’s illegal occupation is funded by the diamond industry.
The blood diamonds complete their circuit in Gaza. Extracted from Congolese conflict zones, laundered through compliant neighbours, certified “clean” by the KP, monetised in Tel Aviv – they become the drones, surveillance systems, and ordnance raining down on Palestinians.
The KP has become their moral laundry service, with manipulated certification masking the reality of carnage.
Feeding the occupation machine
Over 80 countries are signatories to the KP, collectively representing 99% of the global rough diamond trade, yet it is not a legally binding treaty. Its definition of “conflict diamonds” - restricted to gems financing rebel movements - completely voids state violence, occupation, genocide.
The DRC, despite hosting active militias including M23 in North Kivu, has never been suspended. Neither has Israel. Countries that seek to hold Israel accountable at the International Court of Justice (ICJ) for genocide in Gaza, such as South Africa and Namibia, continue to trade stones, conveniently dissociating the diamond trade from war crimes.
The KP relies on self-certification rather than independent verification. Diamonds are laundered through countries with robust security ties to Israel before entering global markets as “clean”.
Israeli penetration of African diamond markets operates through politically connected traders and offshore architecture. A now-sanctioned Israeli-connected trader who secured exclusive DRC diamond export control through the Kabila regime allegedly swapped weapons for mining rights; 2017 US Treasury sanctions accused him of cheating Congo of $1.4 billion. A Dutch court fined his shell companies 25.8 million in March 2026.
Another Israeli-connected trader, convicted in 2021 for bribing Guinean officials, has been linked to DRC deals while reportedly funding the Israeli military’s Givati Brigade (accused of war crimes in Gaza). The pattern is systematic: access minerals at below-market rates, extract profit through tax havens, feed the occupation machine.
Conflict free
The global diamond trade triad – India, Israel and the UAE – has penetrated the KP. Ahmed Bin Sulayem chaired the KP on numerous occasions, first in 2015 and subsequently in 2024 and 2025. India currently chairs the KP for 2026, under the theme “3Cs” Credibility Compliance, and Consumer Confidence,” a play on the 4 Cs in diamond grading.
India’s appointment came after Qatar ceded its candidacy following Israeli objection.
In May 2026, India hosted the KP Intersessional Meeting in Mumbai, where Chair Suchindra Misra emphasised “supporting peace”, while failing to mention state violence, occupation or militias.
India’s dominance of the diamond market stems from processing 90% of the world’s diamonds. But it operates parallel to its occupation of Kashmir, where more than 700,000 troops enforce military rule. Human rights organisations have documented systematic extrajudicial killings, torture, enforced disappearances, and collective punishment, mirroring Israel’s conduct in occupied Palestine, solidified by a Defence Cooperation Agreement signed in November 2025.
The UAE has become the world’s largest diamond trading hub despite having no mines, the commercial nexus connecting Indian processing with Israeli financing and African resources. It is also the triangle’s logistics backbone.
As far back as 2021, Amnesty International alleged UAE complicity in the illicit diamond trade in the Central African Republic.
This triad – India’s Kashmir lockdown, Israel’s Gaza genocide, the UAE’s Sudan war – creates a convergence that transcends commerce. All three profit from weak regulation and manipulation of the KP’s narrow definitions When DRC conflict diamonds pass through Dubai to Surat and Tel Aviv, they traverse an occupation network with a shared interest: maintaining the fiction that these stones are “conflict-free”
A moral question
Amid the chaos, African states are recalibrating. Anglo-American has taken cumulative impairments on De Beers totalling approximately $6.8 billion across three write-downs - slashing the unit’s book value by roughly 75%. On 17 July 2026, Botswana confirmed Anglo-American has selected the “Global Diamond Consortium” as preferred bidder for De Beers, targeting Q4 2026.
Botswana, holding a 15% stake and pre-emptive rights, is weighing whether to exercise them alone, partner with the consortium, or bring in a third party. Angola seeks a 20-30% stake; Namibia has expressed interest. An African-led consortium could command 40% of global production.
This would fundamentally alter the trade. De Beers’ supply chain currently feeds Israeli cutting houses. African control could redirect rough diamonds to local beneficiation, accelerating the IDE’s collapse and subjecting Israeli diamond interests to African oversight.
The crisis is consuming the industry from within. In July 2026, De Beers idled its Venetia mine in South Africa – the country’s largest, employing 4,400 people – just three years after a $2.3 billion underground expansion meant to secure production until 2045.
With Voorspoed already closed in 2018, De Beers now has no operational diamond mines in South Africa. Alrosa suspended mining at Severalmaz for three months; Storm Mountain Diamonds’ Finsch mine entered business rescue, with South Africa’s National Union of Mineworkers warning nearly 1,800 jobs at risk.
The blood diamond economy is consuming its own foundations.
For Africa, this is not merely an economic question but a moral one. If its minerals fortify occupation and genocide, resource sovereignty becomes inseparable from Palestinian justice. The stones leaving African soil, diverted through Dubai, processed in Tel Aviv, bear the invisible scars of exploitation and war.
The Kimberly Process affirmed conflict-free diamonds. It is time to ask: free from whose conflicts and at whose expense?
The Kimberly Process Secretariat was contacted by email for comment on the concerns raised in this opinion piece. No response has been received.

Spain calls for probe into reports government agency blamed Morocco for Ceuta migrant influx
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
10:51:24 UTC
19:51:24 KST

Madrid demanded an explanation from its own police after an explosive leaked police report suggested that Moroccan security forces were involved in transporting and pushing migrants towards the border.
Spain's police chief, Francisco Pardo, has told Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska that there is no police report attributing to Moroccan security forces the planning or execution of the events in Ceuta at the end of July.
The response comes after Marlaska asked police to clarify a leaked report in which Spanish police blamed Moroccan security forces for orchestrating a mass entry of migrants to the enclave of Ceuta last week, ministry sources said on Wednesday.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said on Monday that Morocco was not responsible, instead accusing Israel, Russia and the far right of spreading disinformation about the mass entry of around 70,000 migrants into Ceuta.
Sánchez told Cadena SER radio that "no intelligence service with which the Spanish government normally cooperates" had suggested "any involvement in one way or another of the Moroccan authorities."
Online newspaper El Español reported on Tuesday that Spain's National Centre for Immigration and Borders (CENIF) said the incident "was guided by Moroccan security forces...with an objective other than migration" in an explosive leaked report.
Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska demanded police chief Francisco Pardo to check and clarify the information, which was reportedly sent to a judge collecting information on the incident, according to ministry sources.
In his comments, Grande-Marlaska implies the Spanish government found out through media reports about allegations, which would put in question Madrid's narrative that the influx was mostly led by social reports and amplified by human traffickers.
"Any such information should have immediately been made available to the National Security Council...and to other bodies with powers in this field," the minister said in his letter to the police chief, sent after the newspaper report was published.
More than 70,000 migrants entered the small Spanish territory in north Africa on 30-31 July, swimming or crossing on foot from neighbouring Morocco in an unprecedented rush that left scores dead.
Some analysts have suggested the crisis may have been a message sent to Spain by Morocco over the disputed Western Sahara after Sánchez visited Rabat's historic enemy Algeria in July.
The Western Sahara is a former Spanish colony largely controlled by Morocco but claimed by the Algerian-backed pro-independence Polisario Front.
Political flashpoint
The influx triggered fresh tensions within the European Union over the sensitive topic of immigration and dealt a blow to one of its main achievements, the Schengen free-travel zone.
Italy's right-wing government imposed border checks for one month on travellers from Spain after the crisis, with Madrid reciprocating a week later.
Both governments announced a 15-day extension of the controls on Monday.
Although the vast majority of the migrants returned to Morocco within hours, thousands remain in the tiny territory of 18 square kilometres and 84,000 inhabitants, many living rough on the streets.
Their fate has become a major political flashpoint, with the conservative and far-right opposition demanding that all those who entered Ceuta, including minors, be returned to Morocco.
Ceuta residents have held regular demonstrations over what they say are security and hygiene problems linked to the influx.
Sánchez said that 6,000 spaces at reception centres would soon be available in the territory for migrants, whose status must be verified by the Spanish authorities before any possible return to Morocco.
He also pledged an additional €168 million in aid for Ceuta to respond to the crisis.
At the end of August, Madrid asked the European Commission (EC) for the support from Frontex, Europol and the European Union Agency for Asylum (EUAA) to assist with the screening and processing of migrants who are staying irregularly in Ceuta.

She succeeds Alar Karis, who did not seek a second term. REUTERS

gary chang’s ‘domestic transformer’ makes 32 sqm of hong kong living space work 24 ways
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
10:50:06 UTC
19:50:06 KST

Gary Chang’s apartment treats space as a time-shared resource
In Hong Kong, architect Gary Chang’s Domestic Transformer turns a 32 square meter apartment into a series of living environments, using sliding partitions, fold-down elements, and ceiling-mounted tracks to accommodate up to 24 configurations. The project is a long-running experiment in how domestic space can be reprogrammed, asking whether a limited footprint has to mean a limited way of living.
Chang moved into the apartment in 1976, when he was fourteen, sharing the home with his parents, three sisters, and a sub-tenant. The apartment was divided into small bedrooms, a kitchen, bathroom, and circulation space. Without a room of his own, Chang slept in the central passage on a wooden bench after the rest of the family had gone to bed. The experience led him to question the assumption that domestic functions need to occupy permanently defined rooms.
The architect’s design practice has developed this idea through several iterations of the apartment. The space evolved from its original cellular arrangement into an open-plan experiment, then into a version using curtains as partitions before reaching the mechanized Domestic Transformer completed in 2007.
images courtesy of Gary Chang
Sliding walls let the apartment change throughout the day
Chang concentrates services and storage around the perimeter of the apartment and leaves a flexible central area that can be repeatedly reconfigured. The mechanical system is concentrated overhead, with the main sliding partitions suspended from steel tracks fixed to the concrete ceiling. This keeps the floor clear of tracks and allows the storage walls to move across the apartment with relatively little effort. The walls themselves carry much of the apartment’s contents, including appliances, clothing, and media, so moving a partition also changes what is accessible within the space.
Lightweight honeycomb aluminum panels are used for deployable counters and work surfaces, alongside a hydraulic bed that folds away to reveal the living area. Mirrored surfaces and metal finishes create an impression that the boundaries of the apartment are constantly shifting, reflecting light and making the compact interior appear less materially fixed. Among the arrangements are a larger kitchen, a master bedroom, a guest sleeping area, a spa, a cinema and hammock lounge, an enclosed dining room, a walk-in dressing area, and an open studio configuration.
The transformations are particularly revealing because they demonstrate that the project is not organized around a hierarchy of ‘essential’ and ‘non-essential’ domestic functions. The apartment accommodates amenities that might normally be associated with a substantially larger home, including bathing, entertaining, media, storage, work, and overnight guests. When the bed is deployed, the central area becomes a sleeping chamber. When it is folded away, the same floor returns to a living space. Moving storage partitions can create a more enclosed kitchen or open the apartment into a continuous studio. Other configurations turn the interior toward leisure, including a projection setup and a suspended hammock.
Full-height mirrors, aluminum surfaces, and polished metal details reflect light across the interior, making the boundaries of the space less visually apparent. The apartment does not become physically larger, but its surfaces are made to feel less fixed.
yellow-tinted glazing changes the view and atmosphere of the compact interior
DAYLIGHT AND PRIVACY ARE PART OF THE TRANSFORMATION
The flexibility of the apartment extends beyond its walls and furniture. A motorized screen controls the amount of daylight entering through the window, while a yellow-tinted glazing treatment gives the interior a warmer appearance when the screen is retracted. The intervention changes the atmosphere of the room as well as its physical configuration, using light to alter the perception of the compact interior.
Acoustics present a more difficult problem. Moving partitions need enough clearance to slide freely, which makes it difficult to achieve the airtight seals associated with conventional walls. Chang responds by incorporating acoustic isolation into the wet area, where the enclosed steam shower can also serve as a private space for making phone calls.
The compromise points to one of the less visible realities of kinetic architecture: flexibility can come at the expense of some of the qualities provided by permanent construction. The systems have to balance movement, storage, privacy, acoustics, and everyday use within the same small envelope.
movable walls divide the window into changing views of the Hong Kong streetscape
FROM THE SCHRÖDER HOUSE TO HONG KONG’S STREET HAWKERS
Chang’s approach belongs to a longer history of architecture that questions the permanence of the room. Gerrit Rietveld’s 1924 Schröder House used sliding partitions to alter its interior boundaries, while William L. Murphy’s wall-bed system demonstrated how sleeping could be folded into a single-room apartment. Traditional Japanese fusuma and shoji screens offer another precedent for interiors whose boundaries can change according to use.
Chang also draws on a more immediate Hong Kong reference: the city’s street hawkers. Their stalls expand during periods of activity and contract when they are no longer needed, turning limited physical space into a flexible working environment. The comparison is useful because it shifts the idea of transformability away from high-tech novelty and toward a familiar urban practice of making space available only when it is required.
The Domestic Transformer develops this principle at the scale of the home. Its walls, storage units, beds, counters, and screens become components in a larger system of spatial choreography.
with the partitions moved aside, the window opens onto the surrounding city
THE DOMESTIC TRANSFORMER WAS PART OF A LONGER EXPERIMENT
The ideas tested inside Chang’s apartment also appear elsewhere in his work. One important precedent is the Suitcase House at the Commune by the Great Wall near Beijing, completed in 2002. The linear pavilion uses moving and pneumatic elements to change between more open communal arrangements and configurations that provide greater privacy.
Chang later applied related strategies to commercial residential projects in Hong Kong, including serviced apartments where kinetic cabinetry helps make smaller units more adaptable.
The Domestic Transformer therefore represents one stage in a broader investigation rather than a single isolated solution. The apartment allowed Chang to test these ideas at an intimate scale, where questions of movement, storage, privacy, and everyday routines could be experienced directly.
a sliding element reveals storage and hanging space beside the shower
A SMALL HOME THAT ASKS HOW MUCH SPACE WE ACTUALLY NEED
The lasting interest of the Domestic Transformer lies less in the number 24 than in the question behind it. Chang does not make 32 square meters behave exactly like a much larger apartment. Instead, he demonstrates how the same floor area can support a wider range of activities when rooms are no longer treated as permanent entities.
That flexibility is also demanding. The resident has to operate the apartment, move its partitions, deploy its furniture, and accept a degree of mechanical complexity that would be unnecessary in a conventional home. Transformability is therefore not a substitute for space in every sense; it is another way of organizing it.
But in a city where residential space has long been under pressure, the project offers a different measure of domestic capacity. Its architecture is not defined by how many rooms can fit into 32 square meters, but by how many different lives those square meters can accommodate.
The Domestic Transformer ultimately treats the home as something that can change state. A bedroom does not have to occupy the apartment all day, just as a kitchen, dining room, cinema, or workspace does not have to remain permanently assembled. By allowing functions to take turns, Chang turns time itself into part of the floor plan.

a suspended hammock transforms the central space into a lounge
the hydraulic bed turns the living area into a bedroom

BEIJING, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- The 15th China Intellectual Property Annual Conference (CIPAC) will be held from Sept. 8 to 9 in Beijing, highlighting the high-quality development of the IP sector during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), the country's top intellectual property regulator said on Wednesday.
This year's conference will bring together representatives from government, industry, academia, and research and application sectors at home and abroad to jointly explore new pathways for intellectual property to serve the country's comprehensive innovation, high-quality development, and high-standard opening-up, according to the China National Intellectual Property Administration (CNIPA).

Since its inauguration in 2010, the annual CIPAC has become a high-end platform for showcasing China's development in the intellectual property sector, facilitating exchanges on cutting-edge industry topics, and promoting related services.
The number of high-value invention patents held on the Chinese mainland had reached 2.29 million by the end of last year, growing at a faster pace than that of overall invention patents, according to data from the CNIPA.
The number of valid invention patents held on the Chinese mainland had reached 5.32 million by the end of 2025. The year-on-year growth rate of high-value invention patents was 2.2 percentage points higher than that of the country's total invention patents last year. ■

Feature: Chinese enterprise deepens roots in Kyrgyzstan, forging new chapter of cooperation
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
18:48:46 CST
19:48:46 KST

This photo taken with a mobile phone shows the first batch of equipment for municipal infrastructure projects delivered by China's Guangxi Liugong Machinery Co., Ltd. (Liugong) in Karakol, Kyrgyzstan, July 1, 2026. (Xinhua)
NANNING/BISHKEK, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- In the Tianshan Mountains of Kyrgyzstan, construction is in full swing in August from north to south. At the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan (CKU) railway project site, excavators dig through rock and earth while loaders shuttle materials back and forth.
Deep in the Tianshan Mountains, heavy-duty mining equipment operates at an altitude of some 4,000 meters. On the shores of Issyk-Kul, the "Pearl of Central Asia," construction machinery is supporting urban renewal in the eastern city of Karakol.
These steel machines, coming from China's Guangxi Liugong Machinery Co., Ltd. (Liugong), thousands of kilometers away, cross mountains and ascend plateaus to support construction projects across Kyrgyzstan.
BUILDING ACROSS MOUNTAINS
In December 2024, the CKU railway project was officially launched. As one of the main suppliers of engineering machinery for the CKU railway, Liugong is deeply involved in the project.
"Since 2025, we have deployed successive batches of Liugong loaders and excavators to support construction of the CKU railway, undertaking earthwork excavation and material transportation tasks," said Hou Yubo, Industry Customer Director of Liugong Machinery.
He added that this marked the company's first entry into the Central Asian market with electric engineering machinery.
Since September 2025, Liugong, together with local dealers, has been conducting continuous equipment inspections for the CKU railway project, providing maintenance and technical services for loaders, excavators and other machinery to minimize downtime risks and ensure uninterrupted construction of bridges and tunnels at high altitudes.
In November 2025, Liugong officially registered a subsidiary in Kyrgyzstan, advancing its localization strategy. The professional product knowledge and service experience of Chinese staff, combined with local employees' deep understanding of the environment and customers, have proven highly complementary and well-coordinated throughout project operations.
FROM INTERPRETER TO TECHNICIAN
"When I first came to Liugong, I knew almost nothing about engineering machinery," said Marsel Chokoev, a young Kyrgyz man who joined Liugong's team in Kyrgyzstan in February 2026.
What earned him the job was not prior experience in engineering machinery, but his proficiency in Chinese and a strong willingness to learn.
Six months later, he has learned the basics of loaders, excavators, road rollers and bulldozers, and can independently provide basic service consultations to local clients.
As he became more familiar with the equipment, his language skills began to play a vital role in daily operations. He helps relay Chinese technicians' advice on equipment issues to local clients and dealers, while accurately conveying clients' feedback on operating conditions, equipment performance and service needs to his Chinese colleagues.
"Liugong coming to my hometown didn't just give me a stable job. My Chinese mentors taught me their skills without reservation, and we've become like friends. Here, I've not only gained solid professional skills, but also an understanding of sincere friendship that transcends borders," Chokoev said.
From a language interpreter to a skilled technician, this young Kyrgyz man is carving out his own path of growth through each machine, each service call and each conversation.
His journey has also taken him deep into the Tianshan Mountains, where a high-altitude mining site presents a new set of challenges.
Deep in the Tianshan Mountains, a mining site sits at an altitude of around 4,000 meters, where permafrost makes operations extremely challenging. In recent years, Liugong has delivered batches of large-scale mining equipment to the site for loading, excavation and material transport.
Since August this year, Chokoev and other local employees have been stationed there alongside Liugong's mining service personnel, braving extreme cold and oxygen deprivation to help ensure the machinery operates continuously in the rugged mountain terrain.
STRENGTHENING LOCAL TIES
From railway construction sites to high-altitude mines, Chinese equipment has been delivered in successive batches and put to work on the front lines, handling loading, excavation and material transport. As its equipment applications continue to increase, Liugong is also expanding its presence in the local market and broadening its business reach.
On July 1 this year, Liugong delivered its first batch of equipment for municipal infrastructure projects in Karakol, a highland city in eastern Kyrgyzstan.
During the delivery and acceptance process, Liugong and Karakol municipal officials discussed future cooperation, including expanding its product line into more municipal applications. All equipment is expected to be delivered by the third quarter.
As part of Kyrgyzstan's municipal infrastructure upgrade, the equipment will support road maintenance, municipal construction, environmental management and public facility upkeep, providing reliable support for urban operations.
Liugong's experience is but one example of how Chinese equipment manufacturers are strengthening cooperation with Kyrgyzstan and supporting its development.
Rooted in local communities and serving local needs, Chinese enterprises are writing a new chapter of industrial cooperation, joint development and people-to-people connectivity in Kyrgyzstan. ■

ISTANBUL, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- Two Turkish-flagged ships collided in the Sea of Marmara off Istanbul early Wednesday, leaving 10 crew members missing, Turkish authorities said.
According to the Istanbul Governor's Office, the incident occurred at around 3:00 a.m. local time (0000 GMT) when a cargo ship collided with a tanker.
The cargo ship Tugberk Imamoglu is believed to have sunk in waters about 800 to 900 meters deep, while search and rescue operations are continuing, according to the office.
The incident involved the tanker Alsu, which was traveling from the northwestern province of Kocaeli to Aliaga district in Izmir province, and the cargo ship, which was sailing from the southern port of Iskenderun to Karadeniz Eregli on Türkiye's Black Sea coast.
Tugberk Imamoglu, which was carrying 4,199 tons of coiled steel, failed to respond to calls, and none of its crew members could be reached by phone, local authorities said.
The tanker was found to be empty at the time of the collision and sustained no visible damage, according to authorities.
A total of 14 maritime search and rescue units and two helicopters are taking part in the operation, according to the statement. ■

Road access to mudslide-hit border port restored in SW China's Xizang

Rescue teams, relief supplies and some rescue equipment have entered the core rescue area via the road, rescuers said. (Xinhua/Tenzin Nyida)
GYIRONG, Xizang, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- Road access to the core area of the mudslide-hit Gyirong Port in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region was basically restored at 10 a.m. on Wednesday after days of round-the-clock repair work on the damaged G216 national highway.
Rescue teams, relief supplies and some rescue equipment have entered the core rescue area via this road, rescuers said.
A section of the G216 national highway, the only land route to Gyirong Port, was severely damaged by the mudslide carrying huge boulders, with the restoration of road access critically important in aiding large-scale search operations in the core disaster area.
The repair operation, notably, posed formidable challenges.
"Conditions vary from one section of the road to another," said Zhou Gang from China Anneng, a state-owned engineering and rescue enterprise. The original roadbed remained usable in some sections, but most of it had been severely damaged.
The work zone lay in a narrow mountain gorge, with steep mountainsides on one side and a fast-flowing river on the other. This confined space made it difficult for multiple pieces of heavy machinery to operate simultaneously, severely hampering the work, Zhou added.
An even greater challenge came from the unpredictable conditions inside the gorge, featuring fast-flowing water and lingering risks of rockfalls, landslides and other secondary hazards.
Crews responded by adapting their methods. Along narrow sections, multiple excavators worked in relay, lining up one behind another to dig and pass debris from one machine to the next.
In sections with the strongest currents, excavators pushed into the water to open the way, while crews built diversion structures and used rock-filled steel cages to stabilize the roadbed, advancing section by section.
The mudslide, caused by an ice-rock avalanche in Nepal, hit Gyirong Port on Aug. 26, claiming 16 lives and leaving 546 people missing at the border port as of 6 p.m. on Saturday, according to the regional government's latest update.
Following the disaster, Xizang swiftly activated its highest-level emergency response for natural disasters, mobilizing rescue forces from across the region for search and rescue operations, road clearance and other relief work in Gyirong. ■

China Focus: Digital tech, smart gear reshape farming in China's NE granary
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
18:48:34 CST
19:48:34 KST

A robot stacks packaged rice for shipment at a workshop of Qiaofu Dayuan Agricultural Co., Ltd., in Wuchang City, northeast China's Heilongjiang Province, Aug. 31, 2026. (Xinhua/Ji Hang)
HARBIN, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- Across the fertile black soil of northeast China's Heilongjiang Province, data and technology are helping farmers anticipate weather and growing conditions with unprecedented precision, reshaping how food is grown in the country's agricultural heartland.
For 16 consecutive years, the province has ranked first in the country in total grain output. Behind its sustained productivity is a highly mechanized farming system, with the comprehensive mechanization rate for plowing, sowing and harvesting reaching 99.28 percent.
Now, the province is taking the next step toward smarter farming. From AI-powered crop monitoring and drones to upgraded agricultural machinery, technologies are helping farmers make more precise decisions and boost efficiency.
Heilongjiang's transformation offers a glimpse into China's broader efforts to harness technology to safeguard national food security while advancing rural revitalization.
DIGITAL TECH
Inside Beidahuang Information Company in Harbin, the provincial capital, a massive digital map covering 48 million mu (about 3.2 million hectares) of arable land dominates the wall.
Across the screen, data on soil, crop growth and tractor movements updates in real time, as satellite remote sensing, Internet of Things (IoT) and AI are gradually integrated into every stage of farming, from sowing to harvesting.
"Previously, a farmer could inspect only about 200 mu a day on foot. Now, drones and remote sensing allow us to monitor vast areas and update crop data for the entire reclamation area every five days," said Wang Hao, deputy general manager of the company's market operation center.
Wang noted that such data is now helping shape decisions from field scouting and fertilization to pest control.
The company has developed more than 60 digital systems for farm management. Built on years of agricultural data, its cold-region crop AI model analyzes soil, weather and crop-growth information to generate planting plans and variable fertilization prescriptions.
"Our agricultural service app has improved service efficiency and cut management costs for farmers," Wang said, noting that the app has facilitated online transactions worth over 100 billion yuan (around 14.74 billion U.S. dollars).
"Smart agriculture is moving from validation to acceptance, but large-scale rollout still faces multiple challenges in data, technology fit and adaptability," said Wang, adding that AI models need ample on-site data and repeated verification to overcome environmental variability to actually serve farm production.
In Wuchang, a renowned rice-producing area in Harbin, digital technology is also reshaping the entire production chain.
At Qiaofu Dayuan Agricultural Co., Ltd., robots stack packaged rice for shipment. Qiao Wenzhi, head of the company, said QR codes on the products provide information such as the production base and nutritional content, allowing consumers to choose rice tailored to their needs.
SMART GEAR
At a planting base in Heilongjiang, a four-wheel laser weeding robot glides along the crop rows. Multi-spectral cameras and sensors on the robots scan the ground, and algorithms instantly distinguish crops from weeds, directing laser beams to precisely eliminate the weeds.
"Weeding used to rely on manual labor or chemicals, which were either costly or harmful to the soil," said Li Yongwei, deputy general manager of Harbin Huagong Zhiyun Technology Co., Ltd. "Laser weeding is a purely physical, chemical-free method."
Li added that this technology, which achieves a weed removal rate of over 95 percent and a crop damage rate of less than 0.1 percent, cuts weeding costs by up to 70 percent compared with manual labor.
Agricultural machinery is also upgrading toward intelligence. At Heilongjiang Dewo Technology Development Co., Ltd., rows of electric-drive precision seeders are lined up on its square. Air pressure and seed spacing, notably, can be monitored and adjusted in real time via smart terminals.
"The system makes adjustments more convenient and can reduce seed damage," said Du Mujun, chief engineer at Dewo, revealing that the seeder operates approximately 50 percent faster than traditional mechanical seeders.
Currently, Dewo's equipment accounts for more than 60 percent of domestic high-end electric-drive seeder sales. The company has also begun exporting its products overseas, helping extend China's intelligent farming tools to global markets.
"Domestic agricultural machinery manufacturing has improved to the point where it can compete with international brands, offering targeted designs at prices roughly one-third lower than comparable foreign products," said He Chunling, international sales manager at Dewo.
Since launching overseas operations in 2019, the company has exported potato mechanization equipment to Russia, Kazakhstan, Peru and Zimbabwe, and seeders to the Republic of Korea.
EMBRACE INTELLIGENT FARMING
In 2025, Heilongjiang recorded its 22nd consecutive bumper harvest, with grain output reaching a record 82 million tonnes. It also had 676,000 intelligent agricultural machines, ranking first nationwide.
The province's agricultural transformation did not happen overnight.
During the 14th Five-Year Plan period (2021-2025), the province accelerated the upgrading and intelligent transformation of agricultural machinery, its governor Liang Huiling said earlier this year.
During the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), the province plans to foster industrial clusters focused on agricultural robots, intelligent farming equipment and low-altitude economy, Liang said.
In August, construction began on a national AI application pilot base for crop planting, aimed at tackling common technological bottlenecks and developing scalable applications.
Heilongjiang's technological quest aligns with China's broader plans for agricultural modernization.
The country's 15th Five-Year Plan calls for improving agricultural efficiency through a combination of high-quality land, superior seeds, advanced machinery and effective methods, while a document issued in February pledged to advance agricultural and rural modernization and promote all-around rural revitalization, expanding the use of drones, IoT and robots in agriculture and rural areas.
"Relying solely on manual labor and farming the land the way our ancestors did is no longer realistic," said Hu Jinyou, a professor at China Agricultural University, noting that while smart agriculture is still being optimized, the deep integration of AI and agriculture is an irreversible trend.
As a new generation of well-educated farmers enters the fields, Hu said, digital management will gradually become the norm. ■
