Conservative reshuffle is a response to shifting political tides
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
06:00:25 UTC
15:00:25 KST

When Kemi Badenoch steps up to the dispatch box for prime minister’s questions on Wednesday, she will face a very different opponent. And while all eyes will be on Andy Burnham’s first PMQs, those in the Conservative ranks will be watching their own leader’s performance just as closely.
Badenoch attempted to get out of the traps quickly this week, instigating a reshuffle of her frontbench like a conscientious head girl refilling her pencil case for the start of term. Out went the unassuming shadow chancellor, Mel Stride, replaced by the Thatcherite Andrew Griffith. He will lead a new economic unit alongside the City minister, Richard Fuller, and Claire Coutinho, who will replace Griffith as shadow business secretary and act as his deputy after her parental leave.
Priti Patel was also sacked as shadow foreign secretary and replaced with the former Tory leadership candidate Tom Tugendhat. The attention-grabbing anti-migration MP Katie Lam replaced James Cleverly as the shadow communities secretary, after he resigned from the shadow cabinet to run for London mayor.
The new shadow cabinet will quietly get its first ensemble outing on Wednesday, against the soundtrack of 403 excitable Labour MPs keen to show support for their own new leader. Badenoch’s performance will matter.
“Kemi has to change tack because she’s facing different opposition,” said the Conservative peer and polling expert Robert Hayward. “Like the manager of any football team, you have to adjust to the people you’re playing against. Kemi and everyone in the party knows she will have to adapt.”
In the final weeks of Keir Starmer’s premiership, Badenoch fully embraced her cage-fighter instincts, showing little mercy or grace towards the former prime minister even after he announced his resignation. But early indications suggest she understands that Burnham’s folksy Hovis advert charm may require a different approach. Before the start of recess she referred to him as “a pair of eyelashes and a black T-shirt”, only for Burnham to playfully counter, in a social media video, “it’s dark blue, actually”.
“When your opponent is an unpopular prime minister who’s been there a while, you can afford to take the gloves off,” said the Conservative commenter Henry Hill. “But when they are new and in the first flush of their honeymoon, it requires a little more subtlety.”
While that is a quality that has rarely been associated with the MP for North West Essex, advisers were likely to have told her to keep her powder dry and see how Burnham plays his hand, said the Conservative Home editor, Giles Dilnot. “Kemi has her own way of doing things, but she won’t necessarily have to land a knockout blow on day one.”
Her reshuffle, argued Dilnot, was less a reaction to facing a very different type of leader than a move to make her party battle-ready should Burnham announce a snap election in 2027. “Everything has shifted on its axis,” he said. “She knows they have to be ready.”
Bringing more recognisable figures into the cabinet, including her former rival Tugenhat – seen as one of the party’s surviving One Nation centrists, despite his hawkishness on foreign affairs – indicates that Badenoch’s summer purge of the Wets may have pragmatic limits. The addition of Damian Hinds, seen as more to the centre than his leader, as health secretary backs up the theory. “It gives lie to the accusation that she’s trying to lead a clique,” said Hayward.
Some new faces suggest Badenoch is casting her net wider to find talent. The Scot Andrew Bowie at energy is likely to maintain the “drill, baby, drill” stance that helped the Conservatives win a byelection in Aberdeen South in June. Harriet Cross, the new Scotland secretary, is touted as a rising star.
It also is a tacit recognition that, while Badenoch herself is polling relatively strongly – YouGov found her popularity has improved in recent months, with 38% of Britons now saying she is doing well – the “Keminaissance” has not translated into support for her party: polling remains dire and has fallen from 25% at the end of 2024 to 19% now.
“Her personal polling has gone up, but it hasn’t lifted the party with it,” said Hill. “I think there’s an understanding that if there was a general election now, they would get absolutely hammered.”
The reshuffle is not without risk. Griffith was a Treasury minister during Liz Truss’s mini-budget, and repeatedly defended it during the economic chaos that followed. Critics warn that Tugendhat’s hawkishness could lead the party into dangerous territory. Lam’s incendiary rhetoric may turn off as many voters as it attracts.
But with conference season ahead and a Labour party flushed with the success of Burnham’s first summer, Badenoch had to show she was not only the right woman for the job, but that she had a feasible team to run the country, said Dilnot. “Last year was all about Kemi, and this year it has to be about the brand,” he said.

My autistic son lives in fear of bailiffs from Ovo breaking into his flat

06:00:25 UTC
15:00:25 KST

My autistic son has been bombarded for years by letters to his home from OVO Energy addressed to “The Occupier”, with demands for money and threats of debt collectors. He is supplied by Scottish Gas.
He was required to let an OVO agent into his flat to “prove” he didn’t have an OVO meter. Neither this, nor countless phone calls, has stopped the demands.
Call centre agents confirm that he doesn’t have an account but seem powerless to update the system. He lives in fear that bailiffs will break his door down. 
  LO, Edinburgh
OVO swiftly decided that the bombardment was triggered by address error on the national database. In short, it says, the gas and electricity meters supplying another property had been registered to your son’s address. It corrected the address for the gas, but tells me another supplier owned the electricity meter and had “rejected multiple requests” by OVO to update the database.
In response to my queries, OVO agreed to suspend demands and issued a letter of deadlock to enable your son to complain to the Energy Ombudsman.
The letter, which enables access to the database, discovered that the electricity meter was correctly registered to a neighbouring address and supplied by OVO, but OVO had somehow got your son’s address on its billing system. It was ordered to pay £150 compensation and the bills have now ceased.

Whisky galore – and now plenty more besides: exploring the Scottish island of Islay
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
06:00:25 UTC
15:00:25 KST

The Paps of Jura disappear into the mist as I pedal along the shores of Loch Indaal, and the rain cloud I’ve been racing finally catches up. I stash my hire bike at Port Charlotte youth hostel, quickly change and make it to Lochindaal Seafood Kitchen just before the downpour.
I’m soon warmed, by the welcome then by a bowl of creamy fish chowder. “We’ve plenty of fresh seafood just in,” is all the temptation I need to order the seafood plate. It’s a bowl for one, but a hungry one, and soon I’m picking and cracking my way through piles of fat langoustines and crab claws, with hot whisky-butter scallops and plenty of bread and butter.
The island of Islay, off the west coast of Scotland, is far better known for its drinks than its food. With 10, soon to be 11, working whisky distilleries, Islay is synonymous with rich, heavily peated single malts. But, over several days cycling around the island, I find that whisky does much more than fill warehouses and attract tourists. It is helping to support an island where agriculture, fishing and hospitality have long struggled to provide year-round employment.
At Bruichladdich, one of Islay’s smallest distilleries but the largest private employer, that begins with the barley. When the distillery was bought by a pair of wine merchants after being mothballed several times in the 1990s, they questioned why the barley arriving at the distillery was being sourced from so many different places. Surely, they thought, like vineyards, where the grain was grown would influence the whisky’s terroir.
They began encouraging farmers to grow barley on Islay, which hadn’t been done since before the second world war. Farmers were understandably wary of taking on an unfamiliar crop, particularly as the tens of thousands of migratory geese from Greenland are partial to a field of young barley. When Islay’s last creamery closed in 2000, the dairy industry collapsed, so growing barley offered farmers another way to use their land, and Bruichladdich guaranteed to buy the crop regardless of the yield. Today, 21 Islay farms grow barley for the distillery, producing half of its requirements, and early experiments with rye have been promising.
Eva MacIntyre grew up on Islay, tried living on the mainland and came back. She now works for Bruichladdich as a brand ambassador and takes me up the hill to see the distillery’s water source.
“Growing up on Islay, whisky was a way of life,” she tells me. “It’s not just a drink; it’s all about who you share it with.” Before her whisky presentations, she practises with her grandfather. Her story is not unusual. “Every family has at least one person working in whisky,” she tells me.
I meet Kate Hannett, a full-time forager responsible for gathering the 22 botanicals used in the Botanist gin across peaty bogs and hillsides. Her brother, Adam, is Bruichladdich’s master blender, having started his career as a tour guide. Lisa Matthews, the assistant blender, is also an Ileach (a person from Islay) and the distillery’s first female blender. Her brother is a brand ambassador in the US. There are jobs in whisky, and reasons to stay on the island, that most rural communities could only dream of offering their young people.
The distilleries are woven into Islay life. I hear frequent stories of distilleries helping each other out and lending equipment when machinery breaks down. “It’s really not competitive,” Eva says. As well as the employment opportunities, whisky benefits the infrastructure. There’s a full-time fire service, unusual across rural Scotland. Even the swimming pool is heated by waste energy from Bowmore distillery.
At Islay Ales, another island-made drink begins with barley and soft west coast water. The brewery, founded in 2004, opened a new brewhouse last year. Its spent grain, or draff, goes to local farms for feed and wastewater is treated through a reed bed. On an island where the growing season is short and the weather can change before you’ve finished your pint, making food and drink locally is not necessarily easy. “After the Agricultural Show, which is the third Thursday in August, it’s winter,” I’m told.
Emma Goudie of Islay Cocoa began making chocolates as an easily transportable product that wouldn’t compete directly with other island food businesses. She uses local ingredients where they make sense, rather than simply because they are local.
“It’s quality first, but I’m lucky that the produce we have here is excellent.” Her current range includes Orsay sea salt, Argyll coffee, and sourdough from neighbouring Jura. She also works with the whisky industry, creating chocolates designed to pair with Ardbeg and for Caol Ila tours. “It grew quite organically and in the best way,” she says.
Iain and Alexander MacLellan are the fourth and fifth generations of a family whose hospitality business stretches back to the late 19th century. At Lochindaal Seafood Kitchen, Iain tells me he grew up with the fishers who supply the restaurant and remembers cooking mackerel and scallops on their boats. “I’ve been 52 years behind the bar,” he tells me. The restaurant grew out of the family pub at Lochindall hotel, partly because, as Iain puts it, “we ran out of space to serve our seafood platters”.
Chef Ajish Johny came to Port Charlotte hotel after working in India and Dubai, on cruise ships and in Wales, and has now been here for four years. His menus feature a curry of the day alongside Loch Gruinart oysters, locally caught fish and burgers made with beef from nearby Octomore Farm. “We never compromise on quality,” he says. “People on Islay are well travelled. They know what good food is.”
And then there is Ardbeg House in Port Ellen, a once tired traditional hotel that has been transformed into a maximalist extension of the Ardbeg brand. There are 12 quirkily themed bedrooms, a fishing boat suspended over the bar and a theatrical restaurant with a beaten-metal ceiling, bold lighting and tables made from marble bathroom offcuts. It’s an exuberant place, but the food is excellent and well priced. I eat bread made with eight-year-old Ardbeg and thyme; langoustine bisque with pickled fennel and tarragon, then the catch of the day, sea bass, with cabbage, kale, roast potatoes and split beurre blanc. My taxi driver insisted that I try the sticky toffee pudding. My server does the same, so I take the hint and am rewarded with a treacly wedge of cake with whisky ice-cream. Outside, it’s raining again.
Before the Clearances, about 15,000 people lived on Islay. Today, there are just over 3,000. Islay may have been built, in part, on whisky. But increasingly, the whisky is helping build something back: farms, breweries, restaurants, food businesses and reasons to stay.
Ailsa Sheldon was a guest of Hostelling Scotland and Bruichladdich Distillery. Port Charlotte youth hostel has dorm beds from £28 and private rooms from £78 (open late March to early October). Travel to Islay from the Scottish mainland by Caledonian MacBrayne (CalMac) ferry from Kennacraig or by flying with Loganair from Glasgow. Hire bikes from Islay E-Wheels in Port Ellen from £25 a day for non-electric, £35 for electric, delivery available across the island

UK must end all trade with Israel, says co-founder of BDS movement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
06:00:24 UTC
15:00:24 KST

Britain’s legal and ethical obligation to stop a genocide in Gaza requires it to take bigger steps than halting trade with illegal Israeli settlements or imposing further sanctions, Omar Barghouti, the co-founder of the Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions (BDS) movement has said.
He described sanctions against individual settler groups or extremist ministers as a “smoke and mirrors cop-out and distraction” from the UK’s legal obligation under international law to end all support for Israel, including arms exports, trade deals and academic relations that “may directly or indirectly enable Israel’s illegal occupation” of Gaza, the West Bank and East Jerusalem.
The British foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, promised on Tuesday to introduce a “comprehensive reset” of the UK’s policy on Israel in the coming weeks.
It has been reported that the UK is preparing to ban trade with illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank and Miliband told the Commons the government was looking at how to stop British companies “financing, constructing or advertising new settlements”.
Miliband has called plans for the E1 settlement, which would involve the construction of 3,400 houses through the heart of the West Bank, unacceptable and destructive, adding that, by cutting across the territory, critics say it will render a two-state solution impossible.
Tenders for the settlements are due to be handed out, potentially irreversibly, days before the Israeli elections on 27 October.
The Board of Deputies of British Jews and the Jewish Leadership Council have warned Miliband that a UK ban on trade with settlements may fuel antisemitism in the UK.
A third group of British Jews, Yachad, also met Miliband to highlight “the growing concerns of many British Jews about the entrenchment of occupation and effective annexation of the West Bank”.
Barghouti, an influential advocate for Palestinian rights for more than 20 years, said the litmus test for human rights law and the west still lay in Palestine.
He said: “In July 2024, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) said Israel’s entire occupation of Gaza, and the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, is illegal and amounts to a violation of the racial segregation and apartheid prohibitions under international law.
“Dozens of UN human rights experts have said to fulfil those obligations a set of minimal steps are required: a full military embargo, export import, dual-use transfer and transit.
“They also said you have to end all trade, diplomatic and economic relations and academic relations that enable Israel’s illegal occupation.”
Barghouti added: “Further in January 2024, the ICJ said there is a plausible case of the violation of Palestinian rights under the Genocide Convention.
“The ICJ decided there is a plausible risk of genocide that is sufficient to trigger third state responsibilities. But UK government lawyers seem to ignore that part of the ruling and say the court has not ruled on genocide.
“But the genocide convention is very clear – where there is a risk, the obligation to prevent is triggered, and how do you prevent a genocide? You stop enabling it. You end all forms of complicity.”
The Israeli embassy referred to the warning by Gideon Sa’ar, Israel’s foreign minister, who said: “If Britain acts against the state of Israel, the state of Israel will act against Britain. We have the tools.” He added: “The period is over when people act against the state of Israel and the state of Israel doesn’t respond.”
Explaining why he regards UK sanctions as “totally performative”, Barghouti said: “They have no concrete effect in holding Israel to account or pressuring it to comply with international law.”
He added: “Israel has de facto annexed the occupied Palestinian territory, making it near impossible [to] differentiate so-called settlement goods and services.”
Pressed whether the BDS movement is trying to change the minds of Israelis through economic force, Barghouti insisted sanctions have to be legal and ethical.
“They have to target the perpetrators, whether entities or individuals that are involved in crimes, especially international crimes. They are actually measures of accountability, not sanctions that simply say settlers shall not have vacations in London.”
Despite South Africa feeling forced to return to the ICJ to point out Israel is not complying with court orders, he said he retained his faith in international law – for all its colonial origins – arguing it was not something engraved in stone, but dynamic.
“Humanity has agency to evolve and expand international law. We in the BDS movement have been pushing the envelope of its interpretation.”
Barghouti added: “So, in the BDS movement, we try to hold states, corporations and institutions accountable to end their own complicity in genocide rather than just wait for the messiah of international law to come and save us.
“We definitely need international law, just as we need to maintain the ethical high ground. Both are necessary, but not sufficient. We need people power to achieve liberation. There is no other way.”

Women behind the lens: ‘The women are moving towards the church, but it is not the final destination’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
06:00:24 UTC
15:00:24 KST

This image, called Holy Gang, combines an image of a church in my mother’s home town, Fateng-tse-Ntsho, in Free State province, South Africa, with self-portraits of me, multiplied to form a group of women. Although at first glance the women are moving towards the church, it is not the final destination.
Positioned higher, beyond the church, is what appears to be a rising sun. For me, the sun represents a place where I can meet and be with my ancestors beyond religious limitations, even though they were members of the church and I am not.
I was born in Soweto and moved to Johannesburg’s southern suburbs when I was seven. Throughout my early life, I moved between urban Johannesburg and Fateng-tse-Ntsho, where my mother and I returned each year to visit family or attend funerals. I grew up negotiating multiple ideas of “home” and “belonging” without feeling entirely rooted in any of them. This experience led me towards spirituality as a way of thinking about identity, belonging, and my relationship to a larger collective.
Whenever I visited my family in Fateng-tse-Ntsho, I would walk past the Nederduitse Gereformeerde Kerk in Afrika, or the Dutch reformed church in Africa, that my great-grandmother and her daughters belonged to. It became part of my core visual memory from childhood, and it enters the work as a remembered image rather than as a religious symbol. Its significance lies in its familiarity, its connection to my childhood, and its relationship to the women in my lineage.
The image is part of the Spirit series of digital collages that I began working on in 2021. Through the series, I use self-portraiture and white cloth to embody my female ancestors. The white becomes a visual language of transcendence that allows me to access my forebears and be alongside them. Rather than separating those who belong to the church from those who do not, the white binds us together. I may not subscribe to their religion, but I can still encounter them through lineage, memory, spirituality and our literal DNA.
The title, Holy Gang, introduces another tension. “Gang” in this context suggests agency, solidarity, loyalty, movement and collective force, allowing me to think of the women of my lineage as more than their religious practices and beliefs. Holy Gang is ultimately an imagined meeting place for me and the women who came before me.
In this artwork, I do not “enter” the image to become part of the church; I enter to meet and journey with those women beyond the church, toward the sun. The church becomes the backdrop against which this encounter takes place, a structure that is part of our shared history but not the limit of our spiritual belonging.

'Didn’t think twice': The routine activity that sent Robert to the emergency department
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
05:58:07 UTC
14:58:07 KST

IN BRIEF
- Most gardeners face little risk, but older people and those with weakened immunity can develop serious infections.
- To reduce risk, wet potting mix before use, wear a mask and gloves, open bags away from your face and wash your hands afterwards.
For millions of Australians, gardening is a weekend ritual, but experts warn there can be more than nutrients and organic matter in a bag of potting mix.
Bacteria and fungi are a natural part of the material, and while most pose no threat to healthy people, some can cause serious infections in those who are more susceptible.
One of the best-known examples is Legionella longbeachae, a species of bacteria associated with potting mix and soil that can cause Legionnaires' disease.
'I didn't think twice about it'
For 72-year-old Sydney gardener Robert, that risk became a reality after routinely handling potting mix without taking the precautions recommended on the packaging.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
He told SBS News that he ended up in hospital after developing Pontiac fever, a milder form of illness caused by exposure to Legionella bacteria.
Unlike Legionnaires' disease, Pontiac fever does not cause pneumonia and usually resolves on its own.
But Robert's experience was a reminder that something as ordinary as opening a bag of potting mix can expose people to bacteria capable of causing illness.
While he recovered after a trip to the emergency department, he says the experience has changed how he approaches gardening.
"I never really thought twice about handling potting mix. You just open the bag and get stuck into it," he said.
"After getting sick from it, I'll definitely be wearing a mask and gloves because it's just not worth taking the risk of getting something worse next time."
His case also highlights the spectrum of illness associated with Legionella, from a relatively mild, self-limiting infection to potentially fatal pneumonia.
A microscopic ecosystem
Richard Bentham, adjunct associate professor at Flinders University, says potting mix is effectively a living ecosystem.
"Potting mix is made by microorganisms, so it's very, very rich in microorganisms," he says.
He told SBS News that some microbes can cause infection when they encounter someone who is particularly susceptible.
Legionella longbeachae is one example, but Bentham says other bacteria, including mycobacteria, can also be found in potting mix and potentially cause infection.
But he insists that the presence of microorganisms does not mean potting mix is inherently dangerous.
Bentham said millions of bags are used safely every year and that the risk of serious infection remains low, but the consequences can be severe for people who are more vulnerable.
From potting mix to the lungs
Experts say the main concern is what happens when contaminated material is disturbed, and fine particles can become airborne when dry potting mix is opened or handled, allowing microorganisms to be inhaled.
Bentham said inhalation is considered an important route of infection, although researchers aren't certain it's the only one. Contaminated material could also potentially be transferred from the hands to the mouth.
Legionella longbeachae can reach the lungs and, in susceptible people, develop into serious pneumonia.
The Australian Centre for Disease Control says L longbeachae is most commonly associated with potting mix, compost and garden soil, while other Legionella species are more commonly associated with water systems such as cooling towers.
"This Legionella longbeachae has nothing to do with air conditioning or water systems," Bentham says.

Tencent’s Hy4 model gains in open-source AI rankings after ecosystem-driven training
On the DeepSWE benchmark, the Hy4 preview scored 64.3, surpassing Alibaba’s Qwen-3.8 Max at 56.6 and DeepSeek-V4 Pro at 62.7
Tencent Holdings’ use of its vast product ecosystem to train its new Hy4 preview model gives it an edge in developing AI agents and brings its flagship model suite back into the top tier of open-source offerings, according to analysts.
The Chinese tech giant’s “differentiated product-plus-model strategy”, where preview models were first deployed across Tencent’s suite of products, enabled it to collect user data before feeding the information back into subsequent rounds of training, Goldman Sachs analysts said in a research note on Monday.

They added that the Hy4 preview brought Tencent’s Hunyuan series back to the forefront of open-source models, with notable gains in coding capabilities over Hy3.
Released on Friday, Hy4 preview ranked eighth globally on Tuesday on Code Arena’s WebDev leaderboard – a real-time competition evaluating large language models on real-world coding tasks – just behind Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5 and outperforming Alibaba Group Holding’s Qwen 3.8-Flash-Next in ninth place.
By comparison, Tencent’s previous generation, Hy3, ranked 34th on the same benchmark on Tuesday.

Two commercial vessels collide off Istanbul, 10 crew members unaccounted for

2026-09-02

14:57:22 KST

Two Turkish-flagged commercial ships collided off the coast of Istanbul's Silivri district early on Wednesday, with maritime authorities saying one of the vessels is believed to have sunk after contact was lost with the ship and its 10 crew members, while the Turkish Navy has joined the ongoing search and rescue operation.
The Turkish-flagged commercial vessel Alsu, sailing from Kocaeli to Aliaga, collided around 3 am local time (0000GMT) with the Turkish-flagged commercial vessel Tugberk Imamoglu, which was travelling from Iskenderun Port to Karadeniz Eregli, according to the Istanbul Governor's Office.
The collision occurred 18 nautical miles south of Silivri.
The governor's office said vessels from the General Directorate of Coastal Safety and the Coast Guard Marmara and Straits Command, along with a Coast Guard helicopter, were dispatched to the scene.
Initial assessments by responding teams found no visible damage to the Alsu.
The Directorate General of Maritime Affairs said in a statement that the Tugberk Imamoglu is believed to have sunk after the vessel failed to respond to any radio calls and none of its crew members answered their phones.
“Life-saving equipment belonging to the Tugberk Imamoglu vessel (including the free-fall lifeboat), for which 10 crew members were assigned, has been located on the sea surface; unfortunately, no ship personnel have been detected inside them,” the directorate said.
“Developments regarding the maritime accident are being monitored, and the public will be informed,” it added.
Investigation launched into collision
The Silivri Chief Public Prosecutor's Office launched an investigation into the collision, assigning a deputy chief public prosecutor and two prosecutors to the case.
The prosecutor's office said the Tugberk Imamoglu was carrying rolled steel and construction rebar, while the Alsu was carrying motor oil when the two vessels collided.
It said instructions were issued to conduct expert examinations to determine how and why the accident occurred and identify any possible responsibility.
Authorities were also ordered to secure and collect the vessels' navigation, radar, and communication records, as well as all other documents, footage, and evidence related to the collision.

Queensland police investigate after 5,500 sheep worth $1.7m stolen from farm
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
05:55:51 UTC
14:55:51 KST

Queensland police are investigating after about 5,500 Dorper sheep worth more than $1.7m were allegedly stolen from a western Queensland farm.
Police said the sheep were stolen from a property outside Blackall, about 830km west of Brisbane, between February and May this year.
Detective Sen Sgt Paul Elliot, from the rural and stock crime squad, said the sheep had an estimated value of about $1.7m (£899,000).
They are fitted with white National Livestock Identification System tags and are Dorper sheep, a breed with white wool but a black face. Both ewes and rams were taken.
Elliot urged anyone with information about the theft or who had seen Dorper sheep matching the description in the area to come forward.
“Livestock theft investigations can be complex, often spanning large geographical areas, which is why we work closely with producers, saleyards, transport operators and industry stakeholders to identify offenders and disrupt criminal activity,” he said.
The AgForce general president, Shane McCarthy, said it was a “a concerning amount of sheep that have been stolen” and would have a significant effect on the farm’s bottom line.
“We’re seeing a concerning rise in the number of incidents like this happening across the state,” he said. “We would trust that the police are taking these matters very, very seriously.”
He said a sheep theft of that scale would require a plan, time and more than one person. Sheep rustlers will sometimes take a group into a property where they can be bred to gain the value of their progeny and then slowly sold to abattoirs over time.
Thefts are often discovered at the abattoir, he said.
“I would say that it’s been thought out for a while,” he said. “I would suggest that one or two sheep here and there, even up to you know 10 or so sheep, is opportunistic. When we’re talking these numbers, they’re organised.”
It is not yet clear how the sheep were stolen, such as being loaded on to several trucks or mustered.
Dorpers are bred to be eaten, not for wool.
The Blackall-Tambo mayor, Andrew Martin, said the herd was probably not all taken in one night.
“I’m suspecting a number of smaller hits and sneaking them off to the abattoir or whatever it is they’re doing with them,” he said.
Farms in some parts of Queensland can rival the size of some countries. Stock theft is typically discovered during a muster.
Martin, who has farmed Dorper sheep, said some properties have as many as 25,000 sheep. It is possible to lose thousands by them escaping, from an animal attack or just miscounting them, without noticing for a long period of time, he said.
“This is an age-old problem. Poddy dodging is a bit of an art, and it’s been going on ever since poddies were there to be dodged,” he said, using Australian slang for stock theft.

Largest-ever Italian parliamentary delegation visits Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
05:48:05 UTC
14:48:05 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Italy’s largest-ever parliamentary delegation to Taiwan began a six-day visit Monday.
The 10-member delegation, led by Italian Senate Vice President Gian Marco Centinaio, was welcomed at a lunch hosted by Deputy Foreign Minister Francois Wu (吳志中) on Monday, per Storm Media. The lawmakers are scheduled to remain in Taiwan through Saturday and meet with government officials and other political figures during their visit.
President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) received the delegation Tuesday and thanked Italy’s parliament for its long-standing support of Taiwan’s international participation, according to a Presidential Office press release. Centinaio, a longtime Taiwan supporter, is visiting for the fifth time and previously came to Taiwan in 2024 to attend the inauguration of Lai and Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim (蕭美琴).
Lai highlighted Italy’s passage of legislation protecting foreign cultural artifacts loaned for exhibitions from seizure as a concrete example of parliamentary support for Taiwan. The legislation took more than 20 years and five parliamentary terms to complete, and was passed by Italy’s Chamber of Deputies and Senate this year, providing legal protection for valuable Taiwanese cultural artifacts on display in Italy.
Lai also cited a report released last year by the Italian Chamber of Deputies’ Foreign Affairs Committee that stressed the importance of peace and stability in the Taiwan Strait. He said several Italian senators have repeatedly challenged what he described as China’s distortion of UN General Assembly Resolution 2758 and supported Taiwan’s international participation.
As authoritarianism continues to expand, democratic countries must support one another to safeguard democracy and peace, Lai said. He noted that Italy deployed the aircraft carrier Cavour to the Indo-Pacific for exercises in 2024, while holding the G7 presidency, and has continued to send naval vessels to the region over the past two years.
Lai said that Italy is Taiwan’s fourth-largest trading partner in the EU, and the two sides have highly complementary industries. He said Italy has strong capabilities in automobiles, design, and advanced materials, while Taiwan has established industrial clusters in semiconductors, information and communications technology, and electronics manufacturing.
Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) led an economic delegation to Milan in June, creating additional opportunities for cooperation between the two sides, Lai said. He hoped that the visiting lawmakers would help turn the accumulated goodwill into more tangible economic and industrial partnerships.

Taiwan reveals NT$36 billion budget for Strong Bow missile system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
05:47:56 UTC
14:47:56 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Air Force will spend NT$36.04 billion (US$1.13 billion) through 2032 to develop and procure the indigenous Strong Bow medium-altitude anti-tactical ballistic missile system.
The system is designed to intercept tactical ballistic missiles with ranges of up to 1,000 kilometers and will complement the nation’s existing lower-tier missile defense systems, per Liberty Times. The ministry said the system is being developed as part of a multilayered defense strategy to counter the growing ballistic missile threat from China.
Strong Bow was originally expected to be funded through a proposed NT$1.25 trillion special defense budget, but was not included in the final proposal. The 2027 budget documents submitted to the Legislative Yuan instead show that the program will be funded through the defense ministry’s annual budget.
The Cabinet said Strong Bow was originally among 23 weapons programs planned under the proposed special defense budget, but was shifted to the annual budget after the legislature approved NT$780 billion for US arms purchases, per CNA. The government said the defense ministry has since prioritized programs based on delivery schedules and operational needs, although the broader military buildup timeline has been affected.
The ministry did not disclose the number of missiles or weapons systems to be procured, citing classified information, Liberty Times reported. It said the missiles and associated weapons systems are scheduled for delivery starting in 2028.
The Strong Bow system is designed for mobile deployment to improve survivability and can operate alongside other air defense missile systems under a unified command-and-control structure. Its two-stage missile consists of an interceptor vehicle and booster, uses a composite-material casing, and employs thrust-vector control during the terminal phase to adjust its trajectory and improve interception capabilities at medium and high altitudes.
The missile uses a millimeter-wave radar seeker to detect and track targets, while its fire-control radar is the first domestically developed active electronically scanned array radar, according to Liberty Times. Military sources said the radar has a longer detection range than that of the radars on existing Patriot and Sky Bow III systems.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Financial support measures have saved companies more than NT$4.2 billion (US$132.1 million) in interest costs since August 2025 following US tariff pressures, the Export-Import Bank of Taiwan said Tuesday.
The bank said its trade financing interest-reduction program had received 9,746 applications involving NT$629 billion in financing as of the end of August, per CNA. The program has provided NT$4.22 billion in interest savings and directly assisted 5,536 companies, with small and medium-sized enterprises accounting for 88.7% of the total financing amount.
The program was launched Aug. 7, 2025, as part of financial support measures led by the Ministry of Finance to help companies deal with changes in the global economy, per UDN. The bank said the combined measures have eased the impact of US tariffs on businesses.
The nation’s exports rose 32.9% year-on-year to NT$2.39 trillion in July, marking the 33rd consecutive month of growth. The bank attributed the increase to global demand for high-tech products, including those used in AI and cloud computing.
Wholesale trade accounted for the largest share of applications for interest reductions at 23.59%, followed by fabricated metal product manufacturing at 18.46%, machinery and equipment manufacturing at 10.4%, plastics product manufacturing at 6.29%, and basic metal manufacturing at 5.43%.
The bank has also offered discounts of up to 90% on credit investigation and export insurance fees for companies with a track record of exporting to the US or businesses affected by tariffs. As of the end of August, the program had assisted 813 companies through 15,941 fee-reduction cases, generating total savings of NT$146 million while helping businesses manage trade risks and expand into new markets.

Russia has been secretly helping Iran develop supersonic cruise missiles, London-based outlet The Financial Times reported on Wednesday morning, which experts say would likely have been intended for anti-ship and land attacks.
The program, codenamed C430L, began in 2023 and was arranged by Russia's state arms exporter, Rosoboronexport, in coordination with the US-sanctioned NPO Mashinostroyenia, FT reported.
According to FT, Russian arms export officials and senior NPO Mashinostroyenia engineers traveled to Iran repeatedly in 2023.
Among the engineers who conducted these trips were Alexander Dergachev, chief designer for sea-launched missiles and cruise missile complexes; Alexander Chebakov, head of NPO Mashinostroyenia’s design department for air-breathing propulsion units and a specialist in supersonic ramjet propulsion for cruise missiles; and Yuri Prokhorchuk, head of the aerodynamics and ballistics department.
FT also learned that Vladislav Kuzmichev, head of Rosoboronexport’s department of defense technologies and space, accompanied the delegation on its third trip to Iran, and later negotiated the C430L contract with Iran.
By 2025, NPO Mashinostroyenia had received various Iranian technical materials, which Russian engineers analyzed and responded to with various questions.
In correspondence seen by FT from April 2025, Rosoboronexport proposed sending a delegation of Russian specialists to Iran and asked Tehran to answer the engineers' questions before the trip.
“People often think about technology transfers as being solely about sending blueprints, parts, or entire missiles," Fabian Hinz, an Iranian missiles expert and senior analyst with Conflict Armament Research, a UK-based weapons-tracing organization, told FT, "but getting a 60-year-old engineer to fly over and problem-solve, using their experience, is hugely valuable.”
Iranian president thanks Putin for support against United States
On Tuesday, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian thanked Russian President Vladimir Putin for Moscow's position on the war in Iran and resulting sanctions, and said that together, Moscow and Tehran can resist what he called US "unilateralism."
The two leaders spoke on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in the Kyrgyz capital Bishkek.
During the meeting, Putin told Pezeshkian that Moscow stood in solidarity with the Iranian people in the fight for their interests.
Putin also said that Russia and Iran will maintain their economic and trade relationship despite the current military and political environment.
“During this difficult period, we are striving to provide you with the necessary assistance - as we have discussed - and are supplying you with essential goods,” Putin said.
Pezeshkian accuses US of violating international law
Pezeshkian, in turn, said that the US does not have the right to impose sanctions "whenever they please," and accused them of violating international law and committing acts of aggression.
Russia and Iran, he said, would find ways to circumvent the US sanctions.
"Within frameworks like the SCO and other organizations, we can bypass unilateral measures and cooperate on a multilateral basis,” he stated.
Notably, the US sanctions Pezeshkian was referring to, including Washington’s latest measures targeting Iranian financial networks and IRGC-linked assets, are not in themselves prohibited under international law. Economic sanctions also do not constitute an “act of aggression” under the UN definition.

New paved road smooths journey to historic Engüzekkapı Castle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
05:41:19 UTC
14:41:19 KST

The castle is a popular spot for history and nature buffs. (AA Photo)
Perched on the steep cliffs of the eastern province of Erzurum’s Uzundere district, the medieval Engüzekkapı Castle — a popular spot for history and nature buffs — is now far easier to reach following the completion of a 1,200-meter asphalt road.
Located on 150-meter-high rocky cliffs along the Tortum-Uzundere road, the historic castle is believed to date back to the Middle Ages. Used by the Eastern Roman Empire and several Turkish principalities, the fortress features walls about 30 meters high, with the Tortum Stream flowing below.
For years, poor road conditions made the castle difficult to access. A 1,200-meter hot-mix asphalt road was recently built through cooperation between the Erzurum Governor’s Office and the Erzurum Municipality.
As part of the surrounding improvements, an area of about 800 square meters was paved with natural stone and turned into a suitable space for visitors and parking. Guardrails will also be installed at dangerous points along the road following the necessary approvals.
Erzurum Governor Aydın Baruş said the castle was an important tourism asset that had preserved its beauty despite its age.
“Engüzekkapı Castle dates back to the Middle Ages. It was built with roughly hewn stones but has survived to the present day thanks to repairs and still retains its beauty,” Baruş told state-run Anadolu Agency.
He said the castle’s striking location attracts people traveling along the road.
“Those who see this beauty while passing by always want to stop here. Until now, it was not an easily accessible place. Normal vehicles could not reach it because of the poor condition of the road,” Baruş said.
He added that further restoration work would be carried out to make the castle safer and easier to visit.
“About 500 to 600 people visit here every day. The number increases in summer. We hope the number will rise and that everyone will have the chance to see these beauties. It is our duty to make the natural and cultural assets of our province more valuable and accessible,” Baruş 
said.
Ahmet Yer, director of the provincial culture and tourism department, also invited history and nature enthusiasts to visit the castle, describing it as a remarkable monument where history and nature come together.

The show highlights the historical and mythological connections between Troy and Rome. (AA Photo)
A major exhibition exploring the historical and mythological links between Troy and Rome has attracted more than 2 million visitors at Rome’s Colosseum, Culture and Tourism Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy has announced.
“The story of Troy is meeting millions in Rome,” Ersoy said in a social media post, announcing that the exhibition had reached 2,066,178 visitors.
Titled “Troy and Rome: Myths, Legends and Stories of the Ancient Mediterranean,” the exhibition was organized as part of cultural cooperation between Türkiye and Italy. It features 221 artifacts from museums affiliated with Türkiye’s Culture and Tourism Ministry, alongside works from Italian and Vatican museums, bringing the total number of artifacts on display to more than 300.
The exhibition traces a shared historical heritage stretching from the Trojan War and Homer’s “Iliad” to Aeneas’ journey from Troy to Italy and the Anatolian origins attributed to the founders of Rome.
“Our exhibition, which will remain open until Oct. 18, continues to introduce our cultural values to an international audience and strengthen ties between Türkiye and Italy through cultural diplomacy,” Ersoy said.
The exhibition was prepared as part of cultural cooperation projects between Türkiye’s Culture and Tourism Ministry and Italy’s Culture Ministry. It was officially inaugurated by Ersoy and his Italian counterpart at a special ceremony on June 11 and opened to the public on June 12.
Curated by the Archaeological Park of the Colosseum and the General Directorate of Cultural Heritage and Museums, the exhibition explores the Trojan War, the political landscape of Anatolia at the time, myths and stories from Homer’s “Iliad,” Aeneas’ journey to Italy after fleeing Troy to establish a new homeland and the Anatolian roots attributed to Rome’s founders.
The exhibition highlights the historical and mythological connections between Troy and Rome through a range of artifacts and is part of the Culture and Tourism Ministry’s efforts to promote Türkiye’s cultural heritage internationally through temporary exhibitions.
The project also aims to strengthen relations between Türkiye and Italy by using historical and archaeological heritage as a means of dialogue, sustainable development and socioeconomic cooperation.

Eco-project in İzmİr turns mussel waste into marine habitat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
05:40:35 UTC
14:40:35 KST

The project seeks to provide an alternative by recycling mussel shells while bolstering marine life.
Turning tons of organic waste into new underwater homes, the western province of İzmir’s shell-based artificial reef project has recently welcomed its first documented resident: A nesting octopus.
Izmir-based entrepreneur Nermin Sena Özger is transforming discarded mussel shells into artificial reefs, combining her passion for the sea with industrial design to both recycle waste and create new habitats for marine creatures.
Özger, a diving instructor, industrial designer and entrepreneur who grew up surrounded by the sea in Foça, began exploring ways to improve underwater experiences during her master’s studies at İzmir University of Economics, which she completed in 2019.
During her doctoral studies at Yaşar University, completed in 2026, Özger focused on the potential use of discarded mussel shells in artificial reefs as part of her project titled “Towards Symbiocentric Artificial Reef Design: An Application-Based Study Through Bioreef.”
She established a company at Technopark İzmir within İzmir Institute of Technology and developed the project with support from TÜBİTAK’s Individual Young Entrepreneur Program and the United Nations Industrial Development Organization’s Global Cleantech Innovation Programme (GCIP).
Özger began collecting discarded shells from stuffed mussel businesses and processing facilities operated by companies exporting mussels.
In the first stage, she upcycled about 3 tons of mussel shells and produced four artificial reef prototypes. The prototypes were purchased by İZDENİZ, a subsidiary of İzmir Municipality, and placed in Telgraf Bay in the Sığacık neighborhood of Seferihisar.
The reefs are regularly inspected through monitoring dives to assess their contribution to the marine ecosystem.
Özger said she realized while working on artificial reef designs that mussel shells could be transformed into a material capable of withstanding underwater conditions.
More than 40 tons of mussel shells are estimated to be discarded every month in the Aegean region, she said.
“We focused on mussel shells by bringing together the idea of reducing this 40 tons of waste while transforming it into habitats, and potentially turning these habitats into tourism attractions. In other words, we wanted to return to the sea what comes from the local sea,” Özger said.
Artificial reefs are generally made of concrete around the world. Özger said her project seeks to provide an alternative by recycling mussel shells while supporting marine ecosystems.
She said the team had observed that life began forming on the shell-based reefs faster than on conventional concrete reefs.
“Compared with reefs made of cement, which is normally their main competitor, the most striking point about our prototypes is that life begins on them more quickly. In particular, algae and other plant life forms develop faster,” she said.
According to Özger, the growth of algae subsequently attracts other marine species to the reefs.
During a recent monitoring dive, the team made an unexpected discovery: An octopus had settled inside one of the reef structures.
“This was a very encouraging development during our monitoring dive today. For the first time, we saw an octopus inside one of the shelters in our prototypes. This is actually a historic turning point for us.
The octopus had decorated the shelter, and there were clear signs that it had genuinely settled there,” Özger said.
The team has also observed small fish using the reefs as shelter and protection.
“We witnessed Black Sea bream, Gün and Gelin fish using the reefs around them like a shield. We recorded these moments in video and photographs. This is a very joyful and hopeful development for us,” she said.
As part of the TÜBİTAK project, Özger said 35 more reefs would be installed at Telgraf Bay.
The project aims not only to reduce waste but also to turn the area into a new attraction for divers and underwater photographers.

Uludağ to introduce artificial snow as warmer winters threaten ski season
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
05:40:14 UTC
14:40:14 KST

An operator stands beside a snow-making cannon as it produces artificial snow to prepare the Uudağ ski center for the upcoming season.
Türkiye’s Uludağ, one of the country’s best-known winter tourism destinations in the northwest, is preparing to introduce artificial snow as delayed snowfall and increasingly mild winters threaten the length and reliability of the ski season.
According to the Uludağ Area Presidency’s 2026 Institutional Financial Status and Expectations Report, climate change has increasingly delayed natural snowfall in recent years, causing the winter season to open later. The shorter season has in turn led to reservation losses for hotels operating in the resort.
The report says artificial snow production is needed both to extend the winter tourism season and to ensure the continued hosting of national and international sporting events. Artificial snow is required by the International Ski and Snowboard Federation (FIS) for certain competitions, making snowmaking infrastructure increasingly important for Uludağ’s ability to host races. Authorities will conduct calculations on the required capacity and costs before putting an artificial snowmaking system into operation.
The move comes as ski destinations around the world face mounting pressure from climate change, which is altering snowfall patterns and shortening traditional winter seasons. Türkiye is also expected to experience a relatively mild winter, according to climate forecasts, although regional conditions can vary considerably.
The U.K. Met Office has warned that a strengthening El Nino could contribute to exceptionally high global temperatures in 2027, potentially pushing the year above the current global temperature record set in 2024. The World Meteorological Organization has likewise forecast elevated global temperatures and significant changes in precipitation patterns.
Scientists stress, however, that El Nino will not produce identical conditions everywhere. Its regional effects depend on atmospheric circulation, ocean temperatures and other climate patterns. More fundamentally, El Nino is a temporary natural phenomenon superimposed on a much warmer baseline created by human-driven greenhouse gas emissions.

Both producers urged younger generations to engage in farming, describing agriculture as an open-air factory.

Israel’s 15-second drone revolution: eyes in the sky for emergencies and deterrence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
05:39:35 UTC
14:39:35 KST

- i24NEWS
- INNOV'NATION
- Israel’s 15-second drone revolution: eyes in the sky for emergencies and deterrence
Israel’s 15-second drone revolution: eyes in the sky for emergencies and deterrence
What if emergency responders could see an incident from above just seconds after it happened? An Israeli drone initiative is putting that idea into practice
Walk through the Caesarea business zone and you might notice a drone following your every move.
It is part of ROM360, a system designed to give municipalities, security teams and strategic sites their own fleet of autonomous drones — effectively creating an extra set of eyes in the sky.
The technology is being deployed at locations across Israel, including municipalities and strategic sites, with the aim of changing how authorities respond to emergencies.
The 15-second game changer
Ghil Harly, VP of Sales at Cando and the ROM360 initiative, describes the concept as a “15-second game changing revolution.”
If a terrorist attack, earthquake, missile strike or other emergency occurs, the idea is to get a drone into the air almost immediately and transmit a live picture to a command-and-control center and decision-makers on the ground.
Instead of different emergency services operating with fragmented information, police, firefighters and local authorities can see the same live footage and build a shared picture of what is happening.
Operators can control the drone's camera remotely, moving it left and right, zooming in and out, and sending the live feed directly to the people who need it.
The goal is simple: see more, understand faster and respond sooner.
And that speed can be critical when emergency services are dealing with a rapidly developing situation.
Not just for emergencies
But the drones are not only designed to take off when disaster strikes.
They can also conduct routine patrols, using day-and-night vision and specialized sensors to monitor areas for suspicious activity.
That makes the technology a potential deterrent, as well as a response tool.
In Caesarea, for example, following a wave of arson attacks, a reconnaissance drone was used to spot a suspected arsonist attempting to start a fire. The drone tracked the suspect as he fled, while its live location could be shared with police on the ground.
The drones can also communicate with people below. Operators can use speakers to call out suspicious individuals, while lights can be used to signal that they are being watched.
The message is straightforward: if you know you're being watched, you may think twice before acting.
The future is in the sky
For Harly, however, this is just one step toward a much bigger transformation.
He envisions skies filled with fleets of unmanned aircraft, forming an ecosystem that goes far beyond security and surveillance — eventually supporting logistics, deliveries and even air taxis.
For now, ROM360 is focused on putting eyes above the streets and giving authorities a faster, clearer picture when something goes wrong.
But the broader vision is clear: the skies are becoming another layer of infrastructure — and drones could soon be doing far more than simply watching from above.

The increase in capacity is part of the efforts to develop local processing, increase the added-value generated in the country, and strengthen the competitiveness of the cocoa sector.
Cote d'Ivoire processed 650,000 tonnes of cocoa during the 2025-2026 season, representing a processing rate of around 30 percent, Kone said.
Kone also stressed the need to increase investment in research to develop high-yielding seeds, disease- and drought-resistant plants, as well as solutions to promote the mechanization of agricultural operations and improve the phytosanitary protection of cocoa plantations.
The push to expand processing comes as cocoa farmers face a sharp drop in farmgate prices.
Cote d'Ivoire has maintained the minimum guaranteed farmgate price of cocoa at 1,200 CFA francs (about 2.13 U.S. dollars) per kilogram for the 2026-2027 season, announced Ivorian Agriculture Minister Bruno Nabagne Kone at the event.
The price is down from 2,800 CFA francs (about 4.95 dollars) per kilogram for the 2025-2026 season, a decline attributed to a sharp drop in international cocoa prices.
The Ivorian government has reorganized the cocoa marketing calendar in February, which is expected to facilitate the resumption of bean purchases by multinational companies and local exporters and improve the marketing conditions for cocoa production.
Cote d'Ivoire is the world's leading cocoa producer and is among the major cocoa bean processing countries.
The country has for several years sought to increase the share of its cocoa production processed locally, notably through the establishment of new industrial processing plants. ■

11 EU states push to curb foreign policy vetoes

14:32:09 KST

Eleven European Union countries have called for limits on national vetoes in foreign policy, urging EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas to explore greater use of qualified-majority voting.
The letter was signed by Austria, Belgium, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Romania, Spain and Sweden.
The countries said they remained committed to seeking consensus wherever possible but argued that unanimity should not prevent the bloc from acting.
“We must also ensure that this culture of consensus fosters common action rather than preventing it — otherwise we will have legitimacy but no strength,” the letter said.
The signatories argued that the EU needed to be able to mobilize its political, economic and diplomatic weight quickly and effectively in a more unstable international environment.
They proposed making greater use of “constructive abstention,” avoiding links between foreign policy decisions and unrelated disputes, and examining existing treaty provisions that allow a shift from unanimity to qualified-majority voting in selected cases.
EU foreign and security policy decisions generally require the support of all 27 member states, allowing a single government to block joint action.
The debate intensified during Viktor Orbán’s final years as Hungarian prime minister, when Budapest repeatedly delayed or blocked EU foreign policy decisions.
Orbán’s 16-year rule ended after his election defeat in April.
Any change is unlikely in the short term.
Article 31 of the EU treaty allows the European Council to extend qualified-majority voting to additional foreign policy matters, but activating that provision would itself require unanimous approval.
Decisions with military or defense implications are excluded.

"If You Build Ugly Social Housing, You Will Create Social Problems": An Interview with the OBEL Award 2026 Recipients
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
05:30:00 UTC
14:30:00 KST

On 1 September 2026, the Balearic Social Housing Model was announced as the recipient of the 2026 OBEL Award. The focus of this award's cycle was "Systems' Hack," calling on architecture to critically engage with the systems that underpin contemporary society and to examine how these interconnected networks might be reconfigured in response to accelerating global challenges. The Balearic Social Housing Model, created by economist and independent consultant Cris Ballester and architect and civil servant Carles Oliver, is a six-point approach to public housing developed between 2019 and 2023, providing additional value and comfort to traditional affordable housing by bringing procurement, architecture, materials, energy, tenure, public capacity and learning together as responses to current social, environmental and economic challenges. In this interview with ArchDaily, the model's creators discuss its origins, ambitions, and material challenges in making social housing a desirable place to live.
The model grew out of a need to rethink social housing in the Balearic Islands, where publicly built housing had long carried a reputation for poor quality. As technicians tasked with changing that perception, Cris Ballester and Carles Oliver worked alongside IBAVI, the Balearic Housing Institute. The initial goal was to increase the public housing stock by 50%, a target that ultimately grew to more than 70%. Meeting it within a tight three- to three-and-a-half-year timeframe brought its own difficulties, from navigating multiple regulations to weathering the COVID-19 pandemic and rising raw material prices, all while the model itself took shape gradually through the work rather than starting from a finished blueprint. From the outset, the questions driving the project were how to respond quickly to a genuine housing emergency while still understanding what impact that speed would have, and, on the economic side, how much residents would end up paying, and what the real long-term costs would be.
 These buildings eventually create the limits of the public space. So, if you build ugly social housing, in the end, you will create and develop social problems. So, the moment you invest within a budget for social housing, you invest in something that's better for the people who live in it, but also for the whole neighbourhood.
Related Article
Architecture Awards Must Evolve: A Debate on Their Role and Responsibility at the UIA World Congress 2026
The creators describe a commitment that runs across the entire life of each building, from initial concept through to delivery and everyday living. It took roughly two-and-a-half to three years before the first keys were handed over and tenants moved in, the point, they say, when the model stopped being simply an idea and became something demonstrably possible. That commitment carries into how the buildings are lived in, with ongoing attention to what they describe as the "life cost" of residing there over time. Replicating the model elsewhere, in their view, depends on two things: courage, since strategies can be copied but outcomes will always differ according to local circumstances, and genuine multidisciplinary collaboration. Architects, economists, and legal teams working in isolation, they argue, simply does not work, the different professions involved need to work together.
Precision is a recurring theme: precision in how budgets are divided between passive and active building strategies, and precision in material choice, since a design must be built around a material's specific properties rather than imposed on it regardless of what that material is. This precision extended to working within EU procurement law, which prevents public tenders from naming specific materials outright. The workaround was to describe the required features and qualities of a material instead of naming it directly, a route made possible by climate change legislation favouring low-carbon and local materials wherever feasible. Applying the model in other places, they suggest, starts with building a clear "map of resources", understanding local stakeholders, regulatory gaps and available materials specific to that place. As they put it, these different dimensions should be taken into account from the very beginning.
 What we found out is that the impact on our territory, or let's say using local materials, can also be territory resilience and can also be competitive, can also make a competitive territory. Because it's local labour force, because it's new jobs, because maybe new industries can come, or industries that were about to disappear could suddenly restart and make money for the same place where we were constructing houses.
Watch the full interview to hear Cris Ballester and Carles Oliver discuss the Balearic Social Housing Model in their own words, and explore ArchDaily's coverage of previous OBEL Award cycles to discover other award-winning, non-traditional architectural initiatives.

A search for one exotic particle uncovered two strange new structures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
05:28:30 UTC
14:28:30 KST

A search for one exotic particle uncovered two strange new structures
- Date:
- September 2, 2026
- Source:
- Thomas Jefferson National Accelerator Facility
- Summary:
- A search for one mysterious particle unexpectedly revealed evidence for two different structures that may belong to the bizarre family of exotic subatomic particles known as XYZ states. The findings could help physicists uncover new ways that quarks and gluons combine to create matter.
- Share:
Physicists have spent decades organizing the growing collection of subatomic particles, yet some discoveries continue to resist easy classification. Researchers at the U.S. Department of Energy's Thomas Jefferson National Accelerator Facility have now identified evidence for two unexpected structures that may help clarify part of this increasingly complicated particle landscape.
The signals could shed light on a puzzling group of objects known as XYZ states. These states do not fit neatly into the conventional picture of particles built from quarks, the fundamental building blocks of matter. For the first time, Jefferson Lab researchers detected two such signals created when a beam of high-energy photons interacted with a proton target.
The findings come from the Gluonic Excitations (GlueX) Collaboration in Experimental Hall D at Jefferson Lab and were recently published in Physical Review Letters. The results could help scientists better understand how one of nature's fundamental forces contributes to the formation of matter.
"We went searching for a confirmed XYZ candidate with a photon beam but instead found two other structures," said Malte Albrecht, a staff scientist at Jefferson Lab. "It's new information."
How the Particle Zoo Took Shape
Beginning in the 1950s, high-energy collision experiments started revealing large numbers of subatomic particles collectively known as hadrons. Hadrons are composite particles containing two or more quarks held together by the strong nuclear force. Familiar examples include protons and neutrons, which each contain three quarks (though they had already been identified decades earlier).
Among the newly discovered hadrons were short-lived particles called mesons. These typically consist of a quark paired with its antimatter counterpart, the antiquark. In 1964, physicists introduced the quark model to organize these bound states. The earliest version contained three quark "flavors": up, down and strange. Up and down quarks, for example, are the ingredients that form protons and neutrons. Up, down and strange are also the three lightest types of quarks.
Particle physics changed dramatically again in 1974 with the discovery of the heavier charm quark. The quark model was eventually expanded to include six flavors. The charm quark discovery helped build the framework that became the Standard Model, the broad theory describing elementary particles and fundamental forces, while also expanding the known spectrum of possible hadronic structures.
As particle accelerators became more powerful and detectors grew increasingly sensitive, researchers gained access to subtler physical processes. After the start of the 21st century, experiments began revealing many hadrons with unusual quantum properties that did not fit comfortably within the original quark model.
The discoveries accumulated so quickly that physicists adopted the general label XYZ states for many of these poorly understood particles.
"We are in a new era here, similar to 70-odd years ago," said Frank Nerling, a Jefferson Lab collaborator from Germany's GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research and Goethe University Frankfurt. "First, a zoo of hadrons was discovered. Now, we're facing a zoo of so-called exotic states."
Searching the Strange Quark Sector
Hadrons containing a charm quark and its antimatter partner, an anti-charm quark, occupy a region of the hadron spectrum with similar masses known as charmonium. In the same way, particles containing strange and anti-strange quarks populate the strangeonium region. Many XYZ states have been detected in these two sectors.
In 2006, researchers working on the BaBar experiment at the DOE's SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory reported a possible strangeonium state with a mass of approximately 2.16 billion electron volts (2.16 GeV). Because it was considered an XYZ candidate, the particle was designated Y(2175). BaBar created Y(2175) by colliding negatively charged electrons (e-) with their positively charged antimatter counterparts, positrons (e+), through a process known as e+e- annihilation.
Y(2175) displayed quantum behavior that may be difficult to explain as a conventional quark-antiquark pair. One possibility is that it represents a hybrid state involving two strange quarks and excited gluons, the particles that carry the strong force. Scientists have also proposed that it could be a four-quark configuration called a tetraquark or a molecule-like combination of other composite particles.
Later electron-positron (e-e+) collider experiments, including the Beijing Spectrometer (BES) in China and Belle in Japan, confirmed the existence of Y(2175). Until now, however, Y(2175) had not been observed through a process other than e-e+ annihilation.
"The challenge is that you have many measurements around the world in very different experiments that have to find consensus about what they are seeing," said Klaus Goetzen, another GSI physicist conducting research at Jefferson Lab. "It's more complicated than it sounds, because there are states that are close by in mass and might or might not be the same thing."
The GlueX Collaboration set out to search for Y(2175) using photoproduction. In this process, a photon beam strikes protons held inside a fixed target. Y(2175) did not appear through this production mechanism. Instead, researchers detected something unexpected at nearby masses.
GlueX Finds an Unexpected Pair
The GlueX Experiment at Jefferson Lab was built specifically to investigate hybrid mesons, exotic particles in which excited gluons may directly contribute to the internal structure. Quantum chromodynamics (QCD), the theory that describes the strong nuclear force, predicts that such states should exist.
"Excited gluonic fields are what could be in these mesons where you have more than just the quark-antiquark pair," said Justin Stevens, a William & Mary physics professor and the spokesperson for GlueX. "That's one of the investigations, to try to understand whether there is a gluonic contribution to the structure we see."
GlueX uses the Continuous Electron Beam Accelerator Facility (CEBAF), a DOE Office of Science user facility that supports research by more than 1,700 physicists around the world. An ultrathin diamond wafer converts CEBAF's electrons into a beam of high-energy photons with parallel spins. Millions of these photons strike protons inside a liquid hydrogen target every second. A large-acceptance spectrometer then records the spray of particles produced in the interactions.
"No other experiment has a facility with a photon beam of this intensity at the energy we have available," Albrecht said. "This truly is a unique setup."
The experiment generates enormous quantities of information, enough to fill the hard drive of an average laptop within minutes. Researchers searched through those data for evidence of Y(2175), which had never previously been confirmed through photoproduction.
Instead, they identified two structures with nearby masses, suggesting that the objects could have similarly unusual origins. One appeared at roughly 2.24 GeV and was designated Y(2240). The second, called X(1830), appeared at approximately 1.82 GeV.
"One of the interesting things about this result is that we didn't observe Y(2175) at the place we were searching," Albrecht said. "We found something new using a completely different physics process, and that's really intriguing. But now that these have been observed, that doesn't mean we're done."
How Strong Are the New Signals?
GlueX detected Y(2240) with a very high level of statistical certainty, corresponding to a confidence level of about 99.9994%. Physicists describe this threshold as five sigma (5σ) significance, meaning the probability that the signal is invalid is less than one in a million.
The signal for X(1830) was weaker but still notable. It reached 3σ significance, corresponding to a confidence level of approximately 99.7%.
With the measurements now established at these levels of significance, theorists can begin developing new predictions about what the structures might represent and what additional experiments could distinguish among the possibilities.
"The next step is to figure out which exotic quark configurations nature might have realized here," Nerling said. "Theorists may come to further conclusions and identify measurements that could help pin down the real nature of these particular states."
A New Phase for Exotic Particle Searches
The study also establishes an upper limit on how likely Y(2175) is to be produced through photoproduction. That constraint can help physicists design and interpret future experiments.
For GlueX, the two unexpected signals may mark the beginning of a much broader exploration of exotic hadrons using high-energy photon beams.
"It really opens the door for a whole new set of hadron spectroscopy measurements we can make with GlueX," Stevens said. "We've got much more data to sort through, so this is just the beginning of the story."

The United States and Iran exchanged their heaviest attacks in weeks on Sept. 1, ending a month-long lull as Washington struck Iranian military sites and Tehran launched missiles and drones toward U.S. facilities across the region.
U.S. Central Command said it had completed a wave of strikes against Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps targets, including air defense sites, radar systems, maritime assets and facilities, mine-laying capabilities and communications sites.
CENTCOM said the operation followed recent attempted attacks by the IRGC against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and U.S. service members.
More than 50,000 American military personnel are operating across the Middle East, it added.
Iranian media reported explosions in Qeshm, Bandar Abbas, Sirik, Chabahar and Konarak, while state television said Jiroft airport in Kerman province had been targeted.
U.S. President Donald Trump described the attacks as “large and powerful,” saying they were launched in response to Iranian efforts to lay mines in the strait and missiles fired toward a U.S. base in Jordan.
“If they do respond, they’ll be hit much harder,” Trump told Fox News, warning of a larger attack if Tehran continued its retaliation.
He also dismissed the prospect of a new agreement with Iran.
Iran’s military said it targeted radar facilities and concentrations of U.S. troops at Bahrain’s Sheikh Isa Air Base with drones.
Bahrain said its defenses intercepted and destroyed Iranian drones.
Jordan’s armed forces said 13 ballistic missiles entered the country’s airspace, of which 10 were intercepted and three fell in remote areas.
Two U.S. officials told Reuters that initial assessments showed no American casualties in Jordan.
Kuwait’s military said its air defenses were activated against incoming missiles and drones and urged residents to follow official safety instructions.
Iran also claimed missile and drone attacks on U.S. bases near Erbil in northern Iraq.
Neither Iraq nor the United States immediately confirmed those claims.
Iran’s Red Crescent said five people were killed and at least 50 wounded when a U.S. strike hit a house hosting a wedding near Sirik.
U.S. officials had not commented on the incident.
Iran’s joint military command warned that further U.S. attacks would draw broader and more severe retaliation.
Separately, Peru announced that it was severing diplomatic, but not consular, relations with Iran. Lima cited Tehran’s obstruction of international nuclear inspections, restrictions on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and its role in the regional escalation.
