Stanford's AI Index lead says AI is outpacing the world's ability to measure it at Taipei forum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
02:28:09 UTC
11:28:09 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Artificial intelligence is advancing faster than the institutions responsible for measuring, regulating, and preparing society for it, according to Sha Sajadieh, AI Index lead at Stanford University.
Speaking at the WITSA Global AI Summit in Taipei on Tuesday, Sajadieh said the central message of Stanford’s latest AI report is no longer that AI systems are becoming increasingly capable. The more urgent question, she said, is whether governments, businesses, schools, and other institutions can keep pace with the rapid development.
“What is not catching up is our readiness,” she said, pointing to institutions, evaluation methods, and governance frameworks that are failing to keep pace with the scaling of AI.
Sajadieh leads the Stanford AI Index, an initiative that tracks the development of artificial intelligence across technical, economic, and social dimensions. She described the index as an effort designed to measure AI’s global trajectory rather than simply capture a snapshot of the technology at a particular moment.
The 2026 report, Stanford’s ninth annual edition, has expanded to 500 pages and goes well beyond the technical performance of AI models to examine the technology’s impact on science, medicine, education, the economy, public opinion, and government policy.
Sajadieh said that expansion reflects how quickly AI has moved into high-stakes areas of society.
AI adoption is accelerating
Three figures illustrate the speed of change, Sajadieh said. First, 88% of organizations surveyed globally said they use AI in at least one business function. Second, global corporate investment in AI more than doubled in 2025, with private investment increasing particularly rapidly. Third, generative AI has spread faster than previous major computing technologies, including personal computers, laptops, and mobile phones.
However, the rapid adoption of AI masks an important problem, as the resources required to develop and understand the technology are highly concentrated among a relatively small number of countries and companies. “The levers to building this technology, developing it, and understanding it are very uneven,” she said.
The US remains dominant in several of the most important areas. US private AI investment reached US$285.9 billion (NT$9 trillion) in 2025, more than 23 times the amount invested privately in China, according to the 2026 AI Index. The US also had 1,953 newly funded AI companies in 2025, more than 10 times the number in the next-ranked country.
The US also has a major infrastructure advantage. The country hosts 5,427 data centers, more than 10 times the number in any other country, according to Stanford. “So far, the US leads,” Sajadieh said, citing investment, entrepreneurial activity, and infrastructure.
But that lead becomes less secure when looking beyond capital and computing infrastructure.
US-China AI gap narrowing
Sajadieh said the US continues to produce more notable AI models, but its lead in model performance is rapidly disappearing. “When we look at notable models that are widely used, highly cited … the US releases more notable models than other countries,” she said.
“However, this is where the picture starts to get a little bit more nuanced. That lead is starting to diminish.” The Stanford AI Index says the US-China performance gap has effectively closed, with Chinese and US models repeatedly trading places at the top of performance rankings since early 2025.
As of March 2026, the leading US model held only a 2.7% advantage over the leading Chinese model. Stanford said the gap has remained in the single digits and has fluctuated as new models have been released. Sajadieh pointed to the rapid development of Chinese models as evidence of the changing competitive landscape.
She specifically highlighted Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3, which Stanford researchers have described as one of the most capable open-weight models yet released. Sajadieh said in August that Kimi K3 and Alibaba’s Qwen3.8-Max had narrowed the gap with leading American models even further.
The shift is particularly significant because the US advantage was much larger only a few years ago. “China has been able to close that gap very effectively, very quickly,” Sajadieh said.
Stanford’s data shows that China has also built major advantages in areas such as AI publications, citations, and patent output, while the US retains an advantage in producing notable frontier models and higher-impact patents. South Korea is also emerging as a significant player, with Stanford identifying it as the global leader in AI patents per capita.
Taiwan occupies a critical position
For Taiwan, one of Sajadieh’s most important observations concerned the hardware underpinning the global AI ecosystem. “I don’t have to tell you all this in this room, that you’re all very aware that the supply chain rests on a single point, TSMC here in Taiwan,” she said.
The concentration of AI infrastructure extends beyond software and models, she argued. It also exists in the physical systems needed to run increasingly powerful AI applications.
Stanford’s 2026 AI Index says TSMC fabricates almost every leading AI chip, making the global AI hardware supply chain dependent on a single Taiwanese foundry, although TSMC’s US expansion began operating in 2025. That concentration makes questions about AI measurement and governance more urgent, Sajadieh said.
“If you have that level of concentration showing up in all different layers of the AI ecosystem, it makes it even more important that we understand what we’re dealing with,” she said. The question is no longer simply which country has the most powerful model.
It is also whether researchers, governments, and companies have reliable ways of determining what those systems can actually do.
Benchmarks are becoming obsolete
Sajadieh argued that traditional AI benchmarks are increasingly failing to distinguish among leading systems. As the major models have improved, their performance on widely used evaluations has converged.
“You cannot tell the leading frontier models apart from one another,” she said, describing the growing similarity among leading systems on conventional benchmarks. “That means that either all the models are doing an amazing job, or the way we’re measuring them has aged out.”
Stanford’s 2026 report reaches a similar conclusion. It says AI capability is increasingly outpacing the benchmarks designed to measure it, with evaluations that were expected to remain difficult for years sometimes becoming saturated within months.
Many models have already surpassed human baselines on a range of standardized tests, Sajadieh said. But that does not necessarily mean the systems have achieved broad human-level intelligence. Instead, the results illustrate the limitations of using individual tests to describe increasingly complex AI systems.
“Benchmarks are saturating,” she said. Tests intended to remain difficult for several years can now be mastered by leading models in less than a year. Stanford also found growing concerns about the reliability and potential gaming of benchmarks, including errors in widely used evaluations.
Sajadieh said researchers therefore need to move beyond asking whether an AI model can pass an examination. A more meaningful question is whether the system performs reliably when deployed in the real world.
“Is it a benchmark? Is it how well it does on the chemistry exam? Or is it how effective it is when it shows up in our hospitals?” she asked.
Transparency is declining
The measurement problem is compounded by a lack of transparency from major AI companies. Sajadieh cited Stanford’s Foundation Model Transparency Index, which measures how much information model developers disclose across multiple dimensions. The index’s average transparency score fell in 2025, she said.
Stanford’s published figures show the average score dropped from 58 in 2024 to 40 in 2025, with major gaps remaining in disclosures concerning training data, computing resources, and post-deployment impacts.
“If we, as outsiders, can’t look inside these models, how can policymakers do it?” Sajadieh asked. “How can our educators or administrators do it?” The lack of transparency becomes increasingly consequential as AI moves from experimental environments into everyday life.
Sajadieh said documented AI incidents are increasing and that these incidents are increasingly occurring in real-world situations rather than controlled research environments. Stanford recorded 362 documented AI incidents in 2025, up from 233 in 2024.
Medicine illustrates the gap between promising AI demonstrations and evidence from real-world deployment, Sajadieh said. AI systems that automatically document clinical conversations, often referred to as ambient AI, have already been deployed by hospitals and have shown benefits in areas such as reducing clinician burnout and improving administrative and billing processes.
But there is much less evidence for using AI as a direct diagnostic tool. “We don’t have enough evidence to tell us if AI can look beyond the administrative support and to diagnostic support,” she said. She also questioned how many existing studies accurately reflect real clinical environments.
Many studies comparing AI with physicians do not use real patient data and instead restrict physicians from accessing other resources they would normally use, she said. “That’s not quite fair,” she said. The distinction is important because medical decisions involve complex information, uncertainty, and consequences that cannot necessarily be captured through a standardized examination.
AI may create a new bottleneck
Sajadieh was more optimistic about AI’s potential in scientific research. She said AI is already producing significant breakthroughs in scientific fields and could dramatically increase researchers’ ability to generate new hypotheses.
But this creates another problem. “AI can be wonderful, but it generates way too many hypotheses to validate,” she said. The bottleneck is experimentation.
Even if AI can rapidly propose possible explanations or discoveries, researchers still have to conduct experiments to determine whether those ideas are correct. “Experimenting, for example, is still expensive,” Sajadieh said.
AI therefore does not eliminate the need for human scientific judgment and verification. Instead, it can shift where the bottleneck occurs.
Education, Sajadieh said, may be the area in which society is least prepared for AI. Stanford estimates that roughly four in five university students now use generative AI, but the number of educational institutions with comprehensive policies governing AI use, helping teachers integrate the technology, and establishing clear guardrails for students is far lower.
“We know that students are using this,” she said. “The number of schools, universities, and academic institutions that have policies regulating AI … not even close to 80%, not even close to 50%.” Sajadieh also warned against treating computer science education as a direct proxy for AI literacy. “AI education and computer science are different,” she said.
As AI becomes a standard part of education and employment, countries will need better ways of measuring whether students are actually prepared to work with the technology.
AI's impact on jobs is becoming visible
The economic impact of AI remains one of the most contentious parts of the debate. Sajadieh said consumers generally report finding value in AI tools, but evidence of broad labor-market transformation remains more complicated.
Companies increasingly say they expect to reduce their workforces because of AI, but aggregate employment data has not yet shown the massive displacement that some predictions have suggested. There are, however, early signs of disruption in specific occupations.
Stanford's 2026 AI Index found that employment among software developers ages 22 to 25 fell nearly 20% from 2024, while employer surveys indicate that one-third of organizations expect workforce reductions over the following year.
Sajadieh said the effects are particularly visible in occupations with high levels of overlap between AI capabilities and the tasks performed by workers. That does not necessarily mean AI will eliminate entire occupations, she emphasized.
Instead, AI exposure means that a significant portion of the tasks or skills associated with a particular job can potentially be performed or assisted by AI. Productivity gains have already been recorded in areas such as customer service and software development. Stanford cites reported productivity improvements of about 14% to 15% in customer support and 26% in software development.
The most vulnerable part of the labor market may therefore be the entry-level pipeline, where workers traditionally develop skills before moving into more senior positions.
Public attitudes reveal a geographic divide
Perhaps one of the most striking differences in Stanford's research concerns how people around the world view AI. Sajadieh said public sentiment in East and Southeast Asia tends to be substantially more optimistic than in Western countries. “In East Asian countries, Southeast Asian countries, it's likely very positive,” she said.
The survey data shows strong optimism in those regions about AI’s effects on jobs and people's lives over the next three to five years. The US and France, by contrast, recorded some of the lowest levels of positive public sentiment across multiple surveys.
The divide also appears when people are asked whether they trust governments to regulate AI effectively.
Sajadieh said East Asian and Southeast Asian countries show relatively higher levels of trust, while trust is particularly low in the United States. Stanford's 2026 AI Index found that only 31% of Americans surveyed said they trusted their government to regulate AI effectively, the lowest level among the countries surveyed.
The difference helps explain why AI can generate very different political and social reactions in different parts of the world. In the United States, Sajadieh described an increasingly polarized debate between people who see AI as a technology capable of transforming society for the better and those who view it as an existential or national security threat.
Yet in many Asian countries, she said, public discussion is more optimistic about the technology's potential benefits.
AI sovereignty raises difficult questions
Governments around the world are responding by developing national AI strategies. Sajadieh said the growth of national AI strategies is encouraging, particularly because countries that previously played little role in AI policymaking are now seeking to establish their own positions.
But a strategy is not the same as implementation. “An AI strategy and an AI framework are quite a ways away from implementation and enforcement,” she said.
One increasingly important concept is AI sovereignty, the ability of a country or region to exercise meaningful control over the technology, infrastructure, data, and capabilities on which its AI ecosystem depends.
But Sajadieh questioned what sovereignty means when so many parts of the AI ecosystem are concentrated in the hands of a small number of companies and countries. “If you think about entrepreneurial activity, investment, hardware infrastructure, where the power control rests in only a few actors’ hands,” she said, the concept becomes much more complicated.
The issue is particularly relevant to Taiwan, which occupies a central position in the global semiconductor supply chain while also facing the geopolitical consequences of that concentration.
Measurement may become the most important AI infrastructure
Sajadieh ultimately returned to the central theme of her presentation: measurement. The world needs better ways to determine whether AI systems are actually improving people's lives, organizations, workplaces, schools, and health care systems, she said.
“Measurement is not something to say, ‘Oh, yeah, we will get to it,’” she said. “It’s the shared infrastructure that the world is going to depend on.” The task cannot be handled by one university or research institute, she said.
Stanford's AI Index itself is designed as a multidisciplinary project, bringing together expertise from academia and industry to track AI's development across multiple dimensions. But Sajadieh argued that the next stage will require a broader international effort. “We all need to come together to understand a better way of measuring AI that goes beyond benchmarks,” she said.
That means developing measurements capable of capturing what AI means for the next generation, how it changes workplaces and organizations, and whether it produces meaningful benefits when deployed in the real world.
For Taiwan, the message is particularly relevant as it sits at one of the most concentrated points in the global AI hardware supply chain, while its universities, semiconductor companies, and technology firms are increasingly integrated into the international AI ecosystem.
The Stanford analysis suggests that simply possessing advanced hardware or attracting investment will not be enough to determine who benefits from the AI revolution. The countries and institutions that succeed may instead be those capable of combining technological capability with talent, public trust, education, governance, and reliable ways of measuring whether AI actually works.
As Sajadieh put it, the question is no longer whether AI is moving quickly; it's whether the rest of society can keep up.

Independent review finds Telstra failed to prioritise systems behind major network outage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
02:25:55 UTC
11:25:55 KST

In brief
- An independent investigation has found Telstra failed to prioritise systems that led to a major outage.
- A separate ACMA investigation, that could result in fines of up to $30 million, is ongoing.
Telstra did not prioritise systems that caused a major nationwide network failure and lacked the technical expertise to properly maintain them, an independent investigation has found.
The results of the review into the telco's 8 July network failure, which left thousands of Australians unable to make calls or access data, were released on Tuesday.
The outage sparked chaos with Triple Zero calls and businesses affected, along with failures across train networks and electronic payment services.
A lack of ownership and oversight of the functions that led to the outage were identified as key contributing factors by Technology Audit Partners in the report.
The outage began at 2.50am, nearly an hour earlier than identified by Telstra at the time.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Following the outage, Telstra confirmed it had conducted welfare checks on those who tried to place more than 600 unsuccessful emergency calls.
The investigation also found a further eight Triple Zero calls did not go through to emergency services during the outage. Welfare checks were conducted in relation to those unsuccessful calls, with no adverse outcomes identified, according to the company.
The outage was triggered by a software update not being done on a GPS card, which resulted in incorrect date information.
It was primarily a result of Telstra not treating network timing as a critical capability, the report found.
On the night of the outage, the two primary engineers involved in the botched upgrade were on mandatory stand-down, the report found.
"The overarching finding is we did not prioritise our timing system inside our networks at the highest level as a critical capability, which is exactly what it should have been," chief executive Vicki Brady told media on Wednesday.
"That is a miss on our side."
Brady said additional resources and expertise had been allocated to the impacted area.
Since the outage, just over 30,000 customers have contacted the telco, which has processed credits of just under $1 million for those customers.
Any customers who felt they were impacted and had not been in contact were encouraged to reach out to the company.
Brady was among 10 senior executives whose bonus was cut as a result of the outage. Her total compensation was $6.8 million, 11 per cent more than the previous year.
"I fully accept the board's decision on that," Brady said.
A separate ongoing Australian Communications and Media Authority investigation into the outage could result in fines of up to $30 million.

Response to Nepal flooding enters new phase: UN humanitarians
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
10:22:32 CST
11:22:32 KST

UNITED NATIONS, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- The response to last week's flash floods in Nepal is entering a new phase, with authorities intensifying relief efforts and recovery operations, said the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) on Tuesday.
As of Tuesday, authorities had recovered 1,003 bodies, while nearly 3,900 people remained unaccounted for, with nearly 12,000 rescued, OCHA said.
For thousands of affected families, the priority is now receiving humanitarian assistance, recovering and identifying the remains of their loved ones, tracing missing relatives and reunifying with separated children, and accessing psychosocial support.
Nearly 3,500 displaced people are living in 27 sites across the districts of Nuwakot and Rasuwa, most of them in schools, disrupting education, said the office.
Humanitarians are also concerned about growing public health risks. Overcrowded shelters, contaminated water and damaged health facilities are putting people, especially women and children, at greater risk of disease in the middle of the monsoon season.
The United Nations and its humanitarian partners continue to support the government-led response. On Monday, staff members from OCHA, the UN Resident Coordinator's Office and the World Food Program (WFP) travelled to the town of Bidur in Nuwakot to meet district authorities and visit displacement sites. Partners are working to establish a coordination hub there so assistance reaches the communities most in need, OCHA said.
The WFP has dispatched nearly 80 metric tons of food. The UN Children's Fund is procuring 10,000 cartons of therapeutic food. Eight health teams have reached more than 1,200 people in displacement sites. More than 1,800 people, including hundreds of children, have received psychological first aid, and a 24-hour mental health helpline is up and running. The World Health Organization is supporting disease surveillance efforts in the two hardest-hit districts, it said.
The Nepalese government and UN Resident Coordinator Lila Pieters Yahia have agreed to launch a four-month humanitarian flash appeal on Friday. The appeal will support the government-led response and focus on mobilizing resources to save lives, deliver urgent humanitarian assistance and address the most critical needs of communities affected by the floods, said the office. ■

====================================================================================================

China Focus: Indian expats carve out life journeys in China's economic hub
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
10:22:01 CST
11:22:01 KST

Indian entrepreneurs Mona Bapna (L) and Rajni Aggarwal communicate at Benaras, an Indian restaurant they launched, in Binjiang District of Hangzhou, east China's Zhejiang Province, Aug. 24, 2026. (Xinhua/Zheng Keyi)
HANGZHOU, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- From startup struggles to cross-cultural community building, Indian entrepreneur Tanmay Gokani and his compatriots have carved out a unique life path for themselves in east China's economic powerhouse Zhejiang Province.
A WHOLESALE MARKET TRANSFORMED BY AI
Coming to China in 2002, Gokani worked at a Hong Kong firm's Shenzhen office before shifting his focus to Zhejiang's Yiwu, a county-level city and a basic wholesale center for hardware, toys and daily goods with limited urban facilities. "It was even hard to find bread back then," he said.
To fund his startup venture between 2009 and 2011, Gokani scouted markets for suppliers by day and taught English after work. "I would spend about two hours every night teaching, just to cover the costs of getting my business off the ground," he recalled.
He registered his consumer goods trading company in 2009, relying entirely on offline inquiries and manual price and quality comparisons.
Fellow Indian trade manager Udit Madhwani arrived in Yiwu in 2012 under the same primitive business conditions. Without digital tools, he navigated the sprawling market by consulting local vendors to verify every unfamiliar product.
The transformation since then has been remarkable. "Yiwu is like a child growing bigger and more handsome every year," said Madhwani, whose company mainly does business with South American countries, including Guatemala, Paraguay, Argentina, Brazil and Peru.
Now home to the world's largest small-commodity wholesale market, Yiwu hosts over 38,000 permanent foreign merchants and more than 10,000 foreign-funded enterprises. It has over 1.26 million business entities and supports employment for more than 32 million people.
A key symbol of China's reform and opening-up, it has upgraded from a low-cost bulk trading hub into a digital marketplace where technology, branding and data match industrial scale in importance.
"Many foreign clients who have never been to China are shocked by product quality and design capabilities here," Madhwani noted. "The goods offer great value, and the market has moved from having few local brands to having numerous ones."
Gokani stressed China's ultra-efficient supply chain, further empowered by AI, as its core advantage. He offered a striking example of an Indian client who confirmed a glass bowl order on a Saturday, with complete samples and quotation sheets ready the following Monday, and full shipments delivered by the month's end.
Now, Gokani's firm ships 100 to 200 forty-foot containers yearly across thousands of products, with 90 percent of exports going to India, mostly ornaments and daily-use goods such as stationery, toys, hardware and other product categories, and the rest to the United States and Africa.
"Yiwu's respect for difference and embrace of diversity have created a space where people of varied backgrounds can meet, do business, and gradually understand one another," said Jiang Jiajiang, director of the Institute of Public Policy at the Zhejiang Academy of Social Sciences.
PITAS, TABLA, HOLI AND DIWALI SHARED WITH CHINESE
For Indian entrepreneurs Mona Bapna and Rajni Aggarwal, life in Hangzhou, Zhejiang's capital city over 100 km from Yiwu, extends far beyond business. The pair moved there in 2004 and launched their Indian restaurant Pita's & Tika's in 2016.
Bapna came to Hangzhou with her husband and children as a stay-at-home mother, while textile engineer Aggarwal relocated with her family to run textile-related ventures. Strangers before arriving in China, the two built a close friendship and business partnership, brought together by fate in a foreign land.
Language barriers were their biggest early challenge. "When we came, we couldn't communicate well and couldn't read Chinese. All documents were in Chinese," Bapna recalled. With support from the Zhejiang International Investment Service Center, they overcame regulatory hurdles to launch their catering business.
Now with three branches in Hangzhou and Shanghai, the duo opened the upmarket Indian fine-dining restaurant Benaras in late 2025. For them, the eateries are cultural bridges between two ancient civilizations. "We opened the restaurant because we want to share Indian culture with China," Bapna said.
Over two decades, they have witnessed a striking shift in local attitudes toward foreign food. "Ten years ago, people didn't know much about Indian food. Now Chinese people are better educated, better traveled, and more open to trying new things," Bapna added.
Their venues regularly host cultural events celebrating India's Holi and Diwali festivals. During recent cultural nights, Chinese guests played Indian musical instruments and a young Shanghai performer played the tabla.
"Music is more than rhythm and melody. It's a way to connect cultures, share tradition and celebrate the spirit of India together," Aggarwal said. The pair also embrace Chinese traditions, hosting special celebrations for Chinese Valentine's Day to honor local culture.
MUTUAL GIVING AND COMMUNITY INTEGRATION
The Indian community in Zhejiang has deeply integrated into society, which they often call their "adopted hometown."
Bapna participates in a local women's organization and once spoke at Asian Games community events, while Aggarwal joins her son's school bilingual book club for cross-cultural exchanges. The two also launch regular charity drives to fund migrant children's education and medical insurance. "We believe we have a good life, so we should give back to society," Bapna said.
Gokani assists foreign residents' integration by facilitating international students' enrollment and joining multicultural festival activities, such as traditional sticky rice food zongzi-making for China's Dragon Boat Festival. Madhwani joined a local community volunteer team along with expatriates from more than 10 countries, including India, Pakistan and Nepal.
An Indian restaurant owner once delivered food to thank Madhwani, while a foreign resident's passport issue, which had puzzled him for days, was resolved in two hours with Madhwani's assistance.
For new Indian entrepreneurs, Bapna offered her advice: "Be patient. China is a country of opportunities. If you come with an open mind, you will find that this country is very easy to do business or live in." ■

Dropbox user accounts breached by hackers who accessed data
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
02:21:00 UTC
11:21:00 KST

Dropbox user accounts breached by hackers who accessed data
- Hackers breached about 5,000 Dropbox accounts in August, accessing files on less than a third of them, leading to notifications to affected users and regulators.
- The breach exploited a Lenovo ID issue, allowing hackers to register IDs with users' emails and access Dropbox accounts without multi-factor authentication.
- Dropbox and Lenovo have addressed the problem, with ongoing investigations; Dropbox expects no material business impact from the incident.
AI generated
SAN FRANCISCO – Hackers broke into thousands of Dropbox accounts in August, viewing and downloading material users kept on the cloud storage platform, according to a company statement and records seen by Bloomberg News.
About 5,000 Dropbox accounts were compromised by the hackers, who accessed files on less than a third of them, spokesperson Tim Rathschmidt said in an e-mail.
When Dropbox learnt of the issue, it moved to secure the accounts, he said, adding that the company has since notified regulators and affected users.
Shares of Dropbox fell as much as 6.6 per cent in post-market trading on Sept 1.
Some Dropbox users received an e-mail from the company on Aug 31 saying there was unauthorised access to their accounts between Aug 4 and Aug 21, according to notification e-mails seen by Bloomberg.
The company told some users their files were viewed and downloaded during that time, while others were told there was no evidence of this, the e-mails show.
The compromised accounts were not protected by multi-factor authentication, Rathschmidt said.
The hackers accessed the accounts by using a Lenovo ID, a user name and password that allows users to access products and services made by Lenovo Group, according to the e-mails.
Dropbox users can access their accounts using verified Lenovo IDs, according to one of the e-mails.
Because of an “issue” with Lenovo’s e-mail verification process, the hackers were able to register Lenovo IDs using the emails of Dropbox users, even if they had not set up such an account, the notification e-mails say.
The hackers then used the Lenovo IDs’ to access the accounts.
Lenovo said in an e-mailed statement that it recently became aware of a “legacy integration” between Lenovo ID and Dropbox that “could be used to improperly authenticate certain Dropbox accounts”.
The companies worked together to “mitigate the risk”. Lenovo’s customers were not affected, and an investigation is ongoing, according to the statement.
Dropbox does not expect the breaches to have a material impact on its business, Rathschmidt said. BLOOMBERG

Top US lawmaker Mike Johnson says lying is part of some Iranians’ religion

Top US lawmaker Mike Johnson says lying is part of some Iranians’ religion
The Republican House speaker defends the US-Israel war on Iran and praises Trump’s ‘steady hands at the wheel’.
Mike Johnson, the speaker of the United States House of Representatives, has suggested that lying is part of Iranians’ religion as he defended President Donald Trump’s decision to launch a war on Iran.
Speaking to reporters on Tuesday, Johnson was asked about the increasingly unpopular policies under the Republican president, including his decision to join Israel in launching a war against Iran in February.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Qatar says efforts under way to end Iran-US war and reopen Strait of Hormuz
- list 2 of 3Iran claims attacks on Bahrain, Jordan, Iraq after US strikes kill 11
- list 3 of 3Israel’s multiple wars see finance, defence ministries clash over spending
The House speaker responded by praising Trump, saying the US president has “steady hands at the wheel”. After addressing the US trade war with Canada, he turned his attention to the Iran war.
“The problem has been – and the reason we’ve been frustrated – is that the Iranians simply cannot be trusted. They’ll sit at a negotiation table and say something. They’ll walk away and do the opposite,” Johnson said.
“For some of them, it’s, you know, apparently part of their religion that they can just lie to someone they disagree with, so that’s been a difficult thing.”
Lying is strictly forbidden in Islam. Johnson’s office did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment by time of publication.
The war in Iran has been unpopular with the US public. On Monday, a nationwide University of Massachusetts poll suggested that 54 percent of Americans disapprove of US military actions against Iran.
The conflict is expected to hurt Republicans’ chances of retaining control of the House and the Senate in November’s midterm elections.
The conflict saw Iran shut the Strait of Hormuz, sending oil and gas prices soaring both in the US and around the globe.
But the Trump administration and its allies have repeatedly argued that the war was necessary to address an “imminent” nuclear threat from Tehran.
In Tuesday’s news conference, Johnson returned to that argument, saying that the war was “necessitated” because Iran was close to obtaining a nuclear weapon.
That argument, however, has been undermined by statements from within the US government.
In June last year, for instance, Trump’s then-intelligence chief, Tulsi Gabbard, told lawmakers that Iran was not weaponising its nuclear programme.
“The IC [intelligence community] continues to assess that Iran is not building a nuclear weapon, and Supreme Leader Khamenei has not authorised the nuclear weapons programme that he suspended in 2023,” Gabbard said at the time.
Within days of her remarks, on June 22, 2025, the US military bombed Iran’s three main enrichment facilities, an attack Trump repeatedly said had “obliterated” Iran’s nuclear programme.
The US and Israel attacked Iran again late in February, sparking an all-out regional war that Trump had promised would last six weeks at most.
But the conflict entered its seventh month last week with no end in sight.
Although US officials have said that Washington has loosened Tehran’s grip on the Strait of Hormuz and succeeded in getting millions of barrels of oil through the waterway daily, American consumers are still paying high prices for petrol.
The increased energy costs have also fuelled overall inflation in the US economy.
But Johnson argued that Washington’s allies will get involved in the conflict to help reopen the strait, something they have refused to do so far.
“Right now, the Strait of Hormuz – we have to have stability there for commerce, and in the Red Sea and in the region,” he said.
“Other countries around the world, our NATO allies, the Arab states in the region – they have a bigger stake in that than Americans do. And I think they’re willing to assist in that regard to make sure that commerce stays open, so we have stability in the markets.”

====================================================================================================

Prakrit has already lost her father. As Nepal’s morgues fill, she hopes her DNA can be used to find her mother
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
02:16:31 UTC
11:16:31 KST

An army official calls out a name. A young woman stands, two pieces of identification in her hands. She fills out a form, takes another and moves to the back of the hospital to give a vial of blood.
With so many people killed by Nepal’s floods, and hundreds of bodies being buried because the morgues are full, there is now a push to identify victims through DNA. The woman, Prakrit Gurung, 19, is hoping her DNA will be linked to her mother’s body. Her father’s has been found – her brother recognised his picture on a wall outside the hospital.
At the government’s request, Gurung is one of dozens lining up on Tuesday morning. Earlier, an Australian citizen was one of the first 14 people to attend. He had flown over to be with his family – his brother, a Nepali citizen, is missing.
Authorities are asking relatives abroad to have their DNA profiles sent over. Several Australian families have already had samples taken.
“We are collecting the blood samples here, from their siblings, or direct relatives,” says Rameshwor Adhikari from the army. “People are coming from all over the valley to give blood, and from different places all over the country.”
Adhikari adds: “It is a disaster. A natural calamity.”
The first day they set up 37 people came through but numbers are growing – and the army brings out more shade tents for people to sit under.
Adhikari wants as many people as possible to come forward. There are now more than 1,000 people confirmed dead and nearly 4,000 reported missing. As of Wednesday morning, 38 of them are Australians.
In a statement this week, family members of 25 missing Australians called for more government support to “bring our friends and loved ones back home”.
Nepali families from the worst-hit area, the upper Rasuwa district, have been campaigning for their government to do more to get boots and rescue equipment on the ground.
It has been a week since the floods and contact has still not been established in some places along the Chinese border.
Lhakpa Gha’s village, Timure, is one of them. Standing outside a Buddhist monastery on Tuesday afternoon, the 53-year-old says that if she talks, the tears will come.
And as she lists her relatives who were washed away, they do. Her father, brother-in-law, son, daughter-in-law, their four-year-old daughter, her daughter and her sister’s brother. All seven, gone.
Gha and her husband survived because they were in Kathmandu, looking after two of their grandchildren attending school here.
“I lost my whole family,” she says through a translator. “We’ve lost everyone.”
The monastery is housing about 200 people from the upper region who managed to survive – they were higher up on the mountain when the flood hit. Many watched as their loved ones were swept away, their towns flattened.
“The army has not been able to reach the village,” Gha says. “They keep saying our village is high risk but we don’t understand. We are fighting with them. If it’s high risk, you need to act. But they have just said they can’t get in.”
Her son and daughter were doctors in the village – they stayed in Timure so they could keep providing for the family.
“We have nothing,” Gha says. “We depended on my son for money.”
On Monday a UN report into the conditions in the country’s far north said it could take weeks to reach the upper areas – there are hardly any roads left in, and bridges have been washed away.
If the army cannot get in, nor can the aid groups. Amy Sagitta Lefevre from Save the Children says: “Aid is definitely getting through, but to a point.”
Speaking from the agency’s warehouse in Kathmandu, she says its teams have reached Rusawa by road. Aid they can’t get further is stored at the army barracks.
“The challenging bit for rescue workers is the same challenging bit for aid organisations, because we have the same access issues as they do,” she says.
Save the Children is getting kits up the valley that include makeshift tents, so people have somewhere to shelter. It’s also setting up mobile toilets.
“On the ground we’re giving out non-food items,” Lefevre says, “which are blankets, ropes, tarpaulin sheets – because a lot of people are sleeping exposed to the elements, so just sheets in case they need to be protected from the rain.”
Many of the shelters up the valley are overcrowded, so families are being sent farther afield.
“We’re also giving out things like buckets, just so people can carry things or wash, if need be.
“And then we have what we call dignity kits … they’re aimed at women, but specifically pregnant women – they have an extra sari, some of the mothers need clothes because they’re still wearing the same clothes they were wearing the day of the disaster.”
About 2,600 children are expected to need medical treatment for “severe wasting” and more than 100 may have been separated from their parents.
Lefevre says it’s impossible to put a timeline on anything. But recognising that the full recovery process could take over a year, Save the Children has set up a field office.
Its workers are worried about the spread of disease, water contamination, overcrowded shelters and the potential, in the chaos of the recovery, for children to be trafficked.
“This area of Nepal has historically been a hotbed for child trafficking of girls,” she says. “We’ve heard anecdotally that it may have lessened in recent years, but because of this disaster we are now very concerned about the fact that children or girls … could be trafficked.”

3D printed concrete and cork shape 36 student homes in denmark
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
02:10:52 UTC
11:10:52 KST

Skovsporet shapes 36 3D printed student apartments in Holstebro
Skovsporet, designed by SAGA Space Architects and MS+ Arkitekter, is a 3D printed student housing development in Holstebro, Denmark, comprising 36 ground-level apartments distributed across six low-rise clusters. Located near VIA University College, the project applies 3D printing to residential construction at a larger scale, combining private living spaces with shared outdoor areas, landscaped gardens, walking paths, and bicycle parking.
The development is organised as a small student village, with individual apartments positioned around communal courtyards and gardens. The layout supports independent living while creating shared spaces for everyday interaction. The buildings are integrated into the existing landscape, with the printing beds positioned between the site’s mature trees. This approach allowed 90 percent of the existing trees to be retained.
Each apartment functions as a complete home, incorporating a kitchen, study area, lounge, bathroom, and sleeping area within a compact ground-level layout. Large roof windows introduce daylight into the interiors, while slanted ceilings shape the interior volume. A combination of 3D printed concrete, cork panels, glass, and conventional roof structures establishes the material and architectural character of the apartments.
3D printed concrete and cork form the Apartments’ structure
The structural elements were printed on site using a COBOD BOD3 printer. The concrete incorporates FUTURECEM, a lower-carbon cement developed by Aalborg Portland, as part of the project’s approach to reducing the material impact of construction.
Skovsporet, developed by SAGA Space Architects and MS+ Arkitekter Studio, also introduces 3D printed elements made with MEVOcem, a cement-free material containing 0 percent cement and achieving an 84 percent reduction in CO2 emissions compared with traditional concrete. These elements have been used for the bicycle shed, extending the material research beyond the residential buildings and into the site’s shared infrastructure.
The project places these printing technologies within the practical requirements of residential construction. Skovsporet was delivered under the regulatory and financial framework governing subsidised housing in Denmark. By applying large-scale 3D printing and optimising the construction process, the team completed the development within a tight budget while maintaining its architectural and spatial objectives.
Skovsporet comprises 36 3D-printed student apartments in Holstebro
A low-rise student village integrated into the existing landscape
The arrangement of six buildings creates a sequence of shared courtyards, gardens, paths, and bicycle parking areas between the apartments. This low-rise configuration establishes a residential environment in which private units are connected to communal outdoor spaces.
The preservation of 90 percent of the existing trees forms part of the site’s integration strategy. Positioning the print beds between the trees allowed the construction process to adapt to the existing landscape rather than requiring the site to be cleared for production.
With construction now complete, the 36 apartments will welcome their first students in September. The project also serves as a basis for further research by SAGA Space Architects and 3DCP Group, who are developing and testing new material configurations and manufacturing methods for future 3D printed projects.

Psychedelics may cause slight personality changes, but other factors play a big role
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
02:00:39 UTC
11:00:39 KST

German university students who tried a psychedelic for the first time showed small relative increases in Openness and decreases in Conscientiousness over one year, according to a study published in npj Mental Health Research. The differences became less certain after other factors were considered and were not clearly specific to psychedelic drugs.
Psychedelics such as LSD, psilocybin, and DMT can temporarily alter perception, emotion, and thinking. Clinical trials and observational studies have sometimes linked psychedelic experiences to longer-term personality changes. Yet many studies have involved small clinical or retreat samples, lacked a nonuser comparison group, or measured participants only after use.
Constantin Volkmann of Charité – Universitätsmedizin Berlin led the team in asking whether changes previously reported in controlled settings would also appear among young adults using psychedelics in everyday life for the first time.
The researchers used data from a survey of students at Berlin universities. Participants completed an online questionnaire at the beginning of the study and approximately one year later. Of 9,351 initial respondents, 1,443 completed the follow-up and were eligible for analysis: 102 first-time psychedelic users (average age 23.52; 59.8% male, approximately 61 participants) and 1,066 never-users (average age 23.35; 43.9% male, approximately 468 participants).
Participants completed a 15-item Big Five personality questionnaire (assessing Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Neuroticism) and reported substance use, age, sex, income, and psychiatric diagnoses.
At first, students who used a psychedelic for the first time appeared to become slightly more open to new experiences (higher Openness) and slightly less organized or self-disciplined (lower Conscientiousness), compared to students who had never used one. These differences were small, and there was no clear evidence of changes in sociability, kindness, or emotional instability (Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Neuroticism).
When the researchers also considered factors such as age, sex, income, mental health history, and previous use of other substances, the overall pattern remained. However, the evidence was no longer strong enough to rule out the possibility that the small differences occurred by chance.
The researchers also compared first-time psychedelic users with 24 students who first tried another illicit drug. Differences in Openness and Conscientiousness were substantially weakened, raising the possibility that novelty-seeking, social circumstances, or broader drug experimentation contributed to the main result. In an exploratory analysis, first-time users with a psychiatric diagnosis showed a larger reduction in Neuroticism, while sex did not clearly alter the patterns of change. The psychiatric finding requires replication and is not evidence of a treatment benefit.
As the authors summarized, “Findings suggest small personality changes after first-time psychedelic use, with limited causal interpretability.”
The study had important limitations. Use was self-reported and not randomized, and the study did not record the exact timing, dose, setting, motivation, or subjective intensity of use. A one-year interval also cannot establish whether any changes are long-lasting.
The study, “Personality changes following first-time psychedelic use in college students in Germany,” was authored by Constantin Volkmann, Michael Seitz, Ricarda Evens, Moritz Bruno Petzold, Michael Koslowski, and Felix Betzler.

China approves string of ‘telepathy’ devices amid push to leapfrog Elon Musk
Chinese regulators have approved a group of brain-technology products this year, as local start-ups push to surpass Musk’s Neuralink
China’s health regulators have granted approvals for a string of brain-technology products this year, as domestic start-ups push to transform the treatment of conditions ranging from paraplegia to Alzheimer’s and depression.
The approvals come as Beijing bids to lead the world in brain-computer interfaces – devices that allow patients to control digital devices using thought alone – offering generous policy support to help Chinese firms compete with overseas players such as Elon Musk’s Neuralink.
Among the brain tech products to win Chinese market approval recently is a system developed by a domestic firm named Tiankai Suishi (Tianjin) Intelligent Technology, which helps doctors assess whether a patient’s cognitive functions have been impaired.
The device is a cap studded with electrodes that fits over a patient’s scalp and can be used to read the electrical signals given off by the brain, according to an article posted to the company’s official WeChat feed. It was approved by China’s National Medical Products Administration (NMPA) on August 19, official records show.
Tiankai Suishi also sells BCI devices that aid early diagnosis of cognitive dysfunction linked to conditions such as Alzheimer’s disease and schizophrenia. It is currently seeking regulatory approval for a product to assist with diagnosing depression.
The company, founded in 2023, has registered capital of 10.67 million yuan (US$1.59 million), according to the corporate database Qichacha. It is led by Gu Bin, who completed a doctoral degree at Tianjin University’s medical school, according to Chinese media reports.

Ceuta spirals into chaos as Spain’s Sánchez struggles to regain control
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Ceuta spirals into chaos as Spain’s Sánchez struggles to regain control
Makeshift camps, clashes and growing hostility have become part of daily life in the North African exclave, where thousands of migrants remain a month after the mass crossing.
CEUTA, Spain — Spanish police fired shots into the air Monday morning as they worked to clear several thousand young men from an encampment in a parking lot beside Ceuta’s city hospital.
The chaotic scene, with officers using batons to direct migrants toward the center of the city, was an uncomfortable reminder of the gap between early assurances from Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez and his government that the crisis was largely over — and the reality unfolding in Ceuta’s streets.
At the time, Spanish and EU officials said that nearly all of 72,000 migrants who crossed from Morocco to Ceuta had abandoned the city. But as his police was intervening on Monday morning, Sánchez had to concede in a radio interview that around 5,000 of them remained in the Spanish territory.
Advertisement
That number is disputed by officials like Ceuta Mayor-President Juan Jesús Vivas, who maintains that some 10,000 unauthorized people are still in the city. The CEP police union and Spanish National Police officers who spoke to Axel Springer’s Global Reporters Network agreed with the larger figure.
Among the migrants that remain in the city are some 1,200 unaccompanied minors who are due to be transferred to shelters on the Iberian Peninsula in the coming weeks, Sánchez said Monday.
The prime minister has vowed that his government will resolve the crisis with “dignity” and in accordance with the law. In practice, that means migrants must be allowed to file asylum claims and have their cases considered — a process that could substantially delay any deportations.
The unresolved situation is turning Ceuta into a theater of ongoing violence between locals, Spanish authorities and the remaining migrants.
Several Spanish soldiers were injured after a group of around 40 young migrants pelted them with stones last week. In a separate incident, police arrested three migrants Sunday accused of throwing Molotov cocktails at a platoon patrolling the exclave.
Meanwhile, Spanish police last week intervened to protect migrants after local demonstrators stormed their improvised encampment on Ceuta’s El Trampolín beach and set fire to their belongings.
Advertisement
It’s on El Trampolín that Laarvi and his son Omar, both from Tetouan in Morocco, set up camp. “My son couldn’t find work back home,” Laarvi said. The men said they dream of a better life on the Spanish mainland, and perhaps someday further north in Europe.
But those dreams are unlikely to come to fruition. Sánchez confirmed Monday that those who entered Ceuta for economic reasons would not qualify for asylum and would be subject to deportation.
Escalating violence
The removals cannot come soon enough for locals frustrated with the continued presence of thousands of migrants in the city.
Shelters and tents along Tramoplín beach in Ceuta on Aug. 31, 2026. | Antonio Sempere
“Normally, elderly people spend the summer at the beach, but they can’t do that anymore,” said Jalid Ali Amar, a local resident who owns a restaurant near the encampment on El Trampolín beach.
Ali Amar said the city’s inhabitants had been forced to endure weeks of chaos. He added that he had no respect for the migrants “because they have no respect” for locals, many of whom he said are now too afraid to leave their homes because of the deteriorating security situation.
Sebastián Sützl, a spokesperson for Spain’s CEP police union in Madrid, said crime in the exclave had increased eightfold since July 30, but provided no evidence to substantiate the claim. Spain’s interior ministry declined to confirm or deny a rise in criminality, saying it had yet to receive the latest crime statistics from Ceuta.
Advertisement
During a visit to the exclave last week, however, Attorney General Teresa Peramato confirmed that authorities had detected an increase in criminal assaults and crimes against private property over the past month.
And on Monday, Ceuta’s Public Prosecutor’s Office said it was investigating 22 alleged sexual assaults targeting migrant women and girls, as well as an additional case involving a man belonging to the LGBTQ+ community.
“Many women have been raped,” said Helena Maleno, spokesperson for migrant rights NGO Caminando Fronteras. She added that the true number could be higher than the figure confirmed by Spanish officials, as migrant women may not know how to report sexual assaults or trust authorities enough to do so.
Aid groups are increasingly caught in the middle of the violence.
Nolte Bauer, an activist with Mission Lifeline, a German NGO that works with migrants and internally displaced people, said he had received death threats. He added that unidentified people had attempted to slash the wheels of his truck, from which migrants can charge their phones for free. Protesters have also tried to stop Red Cross vehicles from distributing food to migrants.
“I understand that the current situation is stressful for local residents, and I understand that they are protesting,” Bauer said. “But threatening people with death, hunting people down and setting camps on fire — that crosses a line.”
Advertisement
The activist questioned the lack of solidarity with the migrants. “Europe is over there,” he said. “There is plenty of space.”
Frustration builds
The unresolved crisis is proving to be a major challenge for Sánchez.
A third of the government’s ministers have been summoned to testify in extraordinary parliamentary hearings on the situation in Ceuta, during which lawmakers belonging to political groups that have traditionally supported the prime minister are increasingly expressing their frustration with the situation in the city.
Spanish National Police officers interact with a group of people in Ceuta. | Antonio Sempere
Lawmaker Mikel Legarda, a member of the regionalist Basque Nationalist Party, slammed the government for “negligence” over the factors precipitating the crisis in Ceuta, and its “inaction” in returning the city to normalcy.
“The question is unavoidable: Where is the state?” he asked in parliament.
The Sánchez government on Tuesday unveiled a €309 million stimulus package to reinforce Ceuta’s security infrastructure, reinforce public services, aid local businesses and humanitarian support for migrants.
Advertisement
“The main objective of the decree is to give confidence to both businesses and workers,” said Deputy Prime Minister and Economy Minister Carlos Cuerpo. “We are aware of the urgent need to act to restore the tranquility and confidence that Ceuta’s citizens and businesses need.”
But it remains unclear whether the measures will be enough to heal the lasting rifts the crisis is creating within the exclave.
Ceuta has long prided itself on being a bastion of hospitality and peaceful coexistence between Christians and Muslims on the North African coast, but the migrant influx is testing that identity, with locals like Ali Amar rejecting newcomers he said have “brought chaos” to the city.”
“I am Muslim. I am Spanish. I am a patriot,” he said. “These people have no business being here.”

Rival German lawmakers plot pact to shut out EU far right
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Top lawmakers in the European Parliament want to replace the fragile alliance supporting Ursula von der Leyen with a formal German-style centrist coalition — over fears her group relies too much on the far right to pass legislation.
Niclas Herbst and René Repasi, the respective parliamentary leaders of Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s center-right Christian Democrats and Vice Chancellor Lars Klingbeil’s center-left Social Democrats — the two parties that govern Germany — said they want their pan-European political families to strike a deal to push through policies as a united front rather than bicker over issues they disagree on. In what would be a striking reversal of how their two groups have drifted apart, they want formal governance structures to resolve disputes and take turns promoting their priorities.
“If we don’t have trust, and if we don’t find good solutions, if we do not deliver for the people, the populists and extremists on the left and on the right will decide,” Herbst said, sitting in an armchair next to Repasi, in the center-left lawmaker’s office during a joint interview — itself a stunning case of two rival politicians wanting to put their differences aside to fight what they see as a common enemy. According to a POLITICO poll of polls, the three centrist groups are on course to lose 49 seats at the next election.
Advertisement
The far right’s gains in the 2024 EU election disrupted the longstanding balance between the two political groups that drove lawmaking for decades. The EPP, of which the CDU is a member, has increasingly relied on right-wing majorities due to fraying cooperation with the S&D, to which the German Social Democrats belong. With polls signaling further populist gains across the bloc, Herbst and Repasi warned that unless the center repairs the relationship, more extreme voices will increasingly call the shots in Brussels.
The Herbst-Repasi idea would also help reduce European Commission President von der Leyen’s political stress. Rivalry between the two centrist groups has made Parliament votes on some of her biggest policies increasingly unpredictable ― such as in January when MEPs sent her EU-Mercosur trade deal for judicial review. A coalition agreement would restore stability, giving the Commission and capitals greater confidence in Parliament’s ability to deliver von der Leyen’s program, the MEPs said.
Continued “frustration” and “distrust” stemming from the EPP striking deals with the far-right could eventually drive the two groups completely apart, triggering a “political catastrophe” because the whole Brussels system would be paralyzed, Repasi said.
‘Basis of trust’
With far-right and far-left forces on track to make major gains at the 2029 EU election, Herbst warned that failing to work together would give “even more ammunition to the populists from the left and the right,”allowing them to keep scoring “easy wins” in Parliament.
“If mistrust continues, it will only be amplified by the 2029 elections,” his center-left counterpart added. “The need to talk to each other is going to be even bigger.” He said a potential pact could serve as the “model” for the next legislature.
Since June 2024, the EPP has increasingly joined forces with far-right groups to pass key legislation, including on deportations, cuts to green reporting requirements for businesses, and delays and rollbacks to a deforestation law. The group has also relied on far-right votes to shape the agenda in Parliament’s decision-making bodies.
Advertisement
Borrowing from the German model, the two MEPs said the two main groups should work together more formally and no longer rely on negotiations file-by-file by individual lawmakers.
“If a trade-off is not possible within a file, we need to find a trade-off across files,” Repasi said. Partners need to agree on concessions that are “difficult to digest” for each other. This would create “this joint feeling of mutual trust.”
Compromises on which group gets the leading voice in different areas could be struck across files in advance, giving the two sides an incentive to stick together. The two MEPs also floated the idea of creating a new “governance structure” body to steer coalition disputes and allocate who gets which win, similar to the coalition committee between the CDU and SPD in Berlin.
Ursula von der Leyen delivers a speech during a plenary session at the Strasbourg European Parliament on May 20, 2026. | Sebastien Bozon/AFP via Getty Images
“We need more binding agreements on who will take the lead on which question,” said Herbst, who defended a deal but rejected the term ‘coalition,’ arguing it has different meanings across the EU. “Everybody needs to have some successes.” The EPP is the biggest group and hence needs to get its fair share of “wins,” though, he said.
Will it happen?
Whether Herbst and Repasi’s plan has legs depends on political will across the two groups — and there doesn’t appear to be much.
“This is nothing new,” said a spokesperson for S&D chief Iratxe García. “It was already on the negotiation table in 2024.”
Advertisement
A spokesperson for EPP head Manfred Weber didn’t reply to a request for comment. Herbst said Weber could be open to a broader deal, provided it reflected the rightward shift seen at the 2024 EU election.
After that vote, the two groups, along with liberal Renew, signed a two-page agreement vaguely promising to cooperate. That didn’t prevent the EPP from working with the far-right.
The plan’s key weakness is that lawmakers have fewer incentives to follow the party line than national lawmakers. Unlike in countries, Parliament cannot be dissolved and failure to maintain a majority does not bring down the Commission.
Members of the European parliament take part in an electronical vote. | Jean-Christophe Verhaegen/AFP via Getty Images
That problem was on display when an EPP-S&D deal to cut red tape for businesses collapsed in October when center-left MEPs rebelled against their leadership, prompting the EPP to vote with the far-right.
Involving more MEPs in coalition negotiations would create greater ownership and discipline among lawmakers, Repasi said. In thinly veiled criticism of the groups’ leadership, he argued that the “previous way of how politics was done by two or three people at the very top that decided everything has just come to its limits.”
Forced together
Despite the two groups’ growing mistrust, they will soon have to find common ground on issues such as plans to water down a combustion-engine ban, a package simplifying environmental rules, including the contentious emissions trading system, a revamp of the EU border agency, Frontex, and the EU’s notoriously thorny seven-year budget.
Advertisement
“You might have some success with the far left or the far right on certain issues, but in the bigger picture we have far more in common with liberals and social democrats,” Herbst said.
There’s also the matter of who gets the Parliament presidency. MEPs expect the EPP’s Roberta Metsola to seek a third term as president, but the S&D insist it’s their turn. Failure to find a common candidate would expose the proposed centrist pact’s weakness before it even gets off the ground, Repasi said. Herbst agreed the two groups should agree on a common candidate.
Asked why they were taking the initiative rather than relying on the group leaders, both pointed to Germany’s long tradition of grand coalitions.
“It is good that those who have made positive experiences with this sort of governance try to translate it into the European level … and therefore the impulse is coming from the two German heads of delegations,” Repasi said.
Herbst said he hadn’t directly consulted with Merz about the coalition plan, but that it was important to Berlin to have “good cooperation.” For his part, Klingbeil has been “informed” of the initiative, Repasi said, adding “it is also in the interest of the German government” that things agreed in Berlin are followed through in the EU Parliament.
“Let’s not talk too much about the past or personal relationships but look to the future,” Herbst said.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said on Monday that Israel and Russia spread disinformation about Spain’s migration policy after a rush of migrants arrived in Ceuta, a Spanish exclave in North Africa.
Over 72,000 migrants crossed into Ceuta between July 30 and July 31, with at least 100 people dying in the attempt, according to local authorities. Sánchez, along with Morocco’s Interior Ministry, have blamed the surge on human trafficking networks that exploited misinterpretations of a change in Spain’s border policy.
In Sánchez’s first interview since the border crisis, he also said that Israel and Russia organized internet campaigns to undermine Spain’s government during the chaotic aftermath. Online theories proliferated widely after the Ceuta crossings, including some that said Israel orchestrated the crisis.
“After July 30th and 31st, there was an expansion of these hoaxes and this disinformation by social networks associated with both Russia and Israel, and with an international far-right movement that always uses migration, not only to attack Spain, but also to attack Europe and divide it,” Sánchez said in an interview with the Spanish radio network Cadena SER.
Sánchez said research from the European Union’s European External Action Service showed that Israel and Russia were behind disinformation campaigns, without giving further details on the evidence.
EU spokesperson says Russia tried to 'exploit' Ceuta crisis
An EU spokesperson told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency, “In the case of Ceuta, we saw attempts by Russia to exploit the crisis online. However, we have no conclusive evidence to suggest that the crisis itself was triggered by disinformation from foreign state actors.”
The spokesperson did not specifically address Sánchez’s claim that Israel spread disinformation. They noted that the EEAS shares research with member states “when their interests are affected.”
Sánchez said that it was “evident” that Israel and Russia were motivated by Spain’s political positions “regarding the genocide in Gaza and Putin’s invasion of Ukraine.” He is among Europe’s most vocal critics of Israel’s conduct in Gaza and Iran.

Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov also told the Russian state broadcaster RBC that Russia had no involvement in the migrant crisis or disinformation campaigns.
Spanish-Israeli diplomatic ties, first established in 1986, have deteriorated since the start of the Gaza war in 2023, with Madrid since recognizing Palestine as a state and banning ships carrying arms to Israel from docking in its ports. By 2026, both countries had recalled their ambassadors.

Prior to the new strategy, the US had only prevented Iranian ships from violating the naval blockade.
The tankers were anchored off Iran's coast north of the US naval blockade line, said Axios, when US drones launched missiles and hit their engine rooms.
The White House and US Central Command (CENTCOM) claimed that the wave of strikes launched on Iran were in response to recent Iranian attacks on commercial ships in the strait, as well as American bases in the region. One US official said the strategy was to “mow the lawn” in order to reduce the risk of Iranian attacks on oil tankers and US military assets in the region, said Axios.
Around 100 Iranian targets hit on Tuesday, US official says
Around 100 targets were attacked during Tuesday’s round of strikes, Axios cited US officials as saying.
IRGC air defense sites, radar systems, mine-laying capabilities, communications sites, anti-ship cruise missile launchers and attack drone launchers were among the targets hit, the officials said.
Iran has, in response, launched attacks on Jordan, Kuwait, Bahrain, and Iraq.
The US embassy in Jerusalem issued a security warning for American citizens in the Middle East due to rising tensions.
Similarly, Bahrain's Interior Ministry issued an alert for "potential threats in the country."
The renewed strikes degraded Tehran’s capabilities in Hormuz and “bought at least a month” of lowered threat levels for commercial tankers, a US official told Axios.

mirrors, ribbed glass, and light boxes open up a narrow amsterdam townhouse

Kubota & Bachmann reforms a 1890 home into a fluid living space
Situated on the ground and first floors of a traditional 1890 Amsterdam townhome, this dual-level apartment features a classic deep, transversal layout with a private inner courtyard. Kubota & Bachmann Architectsreimagined the residence to transform its deep, narrow proportions into a fluid, light-filled living environment.
The primary design challenge was bringing natural light deep into the ground-floor living area to dissolve the traditional ‘tunnel effect’ of Amsterdam townhomes. The interior relies on a clean white palette paired with natural wood flooring, tailored wooden shelving, tactile tilework, and clean-lined kitchen cabinetry. Strategically positioned mirrors reflect the courtyard windows, visually expanding the room’s openings and dissolving the boundaries between interior and exterior.
Mirrors, glass, reflective curtains, and light define the residence
Two oversized light boxes are integrated into the living area, acting as artificial skylights to brighten dark zones and disrupt the linear corridor effect. The upper level houses three bedrooms and a master bathroom. While respecting the original structural layout, the design opens up the circulation areas to maximize spatial continuity.
The structural walls around the mezzanine and technical rooms were opened and replaced with ribbed glass partitions and silver reflective curtains. This strategy by Kubota & Bachmann Architects Studio allows soft, diffused daylight to filter through the spaces while preserving privacy. The bathroom features lightweight partition walls and curved corners clad in Japanese kit-kat mosaic tiles, creating a continuous, tactile surface that seamlessly wraps around the space.
